2026-07-25.intro: Saturday. This week the whole ecosystem tilted toward helping you succeed — billions in hands-on support, a fast-growing market for agent skills, and everyday tools handling the busywork. You're perfectly placed to ride it.

trends.title: The reinforcements are arriving to help you win
trends.body: Microsoft and Amazon are pouring resources into hands-on teams whose whole job is helping companies turn AI tools into real results. Microsoft just committed $2.5 billion and roughly 6,000 specialists to its new Frontier Company for enterprise AI deployment (Microsoft, via TechXplore), with AWS adding a $1 billion program of its own. The signal is clear: these tools shine when someone knows how to point them at the right problems — and that someone is you.

slants.strategy: The vendors are betting billions that value comes from deployment, not just licenses — so the leaders who build internal know-how to apply AI capture the upside first.
slants.operations: Expert deployment teams exist because someone has to connect AI to real workflows; the ops leaders who map those workflows become the indispensable link.
slants.pm: These programs succeed when someone translates messy processes into clear, automatable steps — exactly the coordination work you already do, now worth more.
slants.admin: As companies invest in making AI genuinely useful, the people who know how the daily work really flows become the go-to guides everyone leans on.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and pick one process on your team that people complain is slow or clunky.
Paste this prompt: "Act as a deployment consultant. Here's a slow process my team runs: [describe it]. Map it into clear steps and show me exactly where AI could take over."
Pick the single step the AI flagged as the best candidate and try running it with your tool today.
Paste this follow-up: "Now write me a short, plain-language plan to roll this out to two teammates, including what to measure in the first week."
Share in the group the one process you'd most want a deployment expert to help you automate.

trends.title: A whole new market is opening under your skills
trends.body: Directing AI agents is fast becoming one of the most valuable capabilities in business. Gartner projects that agentic AI could power roughly 30% of enterprise application software revenue by 2035 — more than $450 billion, up from about 2% in 2025 (Gartner). Every dollar of that growth needs people who can design, guide, and trust these agents — a career lane that barely existed a year ago.

slants.strategy: A market growing from 2% to 30% is a rare, visible wave — position your team's skills toward it now and you set the agenda instead of reacting to it.
slants.operations: As agents move into the software you run, the operators who know how to configure and supervise them become the ones the whole organization depends on.
slants.pm: Coordinating people and agents together is emerging as a core project skill; getting fluent now widens the scope of what you can lead.
slants.admin: The rise of agents creates a brand-new role — the person who sets them up and keeps them on track — and it's a natural, high-visibility step up.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and think of one recurring task you'd happily hand to a reliable assistant.
Paste this prompt: "Help me design a simple 'agent brief' for this task: [describe the task]. Include its goal, the exact steps, what data it needs, and when it should ask me before acting."
Review the brief and tighten the 'ask me first' rules until you'd trust it running on its own.
Paste this follow-up: "Now run the task once using this brief with this example: [paste a real example], and show your work at each step."
Share in the group the task you think will be first to run agent-style on your team.

trends.title: Let AI handle the meeting so you can lead it
trends.body: The tools you already open are quietly taking the busywork off your plate. Google says over 110 million people used Meet's 'Take Notes for Me' in the past month — 8.5 times more than a year ago (Google Workspace), and it now captures summaries and action items even for in-person meetings or calls on Zoom and Teams. That frees you to actually engage in the room while the recap writes itself.

slants.strategy: When note-taking is automatic, your meeting time converts fully into thinking and decision time — the highest-leverage use of a leader's attention.
slants.operations: Automatic summaries and action items mean nothing slips between meetings, so the handoffs you own run cleaner with less chasing.
slants.pm: Let the AI capture decisions and owners while you steer the conversation, and you can run more meetings without dropping a single follow-up.
slants.admin: With recaps handled automatically, you shift from scribe to orchestrator — the person who turns every meeting into clear, tracked next steps.

steps: Before your next meeting, turn on your company-approved AI note-taker, or open your AI tool ready to paste notes afterward.
Paste this prompt: "Turn these raw meeting notes into a clean summary with decisions, action items, and owners: [paste your notes]."
Send the summary to attendees within an hour and watch how much faster follow-ups happen.
Paste this follow-up: "Draft short, friendly reminder messages for each owner about their action item, due this week."
Share in the group how much meeting time you reclaimed by letting AI handle the recap.

homework.title: Plan a stress-free weekend trip
homework.body: This one practices structured output — asking AI to return information in a specific, ready-to-use format instead of a wall of text. When you tell it exactly how you want the answer organized, you get something you can act on right away.
homework.prompt: Act as a practical travel planner. Build me a weekend itinerary as a simple table with columns for Day, Time, Activity, and Estimated Cost. Keep it relaxed with room to breathe between activities. Here are the details: [paste your destination, dates, and budget here].

2026-07-24.intro: Friday. This week's throughline: the agents are here, they're trustworthy, and they're opening a brand-new seat at the table for people who know how to steer them. You're early — and that's the advantage.

trends.title: Now you can trust an agent with the real work
trends.body: OpenAI just unveiled Presence, a platform for building AI agents that stay inside the guardrails, policies, and escalation rules your team defines. On OpenAI's own support line, Presence already resolves roughly 75% of inbound customer issues without a human stepping in (OpenAI, via Techgenyz) — proof that a well-scoped agent can carry the routine load while people handle the moments that need a human touch.

slants.strategy: Governed agents mean you can finally point automation at customer-facing work with confidence — the leaders who define the guardrails first set the pace for everyone else.
slants.operations: Hand the repeatable, policy-bound tasks to a governed agent and keep your attention on the exceptions, where your experience does the most good.
slants.pm: An agent that escalates cleanly lets you route more work through one predictable system, so you can oversee more without chasing every step.
slants.admin: When a trusted agent handles routine requests, you become the person who designs and supervises it — a visibly higher-value role.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and pick one routine, rule-based request you handle often — a status update, a standard reply, a simple intake.
Paste this prompt: "Act as my process designer. Here's a routine request I handle: [describe it]. Draft a clear step-by-step policy for handling it, including exactly when a human should take over."
Review the draft policy and adjust the escalation point to match your real judgment.
Paste this follow-up: "Now use that policy to handle this specific example end to end: [paste a real example], and flag anything that falls outside the rules."
Share in the group one routine you could confidently hand to a well-defined agent.

trends.title: The tools you already use now come with agents
trends.body: AI agents aren't a separate app you have to go find anymore — they're being built right into the software you open every day. 80% of enterprise applications shipped or updated in early 2026 now embed at least one AI agent, up from 33% in 2024 (Gartner, via Digital Applied). That means the fastest-growing skill isn't installing new tools; it's spotting the agent already sitting inside the ones you have.

slants.strategy: The advantage now goes to leaders who map where embedded agents add the most value — the capability is already in your stack, waiting to be pointed at the right work.
slants.operations: Agents built into your existing apps mean less switching between tools and smoother handoffs, so the workflows you own get quicker to run.
slants.pm: With agents native to the platforms you already coordinate in, you can automate status-chasing and updates, widening your reach across projects.
slants.admin: Being the person who knows how to use the agent already inside your everyday suite makes you the team's go-to expert.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and list the three apps you spend the most time in each week.
Paste this prompt: "Here are the three apps I use most: [list them]. For each, tell me whether it likely has an AI agent or assistant built in, and one practical task I could hand to it."
Pick the suggestion that would save you the most time and try it in that app today.
Paste this follow-up: "Write me a plain-language, step-by-step guide to set up and use that built-in agent well."
Share in the group which built-in agent surprised you most.

trends.title: Reclaim hours every week for the work that matters
trends.body: The time agents hand back is now showing up clearly in the data. Across roles, professionals using production AI agents are reclaiming roughly 5 to 9 hours per week depending on the job (Digital Applied 2026 productivity data) — from reporting and reconciliation to research and campaign prep. That's close to a full workday freed up for the higher-impact work only you can do.

slants.strategy: Those reclaimed hours are a strategic asset — point them at the initiatives that move the business, not the busywork that used to fill the week.
slants.operations: The tasks agents absorb are usually your most repetitive ones, freeing hours you can reinvest in improving the process itself.
slants.pm: Hours back across the team means you can take on the stretch goals that were out of reach, expanding what your projects deliver.
slants.admin: When agents handle routine coordination, you get hours back for the high-visibility work that gets you noticed.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and pick one weekly routine that eats your time — inbox triage, report formatting, meeting prep.
Paste this prompt: "Here's a routine that takes me too long each week: [describe it]. Design a faster way to do it with your help, and complete the first pass for me now."
Time the AI-assisted version against your usual approach and note the difference.
Paste this follow-up: "Turn this into a repeatable routine I can trigger with one message each week — write the exact prompt I should reuse."
Share in the group how many minutes you saved and what you'll do with the time.

homework.title: Plan a stress-free weekend dinner with friends
homework.body: This practices role prompting plus structured output — you give the AI a persona and tell it exactly how to shape the answer. A clear role plus a required format turns a vague reply into a ready-to-use plan.
homework.prompt:
Try this: "Act as a calm, experienced dinner-party host. Build me a plan for a relaxed dinner for [number] guests, organized into three sections: a shopping list, a prep timeline for the day, and a simple menu. Ask me one clarifying question first if you need to. Here are the details: [paste your guest count, dietary needs, and the vibe you want here]."

Notice how a clear role plus a required format gets you a sharper, more usable answer than a plain request would.

2026-07-21.intro: Tuesday. This week's stories share a bright thread: the most capable AI ever built is landing right in your hands, ready to take on real work — and the people who learn to direct it are pulling ahead.

trends.title: AI agents now do the work — you direct it
trends.body: The two biggest AI labs just landed on the same idea: deliver finished work, not chat. OpenAI's ChatGPT Work and Anthropic's Claude Cowork both arrived this month as agents that complete multi-step business tasks end to end. Gartner projects 40% of enterprise apps will feature task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, up from less than 5% in 2025 (Gartner). The ability to delegate clearly — and check the result — is about to become one of the most valuable skills in the building.

slants.strategy: Delegating to an agent is a real edge: the teams that master hand-off and review will ship in hours what used to take weeks.
slants.operations: Your most repetitive multi-step workflows are exactly what these agents are built for — freeing you for the judgment calls only you can make.
slants.pm: An agent that runs a task end to end lets you take on scope you'd normally need extra hands for. Your influence widens, not your workload.
slants.admin: When you can hand routine coordination to an agent and spot-check it, you become the person who makes the whole office run smoother — and it shows.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and pick one multi-step task you own — booking travel, prepping a recurring report, organizing a shared folder.
Paste this prompt: "I want to hand you this whole task, not just one step: [describe the task]. Ask me any questions you need, then give me a complete plan and the finished first version."
Review what it produced and note where it nailed it and where it needs your judgment.
Paste this follow-up: "Here's what I'd change: [your notes]. Deliver the final version with those fixes applied."
Share in the group one task you'd happily hand to an agent from now on.

trends.title: The most capable AI yet is now everyone's
trends.body: OpenAI made its GPT-5.6 family — Sol, Terra, and Luna — publicly available on July 9, 2026, after an initial preview to only about 20 organizations (CNBC). Sol is billed as OpenAI's best model yet for reasoning, coding, and complex problem-solving. The frontier tools that were locked to a handful of partners a few weeks ago are now yours to use — the playing field just leveled up in your favor.

slants.strategy: When the most powerful models are available to everyone, advantage shifts to whoever applies them best — a race you win on creativity, not budget.
slants.operations: A sharper model means the AI you already use for drafts and analysis just got more reliable. Lean on it for the harder tasks you used to hold back.
slants.pm: Stronger reasoning means you can point AI at messier, higher-stakes planning problems and trust the first pass more — simplifying work you used to untangle by hand.
slants.admin: The gap between 'power user' and everyone else is narrowing. Get familiar with the newest model now and you'll be the go-to person others come to.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and think of a task you assumed was too complex to trust to AI.
Paste this prompt: "I used to think this was too complex for AI: [describe the task]. Walk me through how you'd tackle it step by step, then attempt it."
Read the attempt and judge how close it got compared to your expectations.
Paste this follow-up: "Now push further — what's the most advanced version of this you could produce if I gave you more detail? Ask me for what you need."
Share in the group one task the newest models handle better than you expected.

trends.title: Two-thirds see AI gains — the reinventors win big
trends.body: Deloitte's 2026 State of AI in the Enterprise found that 66% of organizations report productivity gains from AI, while only 34% have actually reimagined how they work around it (Deloitte). That gap is the opportunity: the value isn't going to whoever adopts AI, but to whoever rethinks the work itself. You don't need a bigger budget to join that group — you need a better question about what your team could do differently.

slants.strategy: The advantage sits in the gap between 'using AI' and 'redesigning around it.' Ask what your team would build if AI were assumed, not added on.
slants.operations: Productivity gains are table stakes now. The bigger win is spotting one process you could run completely differently — that's where the outsized value lives.
slants.pm: Instead of bolting AI onto your current plan, sketch what the project would look like if you designed it AI-first. That reframing is where influence compounds.
slants.admin: You're often closest to how the work actually flows, which makes you uniquely placed to spot the process worth reinventing — a high-visibility contribution.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and pick one routine process your team runs the same way every week.
Paste this prompt: "Here's a process my team repeats weekly: [describe it]. Don't just make it faster — redesign it as if AI were part of the team from the start. What would change?"
Read the redesign and mark the one idea that feels genuinely different, not just quicker.
Paste this follow-up: "Take that one idea and turn it into a simple 3-step pilot I could try this month."
Share your pilot idea in the group — reinvention beats optimization.

homework.title: Let AI plan a themed dinner night at home
homework.body: This practices role prompting — giving AI a specific persona to sharpen its output. When you tell it who to be, the answers get more vivid and useful than a generic request. Try it on something fun and low-stakes.
homework.prompt:
Try this: "Act as a seasoned chef planning a themed dinner night for me at home. Ask me about the cuisine I'm curious about, my cooking skill level, and any dietary needs — one question at a time — then design a simple menu with a shopping list and a loose timeline. The theme I'm thinking about is [paste your theme or cuisine here]."

Notice how telling AI who to be — a chef, a coach, a tour guide — sharpens every answer it gives.

2026-07-23.intro: Thursday. The week's throughline: a new wave of AI tools now runs the long, multi-step work for you — freeing you to lead, decide, and take on more than ever.

trends.title: Hand off the busywork to your new AI teammate
trends.body: July brought a fresh class of workplace agents built to run entire multi-step tasks for you. Tools like Claude Cowork and ChatGPT Work can now carry long-running email, calendar, and file jobs from start to finish, and firms deploying them at scale report software work productivity climbing by up to 70% (EY agentic AI rollout). Think of it as gaining a tireless teammate who handles the doing while you set the direction.

slants.strategy: The leaders who win this quarter are the ones who point these agents at real workflows first — early fluency is a compounding advantage over slower-moving competitors.
slants.operations: Offload the repetitive, multi-step chores to an agent and reinvest that time in improving how the whole process runs.
slants.pm: An agent that carries tasks end-to-end means you can shepherd more parallel workstreams without adding hours or headcount.
slants.admin: Delegating long coordination jobs to an AI agent frees you for the high-touch, high-visibility work that showcases your value.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and pick one multi-step task you'd love to hand off — planning an event, prepping a recurring report, organizing a shared folder.
Paste this prompt: "You're my delegated assistant. Here's a multi-step task: [describe it]. Break it into a full plan, then complete step one and show me the result before continuing."
Review that first step and confirm the agent is heading in the right direction.
Paste this follow-up: "Looks good — continue through the remaining steps, and flag anything you need my decision on."
Share in the group one task you fully handed off this week and how it went.

trends.title: Agents are going mainstream — get in early
trends.body: AI agents are moving from experiment to everyday tool across the workplace. Gartner projects that 40% of enterprise applications will have task-specific AI agents built in by the end of 2026, up from under 5% a year ago, one of the fastest technology shifts businesses have ever seen. That means the skills you build now will soon be table stakes — and you're getting a head start.

slants.strategy: As agents get embedded in the tools your team already uses, the advantage goes to leaders who've mapped where they add the most value first.
slants.operations: Agents baked into your existing apps mean less tool-switching and smoother handoffs — the workflows you own get easier to run.
slants.pm: With agents native to more platforms, you can automate status-chasing and coordination, expanding your reach across projects.
slants.admin: As agent features arrive inside your everyday apps, being the person who knows how to use them well makes you the go-to expert on the team.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and list the three apps you use most in a typical week.
Paste this prompt: "Here are the three apps I use most: [list them]. For each, suggest one realistic way an AI agent could take a repetitive task off my plate."
Pick the single suggestion that would save you the most time and try it out.
Paste this follow-up: "Write me a simple step-by-step guide to set up and use that one, in plain language."
Share in the group which app-based agent idea you're most excited to adopt.

trends.title: Powerful AI is now built for every team's budget
trends.body: Access to top-tier AI just got simpler and more predictable. As of July 1, Microsoft made its Copilot-included Microsoft 365 Business Standard and Business Premium plans permanent SKUs (Microsoft), giving small and mid-sized teams steady, budget-friendly access to the same agentic tools big enterprises use. The playing field is leveling — and it's tilting toward teams ready to move.

slants.strategy: Predictable pricing on enterprise-grade AI means you can plan adoption with confidence and commit to it as a long-term capability, not a pilot.
slants.operations: Stable, built-in AI licensing removes the guesswork from rollout, so you can standardize how your team works with it.
slants.pm: With AI access locked in across the team, you can build it into your project workflows knowing everyone has the same tools.
slants.admin: Copilot bundled into your everyday suite means the AI assistant is right where you already work — no new logins, more time saved.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and pick one everyday document or message you create regularly.
Paste this prompt: "Here's something I make often: [describe or paste it]. Create a reusable template I can fill in each time, and explain how to adapt it quickly."
Save that template somewhere you'll actually find it next time.
Paste this follow-up: "Now draft a fresh version from this template using these details: [your specifics]."
Share in the group one template you created that you'll reuse every week.

homework.title: Get a personalized packing list for your next trip
homework.body: This practices role prompting plus structured output — you assign the AI a persona and tell it exactly how to shape the answer. Giving it a clear role and format turns a generic reply into a tailored, ready-to-use list.
homework.prompt:
Try this: "Act as a seasoned travel concierge. Build me a packing checklist for [paste your trip details — destination, dates, activities here], grouped into categories like Clothing, Toiletries, and Documents. Ask me one clarifying question first if you need to."

Notice how giving the AI a role plus a required format gets you a sharper, more usable answer than a plain request would.

2026-07-22.intro: Wednesday. This week keeps circling one uplifting idea: as AI takes on more of the doing, your judgment and direction become the most valuable part — and it's never been more affordable to put to work.

trends.title: As AI does more, your judgment matters more
trends.body: Microsoft's 2026 Work Trend Index landed on a hopeful finding: as agents take on execution, people are gaining more control over decisions, not less. 58% of AI users say they're now producing work they couldn't have a year ago (Microsoft), and most treat AI output as a starting point they shape rather than a final answer. The skill rising fastest in value is your judgment about what good actually looks like.

slants.strategy: The edge is shifting to leaders who set clear intent and standards — when agents handle execution, your direction becomes the differentiator.
slants.operations: Let agents carry the repetitive execution so your attention goes to the calls that need a human eye, the part that makes your work matter most.
slants.pm: As AI runs more of the doing, your role expands into orchestration and judgment — steering more scope without adding hours.
slants.admin: You're increasingly the one directing and quality-checking AI output, which puts your judgment front and center where the whole team can see it.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and pick one task where the final call really depends on your judgment — a tricky email, a sensitive schedule, a first-draft plan.
Paste this prompt: "Give me a complete first version of this: [describe the task]. Then list the 3 judgment calls you think I, as the human, should personally decide."
Look at those three judgment calls and confirm they're exactly where your experience adds the most value.
Paste this follow-up: "Here are my decisions on those calls: [your choices]. Revise the work to reflect my direction."
Share in the group one place where your judgment turned a good AI draft into a great final result.

trends.title: Reclaim most of a workday every single week
trends.body: Fresh workforce data shows just how much time AI is handing back. Knowledge workers using production AI agents recover a median 6.4 hours per week per seat, with senior practitioners saving 10–12 hours (McKinsey Global AI Survey / Slack Workforce Index). That's most of a workday freed up — hours you can redirect to the higher-impact work only you can do.

slants.strategy: Those reclaimed hours are a strategic asset — point them at the initiatives that move the needle rather than the busywork that used to eat the week.
slants.operations: The tasks agents absorb are often your most repetitive ones, freeing hours you can reinvest in improving the process itself.
slants.pm: Hours back across your team means you can take on the stretch goals that were previously out of reach, expanding what your projects deliver.
slants.admin: When AI handles the routine coordination, you get hours back for the high-visibility work that gets you noticed.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and pick one time-consuming routine you do every week — inbox triage, calendar juggling, report formatting.
Paste this prompt: "Here's a routine that eats my time every week: [describe it]. Design a faster way to do it with your help, and handle the first pass for me now."
Time how long the AI-assisted version takes compared to your usual approach.
Paste this follow-up: "Turn this into a repeatable routine I can trigger with one message each week. Write the exact prompt I should reuse."
Share in the group how many minutes you saved — and what you'll do with the time.

trends.title: The best AI just got dramatically cheaper for you
trends.body: The cost of running AI is collapsing in your favor. Inference costs have fallen roughly 95% in two years — from about $30 per million tokens to under $0.50 for equal-quality models (Value Add VC analysis). The powerful tools once reserved for the biggest budgets are now within reach of any team willing to pick them up and use them.

slants.strategy: Falling costs mean AI is no longer a budget question — advantage now goes to whoever applies it most creatively, a race any team can win.
slants.operations: Cheaper AI means you can finally automate the smaller tasks you used to skip, compounding time savings across your whole workflow.
slants.pm: With cost barriers dropping, you can build AI into more of your project without a budget fight — simplifying complexity for less.
slants.admin: Affordable, capable AI lands directly in your hands, so you can take on more and make the value you add visible.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and think of a small task you've skipped automating because it felt not worth the effort.
Paste this prompt: "Here's a small, low-stakes task I usually just power through: [describe it]. Show me the quickest way to hand it to you from now on."
Try the AI-assisted version once and notice how little effort it actually takes.
Paste this follow-up: "Now suggest 3 other small tasks like this one that I could easily start handing to you."
Share in the group one 'too small to bother' task that's now effortless with AI.

homework.title: Plan a weekend project with a step-by-step assistant
homework.body: This practices structured output — asking AI to return its answer in a specific, organized format so it's instantly usable. When you tell it exactly how to shape the response, you get a plan you can act on instead of a wall of text.
homework.prompt:
Try this: "Act as a friendly project planner. Help me plan [paste your weekend project here] by returning a table with three columns: Step, What I Need, and Time Estimate. Ask me any questions you need first, one at a time."

Notice how asking for a specific format — a table, a checklist, a timeline — turns a vague answer into something you can use right away.

2026-06-17.intro: Wednesday: the gap between having AI and winning with AI keeps widening. Three things to think about — and a low-key experiment for tonight.

trends.title: 74% of AI's value goes to 20% of companies
trends.body: PwC's 2026 AI Performance Study surveyed 1,217 senior executives across 25 sectors and found a stark divide: 20% of organizations capture nearly three-quarters of AI's total economic value. The differentiator isn't budget or tooling — it's direction. Leaders aimed AI at growth and new revenue, not headcount cuts, and earned 7.2× the financial gains of their peers.

slants.strategy: If your AI business case leads with cost savings, you're optimizing for the smaller prize. Reframe around revenue.
slants.operations: The ops teams winning aren't automating old tasks faster — they're building workflows that didn't exist before.
slants.pm: When leadership asks for the AI ROI story, push for growth metrics alongside efficiency ones. The data backs you up.
slants.admin: If your org is using AI mostly to cut costs, the gains will plateau. The real value is in what AI lets you do that you couldn't before.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool.
Think of one process your team currently uses AI to speed up — drafting, summarizing, formatting, anything.
Paste this prompt: "We currently use AI to do [task] faster. What's a completely new capability or output AI could enable for this team — something we're not doing at all today?"
Read the suggestions. Pick the one that feels most realistic.
Share your best 'new capability' idea in the group — growth ideas beat efficiency ideas.

trends.title: 60% of executives use AI to decide — 5% manage it well
trends.body: Deloitte's 2026 Global Human Capital Trends survey of 9,000+ leaders across 89 countries found something uncomfortable: 60% of executives now regularly use AI to support decisions, but only 5% say they manage that process well. Only 6% report meaningful progress redesigning work for human-AI collaboration. The tool arrived; the governance didn't.

slants.strategy: Your leadership is almost certainly using AI for decisions already. The question is whether anyone's defined when to trust it and when not to.
slants.operations: If AI is shaping decisions upstream but your processes don't account for that, your inputs changed without your knowledge.
slants.pm: Decision logs just got more important. If AI influenced a go/no-go call, that should be traceable.
slants.admin: When an executive's thinking was shaped by AI, the context you provide — what AI didn't see — becomes more critical, not less.

steps: Think of one decision you or your team made recently where AI played any role — even just generating options or summarizing data.
Write down: what did AI contribute, and what did a human add on top?

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "Here's how we made a recent decision: [describe it briefly, no confidential details]. What's the biggest risk of relying on AI at the step where we used it? What safeguard would you add?"
Decide whether the suggested safeguard is worth adopting.
Share one decision-making safeguard you'd recommend in the group.

trends.title: The proficiency multiplier
trends.body: Gartner's 1Q26 Global Labor Market Survey of 12,004 employees across 40 countries found that AI-proficient workers are 2× as productive, 2.3× more likely to deliver high-quality work, and 3.2× more likely to drive process improvements. But only 17% of employees qualify as "AI Champions" — while 56% remain resisters. The gap isn't access. It's practice.

slants.strategy: Proficiency compounds. A 2× productivity edge today becomes a career-defining gap in two years. Invest the reps now.
slants.operations: The 3.2× process improvement number is the one that matters most for ops. The people fixing workflows are the ones using AI to find what's broken.
slants.pm: If your team has a few AI Champions and mostly resisters, velocity is capped by the resisters. Make proficiency a team goal, not an individual one.
slants.admin: You don't need to be a power user overnight. Moving from 'never' to 'sometimes' is where the biggest quality jump happens.

steps: Honestly assess yourself: are you an AI Champion (use it regularly, feel positive), an occasional user, or a resister?
Pick one task you did today without AI — an email, a summary, a plan.
Redo it with your company-approved AI tool. Time both versions.
Note not just speed but quality: did AI catch something you missed, or did you catch something AI got wrong?
Share your self-assessment and one observation from the comparison in the group.

homework.title: Tonight, let AI help you explain something you already know.
homework.body: The fastest way to build AI confidence: use it on a topic where you're the expert. You'll learn to direct, correct, and refine — with zero stakes. Open any free tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity):
homework.prompt:
"I know a lot about [something personal you're genuinely good at — cooking, a sport, a craft, a subject]. Help me explain it to someone who's brand new. Ask me 3 questions about my audience first, then draft a short explanation I can review and edit."

The ask questions first, then draft pattern works everywhere. Tonight you'll see why editing AI is more useful than writing from scratch.

2026-06-18.intro: Thursday: AI budgets are getting real, and governance gaps are showing up fast. Three things worth your attention — and something low-stakes for tonight.

trends.title: The real AI bottleneck isn't the model — it's the data
trends.body: Gartner surveyed 353 data and AI leaders and found that organizations with successful AI initiatives invest up to 4× more in data quality, governance, and change management than those with poor outcomes. Only 39% of tech leaders are confident their current AI investments will pay off financially. And 60% of AI projects are expected to be abandoned this year — not because the AI failed, but because the data wasn't ready.

slants.strategy: If your AI roadmap doesn't have a data quality line item, it's a wish list. The 4× gap is real.
slants.operations: Before you pilot another AI tool, audit the data feeding it. Clean inputs beat clever models every time.
slants.pm: Add 'data readiness' as a gate in your AI project plan. It's the step most teams skip — and most failures trace back to.
slants.admin: When someone says 'the AI isn't working,' the first question is often about the data, not the tool. You're closer to that data than you think.

steps: Pick one report or dashboard your team relies on for decisions.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste this prompt: "I rely on a [type of report] for [what decisions]. What are the most common data quality problems that would make AI unreliable for this kind of work? Give me a 5-point checklist I can use to audit it."
Run through the checklist against your actual report. Note which items pass and which don't.
Share one data quality gap you discovered in the group — and whether it surprised you.

trends.title: 25% of AI budgets just got pushed to next year
trends.body: Forrester's 2026 technology predictions flagged a hard correction: enterprises will defer 25% of planned AI spend into 2027 as financial rigor catches up to vendor promises. Only 15% of AI decision-makers reported an EBITDA lift in the past 12 months, and fewer than one-third can tie AI's value to their organization's financial growth. The CFO is now the gatekeeper.

slants.strategy: The AI business case just shifted from 'possibility' to 'proof.' If you can show measurable value on a small project, you'll survive the budget cut.
slants.operations: Budget tightening means fewer new tools and more pressure to prove the ones you have. Document your wins now — you'll need them.
slants.pm: Expect AI project portfolios to shrink. The surviving projects will be the ones with clear ROI timelines, not the flashiest demos.
slants.admin: If AI tools at your company feel like they're stalling, it's not just you. Budgets are tightening, and proven use cases get priority.

steps: Think of one AI tool or feature your team currently uses (or has been piloting).
Write down, in one sentence, the specific value it delivers. If you can't, that's the finding.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "Help me write a 3-sentence business case for continuing to use [tool/feature] based on this value: [your sentence]. Make it specific enough for a finance review."
Read the draft. Could it survive a CFO asking 'so what?'
Share your one-sentence value statement in the group — brevity is the test.

trends.title: The binary governance trap is killing AI agents
trends.body: Gartner's May 2026 research warned that 40% of enterprises will demote or decommission autonomous AI agents by 2027 because of governance gaps discovered only after production incidents. The root cause: organizations are treating agent governance as binary — either fully locked down or fully trusted. Over-restricting simple agents slows delivery; under-restricting autonomous ones creates real risk.

slants.strategy: Agent governance is a strategy decision, not an IT checkbox. Define tiers of autonomy before your first production incident does it for you.
slants.operations: The ops team that builds a clear escalation path — 'agent handles X, human reviews Y' — becomes the template everyone copies.
slants.pm: Scope every AI agent like a team member: clear authority, clear boundaries, clear escalation. Ambiguity is where incidents start.
slants.admin: If an AI agent can send on your behalf or access shared systems, someone should have defined exactly what it's allowed to do. If they haven't, flag it.

steps: List any AI tools or agents at your workplace that can take actions — scheduling, sending, approving, editing — not just answer questions.
For each one, write down: "What can it do without asking a human first?"
If the answer is vague or you're not sure, that's the governance gap Gartner is warning about.
Open your AI tool and ask: "What's a simple 3-tier framework for governing AI agents based on their level of autonomy? Make it practical for a non-technical team."
Share the most useful tier distinction you found in the group.

homework.title: Tonight, let AI help you prepare for an awkward conversation.
homework.body: Everyone's got one — a message to send, a boundary to set, a favor to ask, a topic to raise. No work context needed. Open a free tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity):
homework.prompt:
"I need to [describe the conversation — ask a neighbor something, bring up a topic with a friend, negotiate with a contractor, talk to a family member about X]. Give me 3 different ways to open the conversation, ranked from most direct to most gentle. For each, tell me what tone it sets."

The ranked with tone labels trick helps you choose consciously instead of defaulting to whatever feels safest.

2026-06-19.intro: Friday — and Juneteenth. A federal holiday that honors freedom, community, and the ongoing work of building something better. The AI industry didn't pause, so here's what moved this week as the world observed.

trends.title: Apple Makes AI Personal — and Private
trends.body: Apple's WWDC follow-up sessions this week detailed exactly how Apple Intelligence handles on-device processing for the vast majority of tasks, with Private Cloud Compute reserved for complex requests. Third-party app developers now have access to Writing Tools and summarization APIs, meaning AI-assisted features will appear across virtually every major iOS app by fall 2026 (9to5Mac, June 2026). The move cements Apple's bet that privacy-first AI is the winning differentiator for the billion-plus device ecosystem.

slants.strategy: When Apple's entire app ecosystem gets AI Writing Tools, your customers' baseline expectations for AI-assisted experiences shift — build AI into your product roadmap assuming it's table stakes, not a differentiator.
slants.operations: On-device AI processing with Private Cloud Compute means sensitive workflows can use AI without data leaving the device — reassess which AI use cases you've been holding back for privacy reasons.
slants.pm: Third-party APIs for summarization and writing mean the next wave of productivity apps in your stack will ship AI features by default — plan your tool evaluations accordingly.
slants.admin: Apple Intelligence Writing Tools coming to every major app means your daily drafting, summarizing, and email work will have an AI assist layer whether you opt in or not — get ahead of it now.

steps: Think about the app you use most for communication — email, Slack, Teams, or another tool.
Check whether it has an AI drafting or writing assist feature you haven't used yet.
Write your next status update, reply, or summary using the AI assist feature instead of from scratch.
Compare how long it took versus your usual approach and what edits you made.
Share the prompt or approach that worked best in the group.

trends.title: The 'AI Colleague' Is Becoming a Real Job Title
trends.body: LinkedIn's latest Workforce Report (June 2026) found that job postings mentioning 'AI collaboration' or 'AI-augmented work' grew 340% year-over-year, with the fastest growth in administrative, project management, and operations roles. Critically, the highest-salary AI-augmented job postings aren't for engineers — they're for strategic operators who use AI to do the work of teams (LinkedIn Economic Research, June 2026). The emerging title: 'AI Strategist' or 'AI Operations Lead.'

slants.strategy: The salary premium is going to people who deploy AI strategically, not those who merely use it — invest in building AI-powered workflows, not just AI prompting skills.
slants.operations: Operations roles that pair AI fluency with process expertise are commanding salary premiums — document your AI workflows and present them as operational infrastructure, not personal tricks.
slants.pm: Project management is one of the fastest-growing categories for AI-augmented roles — the PMs who demonstrate AI-powered delivery will have the most negotiating leverage in the next hiring cycle.
slants.admin: Administrative roles that use AI to do the work of larger teams are among the highest-value positions in this new landscape — you're already ahead if you're building AI into your daily workflow.

steps: Open LinkedIn and search for 'AI Operations' or 'AI Strategist' in your industry.
Read 2–3 job postings and note which AI skills and tools they mention.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "Based on the following job description, tell me which skills I should develop and how to demonstrate them in my current role: [paste the job description]"
Identify one skill gap and one skill you already have.
Share one job posting that surprised you and what it signals about your industry.

trends.title: Real-Time AI Translation Is Quietly Becoming Infrastructure
trends.body: Google expanded its Live Translate feature to 12 additional languages in Google Meet this week, with Microsoft following by enabling real-time captions with translation for Teams across all enterprise tiers. In a study of 50,000 cross-language Teams meetings, productivity metrics — including action item completion and decision accuracy — improved 28% when real-time translation was enabled (Microsoft Research, June 2026). The implication: language is no longer a barrier in AI-augmented workflows.

slants.strategy: Removing language barriers in real-time collaboration expands your effective talent pool and partner network globally — revisit any cross-border initiatives you've slowed due to communication friction.
slants.operations: Real-time translation in your collaboration tools means you can run globally distributed operations with fewer coordination delays — test it in your next cross-regional sync.
slants.pm: Language-barrier-free project communication means your global stakeholder alignment meetings can be more frequent and more substantive — rebuild your cadences with this in mind.
slants.admin: Live translation in meeting tools means supporting international executives, guests, or clients now requires significantly less preparation — try enabling it in your next cross-language meeting.

steps: Check whether your team's video meeting tool (Zoom, Teams, Meet) has live captions or translation enabled.
If it does, turn it on for your next meeting even if everyone speaks the same language — practice using AI-generated transcripts for meeting notes.

After the meeting, paste the auto-transcript into your company-approved AI tool: "Summarize this meeting transcript into: (1) key decisions made, (2) action items with owners, and (3) open questions that need follow-up."
Review the summary against what you actually remember from the meeting.
Share one thing the AI caught that you might have missed.

homework.title: Use AI to reflect on the week's big ideas
homework.body: Juneteenth is a day for reflection and intention. Try using AI to help you process what you've learned this week — about AI, your work, or your goals. Structured reflection with AI as a thinking partner is one of the most underused applications of the technology.
homework.prompt: Act as a thoughtful coach. I want to reflect on something I learned or observed this week. Ask me three questions to help me go deeper — then help me identify one concrete thing I want to do differently next week based on what came up.

2026-06-20.intro: Saturday. The week's news cycle slows down, but your relationship with AI doesn't have to. Weekend drops focus on tools and techniques you can try without a work context — low stakes, high upside.

trends.title: AI Is Getting Better at the Tasks You Hate Most
trends.body: A survey of 8,000 knowledge workers conducted by Slack's Workforce Lab (June 2026) found that the top three tasks people most want AI to handle are: scheduling and calendar management, summarizing long email threads, and generating first drafts of reports and presentations. Workers who regularly offloaded these three tasks to AI reported 23% higher job satisfaction — even when total work output stayed the same (Slack Workforce Lab, June 2026). The insight: it's not just about speed, it's about energy.

slants.strategy: Satisfaction gains from AI come from eliminating low-energy tasks, not just completing more of them — design your team's AI adoption around what drains people most, not just what takes longest.
slants.operations: Scheduling, email triage, and report generation are your three highest-return AI investments — if you haven't built AI workflows around all three, start there before anything more complex.
slants.pm: AI-generated first drafts of status reports, briefs, and decks are one of the clearest time-return plays for PMs — build a template library of your most common report types and draft prompts for each.
slants.admin: The three tasks in this survey are the core of most administrative roles — if you've been treating AI as optional, this research makes the case that it's now the baseline for sustainable, high-performance admin work.

steps: Identify your single most dreaded recurring task — the one you procrastinate the longest.
Open your company-approved AI tool and describe the task in detail: what it is, who it's for, and what a good result looks like.
Ask: "Help me build a step-by-step approach to completing this task using AI, from gathering inputs to delivering the final output."
Test the approach on this week's version of the task.
Share how it went and what you'd change about the workflow.

trends.title: Video Generation Just Crossed a Key Quality Threshold
trends.body: This week OpenAI quietly updated Sora's output quality with a new rendering pipeline, and Runway released Gen-4 Turbo — both achieving what reviewers are calling 'broadcast-quality b-roll' for the first time from consumer tools. Marketing teams at several mid-size companies reported replacing stock video subscriptions with AI-generated footage, cutting video production costs by 60–80% (Adweek, June 2026). The timeline for AI video becoming standard in content production has accelerated significantly.

slants.strategy: When video production costs drop 60–80%, every team — not just marketing — can tell richer stories; revisit every communication you've declined to make visual because of cost.
slants.operations: Training videos, process documentation, and internal communications are about to get dramatically cheaper to produce with motion and visual context — plan this into your next operations content cycle.
slants.pm: AI video can make your product demos, release notes, and stakeholder presentations significantly more compelling at no additional cost — prototype one visual explainer this quarter.
slants.admin: Onboarding materials, executive briefings, and office communications are all candidates for AI-generated video upgrades — even a short AI-generated visual summary can make dense information more digestible.

steps: This is a weekend experiment: try a free-tier AI video tool (Runway, Pika, or Kling) with no work stakes.
Write a short 2-sentence description of a scene — something simple like a coffee shop, a team meeting, or a product being used.
Generate a 5-second clip and watch it.
Generate 2–3 variations by changing a detail in your description.
Share your best result and note what surprised you most about the quality.

trends.title: Weekend Prompt: Make AI Your Personal Research Assistant
trends.body: One of the highest-value uses of AI outside work is helping you make better personal decisions. Whether it's a major purchase, a health question, a financial choice, or a trip you're planning — AI can help you research and evaluate options far faster than traditional search. Users who use AI for structured personal research report making decisions 3x faster and feeling significantly more confident in their choices (Anthropic user research, May 2026). The key is structuring your question well.

slants.strategy: The same structured research skills that make AI useful at work transfer directly to personal decisions — the mental model of 'clear goal, relevant context, specific question' works everywhere.
slants.operations: Personal AI research practice builds the evaluation and prompting skills that make you more effective in professional AI contexts — don't silo your AI experimentation to work hours.
slants.pm: Weekend research projects are low-stakes environments to test multi-step AI reasoning and source evaluation — experiment now so you're not learning on the job when it matters.
slants.admin: Using AI for personal research builds familiarity with context-setting and follow-up prompting that directly translates to more effective professional use.

steps: Pick a personal decision you're currently weighing — anything from a purchase to a trip to a life question.
Open your preferred AI tool and start with: "I'm trying to decide [what]. Give me the 5 most important factors I should consider, and the 3 questions I should answer before deciding."
Work through the AI's questions one by one.
Ask for a recommendation based on your answers.
Share whether the AI's recommendation matched your gut, and what it surfaced that you hadn't considered.

homework.title: Ask AI to plan your ideal Sunday
homework.body: Low stakes, purely for fun — and for practicing specific, context-rich prompting. The more detail you give AI, the better it performs. Your weekend plans are the perfect low-pressure sandbox.
homework.prompt: Help me plan my ideal Sunday. Here's my context: [how many people, location, time of year, budget range, energy level today]. Ask me two clarifying questions, then give me a morning-to-evening itinerary with options at each stage.

2026-06-21.intro: Sunday check-in. The AI adoption numbers are in, and the gap between organizations that have AI and those using it well keeps growing — and the cause isn't the technology.

trends.title: The 'enablement illusion' is the new AI risk
trends.body: Most leaders are measuring AI adoption by access, not by whether it changes anything. Gartner's May 2026 global survey of 12,000+ employees found that workers who are AI-proficient across multiple use cases are 3.2 times more likely to drive effective process improvements than those with basic access. By 2027, Gartner predicts half of enterprises without a people-first AI strategy will lose their best AI talent.

slants.strategy: Reframe your AI KPIs: shift from 'licenses deployed' to 'workflows meaningfully changed' — that's where the ROI signal actually lives.
slants.operations: Audit which teams have AI access but no structured time or training to use it — that's where the enablement illusion costs the most.
slants.pm: Build AI proficiency as a project success criterion, not just adoption rate — capability depth drives results, not tool access alone.
slants.admin: If you've been given AI tools but no clear guidance on using them, that's your organization's gap to close, not yours — advocate for a structured use-case session with your team.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool.
Think of one recurring task you do weekly that feels repetitive — a status update, a summary, or a data lookup.
Paste this prompt: I need to [describe your task]. Walk me through how AI could help me do this faster, and give me a sample prompt I can use next time.
Try the sample prompt on a real, non-sensitive example.
Note what worked and what you would adjust.
Share your task and the sample prompt in the community group — help others see what's possible.

trends.title: Agents are in production, but half of companies skipped the redesign
trends.body: Active AI agents in the Microsoft 365 ecosystem grew 15x year over year, per Microsoft's 2026 Work Trend Index of 20,000 knowledge workers. Deloitte found that nearly half of organizations introduced AI without redesigning the workflows or roles around it — so agents are running on top of broken processes instead of better ones.

slants.strategy: Before scaling agentic AI, map one existing workflow end-to-end and identify what's being automated versus what's just being accelerated — that difference determines your actual efficiency gain.
slants.operations: If your team uses agents to speed up a manual handoff, the handoff is the problem — use this as a trigger to redesign the process, not just automate it.
slants.pm: Add a workflow redesign checkpoint to your AI rollout process — deploying an agent without it is like adding a faster engine to a car with no steering.
slants.admin: If a new AI tool was added to your workflow without explanation, it's fair to ask how it changes what you're supposed to do — that question is worth raising.

steps: Pick one process your team uses regularly that has more than three steps.
Open your company-approved AI tool and type: Here is a workflow my team uses: [describe it in plain English]. Which steps could an AI agent handle, and which require human judgment?
Review the response — does it flag any steps you hadn't considered?
Write down one step that could go to AI and one that definitely shouldn't.
Share your findings in the community group — what was the most surprising step to keep human?

trends.title: How managers model AI use shapes outcomes more than tools do
trends.body: Microsoft's 2026 Work Trend Index found that when managers actively model their own AI use, employees report a 30-point lift in trust in agentic AI and a 22-point lift in how critically they evaluate AI output. Organizational culture accounts for more than twice the impact on AI value as individual employee mindset — 67% versus 32%.

slants.strategy: If AI adoption is stalling in your org, look at your managers before your tech stack — culture and manager behavior are 2x more predictive of AI ROI than individual mindset.
slants.operations: Have team leads share one AI-assisted output per week in team meetings, with a note on what worked and what needed fixing — that's the modeling that moves metrics.
slants.pm: Psychological safety around AI experimentation is measurable: teams where managers encourage trying and failing with AI tools report up to 20 points higher AI readiness — build that into your team norms.
slants.admin: When your manager shares how they use AI, pay attention — it signals what the organization considers safe to try, and it's worth taking note of.

steps: Think about the last time you shared work that AI helped you with — did you mention the AI, or leave it invisible?

Open your company-approved AI tool and use this prompt: Write a casual 3-sentence note I could share with a coworker explaining one way I used AI this week. Keep it conversational and honest about what it did well.
Edit the draft to sound like you.
Share it in the community group — modeling starts with one person going first.

homework.title: Plan a trip you've been putting off
homework.body: Got a summer trip living in your head as 'someday'? Turn it into an actual plan — no work data, no risk. Try this in ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini (all free):
homework.prompt:
I want to plan a trip to [your destination or 'somewhere new within a few hours of me']. Before you give me suggestions, ask me 3 questions that will help you understand my travel style and budget.

After I answer, give me a 3-day itinerary with one 'splurge' option and one 'budget-friendly' version for each day.

2026-06-22.intro: Monday. Most companies have AI agents in production now — so this week's real question isn't whether to deploy, it's whether anyone's actually steering them. Three things to think about, and a five-minute experiment to start the week.

trends.title: Most AI agents are running without a kill switch
trends.body: Writer's 2026 AI Adoption in the Enterprise survey (with Workplace Intelligence, covering 1,200 executives and 1,200 employees) found that 36% of organizations have no formal plan for supervising AI agents, and 35% admit they couldn't immediately 'pull the plug' on one that went rogue. Meanwhile 67% of executives believe their company has already suffered a data leak from unapproved AI tools, and 55% describe AI use at their company as a 'chaotic free-for-all.'

slants.strategy: Governance is now a competitive advantage, not a compliance tax — the orgs that can safely say 'yes' to AI will out-execute the ones still saying 'wait.' Make agent oversight a metric leadership actually reviews.
slants.operations: For every agent your team runs, write down two things this week: who owns it, and how you'd stop it. If you can't answer either, that's your highest-priority fix.
slants.pm: Add a 'named owner and documented off-switch' line to your AI deployment checklist — an agent without both isn't production-ready, no matter how well it demos.
slants.admin: If you're using an AI tool that was never officially approved, you're not alone — but flag it so it can be made safe rather than hidden. Shadow AI only becomes a breach when nobody knows it's there.

steps: List every AI tool or agent you personally use for work — including the unofficial ones.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: Here is a list of AI tools I use for work: [your list]. For each one, ask me a question that would help determine whether it's touching sensitive company data.
Answer the questions honestly for yourself.
Flag anything that touches sensitive data to your manager or IT — frame it as 'help me use this safely,' not a confession.
Share one thing you learned about your own AI footprint in the community group.

trends.title: 97% deployed agents. Only 29% are seeing returns.
trends.body: The same 2026 enterprise research found that while 97% of organizations deployed AI agents in the past year — and 80%+ of the Fortune 500 now run them in production — only 29% report significant ROI, and 79% say they're facing real challenges scaling AI, a double-digit jump from 2025. The bottleneck isn't access to agents; it's the workflows and oversight around them.

slants.strategy: If your ROI story is still 'we deployed X agents,' you're measuring activity, not value. Trace one agent to a dollar saved or an hour freed — if you can't, that's the gap to close before deploying the next one.
slants.operations: Resist adding another agent this week. Take one you already have and remove a step of friction around it — most agent ROI leaks out through the human handoffs at the edges.
slants.pm: Treat every agent rollout like a product with a success metric defined before launch. 'It's live' is a milestone, not an outcome.
slants.admin: If an agent is supposed to save you time but you're spending more time double-checking it, that's real signal — surface it. The fix is usually upstream, not your patience.

steps: Pick one AI agent or automation your team already uses.

Open your company-approved AI tool and type: An AI agent at my company does [describe what it does]. Help me figure out whether it's actually saving time — ask me 3 questions about how the work flowed before and after.
Answer the questions and notice where the real time goes now.
Identify one handoff or check around the agent that could be smoothed.
Share the friction point you found in the community group — odds are someone else has it too.

trends.title: The people going deep with AI are pulling away
trends.body: Across 2026 workforce research, the divide keeps widening between casual users and 'super-users' who weave AI through multiple tasks: super-users report saving roughly nine hours a week and are several times more productive than slow adopters. Yet 56% of the global workforce says they've had no recent AI training, and 57% lack access to mentorship. The capability is available; the structured chance to build it often isn't.

slants.strategy: Your biggest AI ROI lever this quarter may be training, not tooling — the proficiency gap, not the access gap, is what separates your top performers from the rest.
slants.operations: Block 30 minutes this week for your team to swap one AI workflow each. Peer learning closes the proficiency gap faster than any vendor webinar.
slants.pm: Build skill-building into project timelines, not as an afterthought — a team that's nine hours a week more efficient pays back the training time inside the first sprint.
slants.admin: You don't need permission to get better at this. Pick one task you do often and spend 15 minutes finding a sharper way to do it with AI — that compounds.

steps: Think of one task you did with AI this week that felt just 'okay.'

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: Last time I used AI for [task], I [describe what you did]. Suggest three ways I could have gotten a better result, and rewrite my approach as a reusable prompt.
Save the reusable prompt somewhere you'll find it again.
Use it on your next real task.
Share your reusable prompt in the community group — give someone else a nine-hours-a-week head start.

homework.title: Design your ideal Saturday
homework.body: Mondays are easier when there's something to look forward to. Use AI to plan one genuinely good day off — no agenda, no obligations, no work data. Try it in ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini (all free):
homework.prompt:
I want to design my ideal Saturday with zero obligations. Before suggesting anything, ask me 3 questions about what actually recharges me — whether that's quiet, adventure, people, or none of the above.

Then give me a loose hour-by-hour plan for the day, with one option that costs nothing and one small 'treat yourself' upgrade.

2026-06-23.intro: Tuesday. Three new data points this week confirm what most leaders already sense: AI is forcing a rethink of how work is organized — not just what tools are on the menu.

trends.title: Leadership alignment is the real AI bottleneck
trends.body: Microsoft's 2026 Work Trend Index found that 82% of leaders call 2026 a pivotal year to rethink strategy and operations — but only 1 in 4 AI users say leadership is consistently aligned on what AI should do. The gap isn't tooling; it's direction.

slants.strategy: If your AI investments aren't paired with a clear owner and measurable outcome, they're experiments, not strategy — and experiments don't show up in next year's budget.
slants.operations: Misaligned leadership means mixed signals for the people actually running the tools — define what 'good AI use' looks like on your team so your staff isn't guessing.
slants.pm: Leadership misalignment surfaces in your project — as scope creep, last-minute AI requests, and post-launch pivots. Surface the question of AI governance in kickoff, not retrospective.
slants.admin: When AI strategy is unclear from the top, frontline staff get asked to figure it out themselves — your practical experience using these tools is exactly what leadership needs to hear.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool.

Paste: "Our organization is adopting AI but leadership alignment is weak. What are 3 practical questions a team lead or senior contributor could raise in the next all-hands to push for clearer direction?"
Pick the one question that feels most relevant to your team.
Ask a follow-up: "Rewrite that question as a 2-sentence message I could send to my manager before our next 1:1."
Share your question in the community group — even if you haven't sent it yet.

trends.title: AI agents are now an enterprise infrastructure problem
trends.body: Gartner projects that 40% of enterprise applications will include task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, up from fewer than 5% in 2025. Microsoft shipped its Work IQ APIs (June 16) to help IT teams build controlled agents inside Microsoft 365 — signaling that agents are moving from pilot to plumbing.

slants.strategy: Every agent your organization deploys is an infrastructure commitment — before approving the next one, ask who owns it, how its output gets reviewed, and what happens when it makes a mistake.
slants.operations: The people who feel agent sprawl first are ops: someone has to define the handoffs, catch the edge cases, and own the process when an agent does something unexpected — start designing that role now.
slants.pm: Agent integrations belong in your project charter, not your backlog — scope includes who monitors the agent, what triggers human review, and what the rollback plan is.
slants.admin: As agents handle more routing, scheduling, and drafting, the value you add shifts to quality control and judgment — make sure you know what the agents in your stack are doing each day.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool.
Paste: "What is an AI agent, in plain language? Give me 3 examples of AI agents a typical office professional might already be using without realizing it."
Identify whether any of those sound familiar in your own work.
Ask a follow-up: "For one of those agent types, what are 3 questions I should ask before trusting its output at work?"
Share one agent you recognize in your workflow in the community group.

trends.title: The job market is splitting — and human skills are winning
trends.body: PwC's 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer (June 15) found that roles where AI elevates human judgment are seeing twice the job growth and 42% faster salary growth than roles where AI simply handles the work. The finding flips the common fear: AI isn't replacing expertise — it's making it worth more.

slants.strategy: The competitive talent question isn't 'who can use AI' — it's 'who can use AI to think better.' Redesign roles around the judgment AI can't replicate, and you'll have something harder to commoditize.
slants.operations: Process design, exception handling, and cross-functional coordination are growing more valuable — not less — as AI handles the routine. These are exactly what great ops people are already good at.
slants.pm: The PM skills AI amplifies most are prioritization, stakeholder alignment, and judgment under uncertainty — all things you build through practice, not prompts. Keep investing there.
slants.admin: The admin functions with the strongest outlook require relationship management, organizational knowledge, and contextual judgment — these are not automatable, and they're increasingly rare.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool.

Paste: "I work in [your role or field]. What specific skills in my role are becoming MORE valuable as AI handles routine tasks? Give me 3, with a concrete example of how each shows up in day-to-day work."
Pick the skill you feel least confident about right now.
Ask a follow-up: "Give me one 15-minute practice scenario I can try this week to strengthen [that skill] — keep it personal, not work-related, so there's no risk."
Share what skill you're focusing on in the community group.

homework.title: Decode your summer utility bill with AI
homework.body: Try this at home: use AI to decode a bill that always feels like a mystery. The technique is called structured output — you tell the AI exactly what sections you want back, which makes the answer far easier to act on. Try this in ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini (all free).
homework.prompt:
I'm going to paste my electric or gas bill. Please analyze it and give me: (1) a plain-English summary of what I'm paying for, (2) the 2–3 biggest cost drivers this month, (3) one practical thing I can do to reduce the bill without major changes, and (4) any charges or fees I should question or look into.

Here is my bill: [paste your bill text here]

2026-06-24.intro: Wednesday. This week's AI signals are pointing in one direction: the professionals treating AI as a full workflow partner — not just a single-task helper — are unlocking a level of output that's changing what "good work" looks like. The opportunity to be one of them is wide open.

trends.title: Your AI Tool Can Now Run the Whole Play
trends.body: The biggest shift in AI productivity in 2026 isn't a new model — it's a new mode of working. Today's leading AI platforms don't just answer questions; they complete entire workflows: researching, drafting, formatting, and delivering — all in one pass. The AI productivity landscape has shifted decisively from single-task assistants to multi-step agents capable of owning full workflows from research through final output, with over 20 major platforms releasing agentic features in the first half of 2026, per aisofting.com's 2026 AI Productivity Tools Update. For working professionals, this means the unit of delegation is no longer a prompt — it's an entire process.

slants.strategy: If your team is still using AI one question at a time, you're running a 2024 strategy with 2026 tools — the competitive advantage now lives in delegating whole workflows, not individual tasks.
slants.operations: Full-workflow AI means a process that used to take your team a full day — intake, research, draft, format — can now return a polished output in under an hour, compressing turnaround and freeing capacity for higher-value work.
slants.pm: Think of AI agents as a force multiplier on your projects: research briefs, status summaries, and stakeholder updates can now be produced autonomously, letting you focus on the decisions and relationships that need your judgment.
slants.admin: Multi-step AI means you can hand off a complex support task — travel research, meeting prep, briefing documents — and get back a finished, ready-to-share result, making your contribution feel more strategic than ever.

steps: Identify one recurring multi-step task you do weekly — something that involves research, then writing or summarizing a result.

Open your AI tool and paste this prompt: "You are my expert assistant. Complete this task from start to finish: [describe your task in 1-2 sentences]. First, gather the key information. Then organize the main points. Then write the final output."
Review the full output — note where it landed well and where it missed the mark.
Run this follow-up to refine: "Revise the output with these changes: [your specific edits]. Format the final version as [your preferred format — bullet list, email, one-pager, etc.]."
Save your two-prompt sequence as a reusable template for this task going forward.

trends.title: AI Meeting Notes Just Crossed the Unicorn Line
trends.body: The AI meeting intelligence category just had its defining moment. Granola — which automatically captures, structures, and summarizes your meetings — closed a $125M Series C and reached a $1.5 billion valuation, up from $250 million just one year earlier, according to TechCrunch (March 2026). The message from investors and enterprises alike: AI-powered meeting context is becoming foundational infrastructure, not a productivity add-on.

slants.strategy: A $1.5B bet on meeting intelligence signals that the companies winning right now treat meeting context as a strategic asset — if your team's decisions are still scattered across personal notes and inboxes, now is the time to centralize.
slants.operations: AI meeting tools close the gap between what was decided and what actually gets done — every action item, owner, and deadline surfaces automatically, making follow-through a default rather than an extra effort.
slants.pm: When AI captures every meeting decision and next step automatically, your status updates practically write themselves and your projects move faster — this is leverage that makes you look like you have more bandwidth than anyone else in the room.
slants.admin: AI meeting tools transform the admin role from manual transcription to strategic review — you're distributing clean summaries and clear action items, a visible upgrade that showcases your value to the whole team.

steps: Before your next meeting, open your AI tool and have it ready — you'll use it right after.

After the meeting, paste your raw notes with this prompt: "Here are my notes from a [type of meeting] meeting. Please extract: (1) key decisions made, (2) action items with owners, (3) open questions still unresolved, and (4) a 3-sentence summary. [paste notes here]"
Review the output and correct any misattributions or items that were missed.
Follow up with: "Format this as a brief recap message I can send to the attendees. Keep it under 150 words and use a professional but warm tone."
Send the recap (or save it as your post-meeting template) — and track how much time you just recovered.

trends.title: Enterprise AI Spending Just Hit Warp Speed
trends.body: The numbers behind enterprise AI adoption in 2026 are now hard to ignore. Anthropic's annualized revenue surpassed $30 billion — up from approximately $9 billion just six months earlier — with over 1,000 businesses now each spending more than $1 million annually, a number that doubled in under two months, per Anthropic. When organizations are committing at this scale, AI fluency has moved from a résumé bonus to a baseline professional expectation.

slants.strategy: Revenue growth at this speed signals that enterprise AI adoption has crossed into the mainstream — strategy leaders who haven't built AI into their operating model aren't early movers anymore, but there's still real advantage in moving now.
slants.operations: As your organization's AI tools become more capable and embedded, the ops professional who already knows how to leverage them becomes the go-to resource — positioning you ahead of the next wave before it arrives.
slants.pm: As AI becomes standard across enterprise stacks, PMs who can define AI-augmented workflows will have a decisive advantage in velocity, quality, and the confidence of their stakeholders.
slants.admin: The faster enterprise AI adoption accelerates, the more valuable the admin who already knows how to use these tools well becomes — now is the moment to build that expertise and let it be visible.

steps: Choose one deliverable you produce regularly — a report, brief, summary, or proposal — and note how long it currently takes you from scratch.
Open your AI tool and try this prompt: "Act as an expert in [your field or role]. Draft a [deliverable type] based on this input: [paste your source material, bullet points, or key facts here]."
Time how long it takes from first prompt to a polished draft — compare it to your usual time.
Refine with: "Tighten the language, cut anything repetitive, and add one specific example or stat to strengthen the main point."
Track your time savings across three uses of this workflow, then share the result with your manager as a case for formalizing the process.

homework.title: Plan Your Weekend Menu in Five Minutes
homework.body: Tonight's homework is a low-stakes way to practice structured output — the prompting technique where you tell AI exactly what format and categories you want in the response. It's one of the highest-leverage skills you can build, because it transfers directly to any work task where you need organized information fast: briefings, comparison tables, action plans, project summaries. Use your fridge as the dataset and see how precisely AI organizes to your specs.
homework.prompt: Act as a practical home meal planner. Based on these ingredients and constraints: [paste what's in your fridge plus any dietary preferences or time limits], create a weekend plan — Saturday dinner and Sunday brunch — that requires no special shopping. Format each meal as: Meal name | Key ingredients | Cook time | One reason we'll love it.

2026-06-25.intro: Thursday. This week's biggest AI moves are all about the ecosystem growing up: new career tracks, smarter agents, and policy clarity that lets your organization say yes to AI with confidence.

trends.title: A New AI Career Track Just Opened — At Scale
trends.body: OpenAI launched its Partner Network with a $150 million commitment targeting 300,000 certified AI consultants by the end of 2026 — a credentialing wave roughly the size of Accenture's entire global workforce (OpenAI, June 14).
