A separate Salesforce survey found 78% of managers feel personally responsible for their team's AI adoption, yet only 32% work in organizations with formal AI tracking (Salesforce, June 2026).

slants.strategy: This is a planning gap, not a people gap — build the validation and coaching load into role design before you set adoption targets, not after.
slants.operations: Treat AI output review as a workflow step with its own time and owner, the same way you'd account for QA on any process change.
slants.pm: Add a lightweight 'AI-assisted' checkpoint to your project status template so review time doesn't quietly disappear into someone's evenings.
slants.admin: If you support a manager who's drowning in AI review work, ask what parts of that checking process you could take a first pass at.

steps: Pick one AI-assisted output from this week — a draft email, summary, or report.
Open your company-approved AI tool and ask: "Give me a 5-point checklist I can use to validate accuracy and tone before I send this kind of AI-assisted work to a manager."
Run your own output through that checklist and note anything it catches that you missed.
Add one item to the checklist based on what you just learned.
Share your checklist in the group so others can borrow it.

trends.title: AI agents want the whole task now, not just your questions
trends.body: A Harvard Business School analysis of hundreds of millions of user interactions found knowledge workers are the heaviest users of agentic AI, and the pattern is a real shift: moving from asking AI for answers to delegating the entire task (HBS Working Knowledge, June 2026). Researcher Jeremy Yang put it plainly — the tools take "objectives and preferences, instead of step-by-step instructions" (HBS Working Knowledge, June 2026).

slants.strategy: Start writing goals and guardrails for agents into your planning docs, not just task lists — that's the unit of work now.
slants.operations: Pick one recurring, well-defined process and hand it a goal instead of a script; see where it needs a human checkpoint.
slants.pm: Rewrite one recurring deliverable as an outcome statement instead of a sequence of steps, then let the agent ask you what it needs.
slants.admin: Try describing what you want done, not how, and see whether the tool asks smarter clarifying questions than you'd have thought to answer.

steps: Pick a recurring task you usually do step-by-step, like a weekly status update.
Instead of instructions, describe the goal: "I want a weekly status update summarizing progress, risks, and next steps for [project]. Ask me for the info you need, then draft it."
Notice what it asks you before drafting — that's the gap between a tool and a delegate.
Compare the result to how you'd normally write it and flag anything it missed or got right.
Share your prompt and takeaway in the group.

trends.title: The data says AI adopters are hiring, not cutting
trends.body: A new Ramp and Revelio Labs study of over 21,000 U.S. firms found companies that invest heavily in AI grow headcount 10% over the two years following adoption, with entry-level headcount up 12% (Ramp, June 2026). The catch: gains show up "roughly 6-12 months after adoption", once firms build real workflows around the tools rather than bolting them on (Ramp, June 2026).

slants.strategy: Use this data to reframe the AI-and-headcount conversation in planning meetings — the story isn't automation replacing people, it's slow, workflow-dependent payoff.
slants.operations: Expect a lag between rollout and results — set expectations with leadership now so a quiet first two quarters doesn't get read as failure.
slants.pm: Build project resourcing plans assuming teams grow alongside AI tools over time, not shrink the day after rollout.
slants.admin: If a colleague is anxious about AI and job cuts, this is a real number to bring to that conversation, not just reassurance.

steps: Think of a recent headline or hallway comment about AI cutting jobs.
Ask your company-approved AI tool: "Summarize the strongest evidence for and against AI adoption causing layoffs, using recent labor market data."
Compare the summary to what you assumed going in.
Write one grounded sentence you'd use to reassure a nervous colleague.
Share it in the group.

homework.title: Let AI plan your next low-key weekend
homework.body: Pick any free tool — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity — and let it plan a short trip with you instead of for you. This one teaches the 'ask me questions first' technique, which is one of the most useful prompting habits you'll ever pick up.
homework.prompt: "I want to plan a low-key weekend trip within 3 hours of [your city]. Before you suggest anything, ask me five questions about my budget, interests, and travel style, then give me three ranked options."

2026-07-06.intro: Monday. This week is already stacked with momentum — a landmark government AI deployment, a global commission putting world leaders behind AI for everyone, and the most capable everyday AI model yet just became your default tool.

trends.title: State Government's Biggest AI Bet Opens Doors for Everyone
trends.body: California Governor Newsom announced a landmark partnership with Anthropic, making Claude available to every state agency — and optionally every city and county — at a 50% discount. Over 2,800 state employees across 67 departments are already piloting the tool (TechCrunch, June 2026), handling everything from Medicaid case management to document drafting. This is the largest US state government AI deployment in history, and a clear signal that AI-powered work is becoming standard at every level of public and private service.

slants.strategy: When a state the size of California standardizes on AI for day-to-day government operations, it signals that AI fluency is moving from competitive advantage to table stakes — position your team now.
slants.operations: State-scale AI deployment means the tool you're using is proven at volumes and complexity levels far beyond most organizations — your confidence in building AI-powered processes should grow accordingly.
slants.pm: Government project managers are using AI for Medicaid case management and document summarization — the same productivity gains are available in your projects, with no procurement process required.
slants.admin: The tasks state workers are using AI for — drafting, summarizing, analyzing documents — are exactly what you do every day; this is your clearest signal yet that AI-assisted admin work is the new professional standard.

steps: Identify one document you regularly draft or summarize — a meeting summary, status update, or briefing.
Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "You are a professional analyst. Summarize the following document in 5 clear bullet points for a non-technical audience: [paste your document here]"
Review the summary and note what it got right and what it missed.
Refine it with: "Rewrite this summary as a 3-sentence executive briefing for a director. Lead with the most important finding."
Save both prompts as a reusable template for this document type.

trends.title: Global Leaders Make AI Access for All a Shared Mission
trends.body: The United Nations and ITU launched the AI for Good Global Commission on July 2, co-chaired by Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff and Rwandan President Paul Kagame. More than 40 founding members — including the CEOs of Amazon, Nvidia, and Microsoft — have committed to ensuring AI-driven economic gains reach developing nations (Axios, July 2026). Their inaugural meeting is happening this week at the AI for Good Global Summit in Geneva.

slants.strategy: When tech CEOs and heads of state align on a shared AI agenda, the organizations building AI fluency right now will have a meaningful voice in how this unfolds — don't wait to get comfortable with the technology.
slants.operations: Global AI governance frameworks create clearer standards for data, privacy, and procurement — getting your operations AI-ready now means less scrambling when those standards land.
slants.pm: International AI frameworks will shape compliance requirements in your roadmaps — understanding the landscape today puts you ahead of the planning curve tomorrow.
slants.admin: Major commissions generate constant streams of reports and briefings — AI is your best tool for staying current on complex global trends so your executive always has the context they need.

steps: Find one recent AI-related headline from this week — the AI for Good Commission launch is a great starting point.
Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "Summarize this story and explain what it means for professionals in [your industry]: [paste the headline or article text here]"
Identify one implication that's relevant to your team or role.
Draft a short briefing: "Write a 3-sentence summary I could share with my manager about why the UN AI for Good Global Commission matters to our organization."
Share your summary in your team channel or with a colleague as a trends-to-watch post.

trends.title: Your AI Assistant Just Got a Significant Upgrade — for Free
trends.body: Anthropic launched Claude Sonnet 5 on July 1 as the new default model for Free and Pro users, bringing near-Opus-level performance at a fraction of the cost. The model features a 1-million-token context window, dramatically stronger multi-step reasoning, and improved tool use — making complex workflows that once required premium-tier models available to everyone. Introductory pricing runs at $2 per million input tokens through August 31, 2026 (Anthropic, July 2026).

slants.strategy: A model approaching top-tier performance at standard pricing means your team can run more sophisticated AI workflows without a budget increase — the gap between enterprise AI and everyday AI just narrowed significantly.
slants.operations: Sonnet 5's stronger multi-step reasoning means you can automate longer, more complex processes — giving ops teams the kind of leverage that used to require custom development.
slants.pm: The 1-million-token context window means you can paste an entire project plan, contract, or sprint backlog into one prompt for analysis, summarization, or risk identification.
slants.admin: With a more capable default model, routine tasks like drafting emails, prepping agendas, and summarizing meeting notes are noticeably faster and more accurate — your everyday AI just got a meaningful upgrade.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and check which model you're currently using (look in settings or the model selector).

Paste a long document — a meeting transcript, project brief, or email thread — and try: "Analyze this document and identify the top 3 action items, who should own each one, and the suggested deadline based on what's discussed: [paste here]"
Review the extracted action items and refine any that need more context.
Try a multi-step follow-up: "Now draft a follow-up email to the team summarizing these action items in a friendly, professional tone. Keep it under 150 words."
Send or schedule the email and note how much time the two-prompt workflow saved you compared to your usual process.

homework.title: Design Your Dream Room with AI
homework.body: This one's purely for fun — and for practicing structured prompting with rich context. Give AI a detailed picture of your style, constraints, and wish list to generate a room redesign or home decor plan you'd actually love. You're building the same skill that makes your work prompts dramatically more specific and useful.
homework.prompt: You are an interior designer. Using the information below, suggest a complete redesign for my [room type] — including color palette, furniture arrangement, lighting ideas, and 3 specific styles or pieces to look for. My current setup: [describe it]. My style preferences: [describe your taste]. My budget: [range]. My biggest pain point with this room: [what bothers you most about it].

2026-07-07.intro: Tuesday. Post-holiday week is often the most productive week of the summer — clear heads, reduced meeting load, and momentum to reset. Three AI moves from last week you need to know before the real work resumes.

trends.title: Meta's AI Assistant Reaches 1 Billion Users
trends.body: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced last week that Meta AI has surpassed 1 billion monthly active users across WhatsApp, Instagram, Messenger, and Facebook — making it the most-used AI assistant in the world by a significant margin. The fastest-growing use cases are WhatsApp-based: recipe help, travel questions, and real-time information lookup, with over 60% of usage coming from users in India, Brazil, and Southeast Asia (Meta, July 2026). The scale signals that AI assistance is now a mainstream consumer expectation, not a tech enthusiast behavior.

slants.strategy: When 1 billion consumers use AI daily for real-life questions, the expectation for AI-powered experiences in every product rises accordingly — your customer experience strategy needs an AI interaction layer.
slants.operations: The most-used AI features globally are information lookup, summarization, and task help — the same things your team uses AI for. The tools are converging on what actually works.
slants.pm: Meta AI at 1B users means your end users are increasingly sophisticated AI consumers — design your product's AI features assuming users already know how to prompt, not that they need hand-holding.
slants.admin: 1 billion people using WhatsApp AI for everyday questions means your executives, stakeholders, and colleagues are already AI-comfortable in their personal lives — the professional adoption curve is shorter than you think.

steps: If you use WhatsApp, open Meta AI and ask it a practical question you'd normally Google — something about travel, food, or a local recommendation.
Note how the experience compares to your usual AI tools in terms of speed, tone, and usefulness.
Now ask the same question in your professional AI tool (Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot).

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "What are 3 ways a 1-billion-user AI assistant embedded in messaging apps will change how customers expect to interact with businesses in the next 12 months?"
Share one implication that feels most relevant to your role.

trends.title: AI Is Closing the Productivity Gap Between Junior and Senior Workers
trends.body: New research from MIT Sloan (July 2026) tracked 3,200 knowledge workers for six months after AI tool adoption and found that the largest productivity gains went to workers in their first five years of experience — not experienced workers. Junior employees using AI saw a 35% performance lift, narrowing the gap with senior colleagues to just 8% on complex writing and analysis tasks, down from 22% before AI adoption (MIT Sloan Management Review, July 2026). Senior workers still lead on judgment and strategy, but the execution gap is closing fast.

slants.strategy: The closing performance gap between junior and senior workers means your competitive advantage increasingly comes from judgment and vision, not execution speed — invest in developing those distinctly human capabilities.
slants.operations: If junior team members are closing the gap with AI, your onboarding ROI improves significantly and your output per headcount increases — this changes how you structure your team.
slants.pm: Junior PMs with AI tools can now produce senior-quality first drafts, research, and analysis — the highest-leverage PMs are those who direct this output toward the highest-value strategic work.
slants.admin: Early-career admins using AI are already performing at a higher level than their experience would predict — if you're new to the field, AI gives you a once-in-a-career shortcut to credibility and impact.

steps: Think of a task where you typically rely on experience or institutional knowledge to produce a good output.
Describe that task to your company-approved AI tool and ask it to help you complete it as if you're teaching a junior employee.
Compare the AI-assisted result to what you'd produce without it.
Ask: "What judgment calls or context did the AI miss that required my experience to catch or correct?"
Share what the AI got right that surprised you, and what it got wrong that required your expertise.

trends.title: AI Code Review Is Now Standard at the Top Tech Companies
trends.body: Google, Meta, and Microsoft all confirmed this week that AI-powered code review is now part of their standard engineering workflow — not a pilot, not optional. Google's internal tools flag potential security issues and performance problems before human reviewers see the code. GitHub's Copilot Enterprise customers reported a 40% reduction in code review cycle time and a 28% drop in post-merge bugs in the first quarter of adoption (GitHub, July 2026). The era of unassisted code review is ending at scale.

slants.strategy: When the top three tech companies standardize AI code review, the downstream effect on their vendors, partners, and competitors is faster, higher-quality software across the industry — your software supply chain is about to improve.
slants.operations: Faster code review cycles mean faster deployments and shorter feedback loops — if you're coordinating technical releases, AI-assisted review shrinks your timeline assumptions.
slants.pm: 40% faster code review directly compresses sprint cycles and release planning — rebuild your engineering velocity estimates to reflect this new norm.
slants.admin: Even if you don't write code, understanding that AI is now part of the technical workflow helps you set realistic expectations for development timelines and communicate them accurately to stakeholders.

steps: Ask a developer colleague or your AI tool: "Explain how AI-assisted code review works, and what kinds of issues it catches that human reviewers miss most often."
Identify one non-technical process you own that has a 'review' step — proposals, reports, communications.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste your next review-ready document: "Act as a critical reviewer. Identify the 3 most significant gaps, logical errors, or missing information in this document: [paste]"
Fix the issues the AI flagged before you send for human review.
Share how many issues the AI caught that you would have missed.

homework.title: Use AI to clear the post-holiday backlog
homework.body: Long weekends create email debt. Instead of trudging through it manually, let AI help you triage and respond efficiently. This is one of the clearest high-ROI uses of AI for professionals — especially coming off a holiday.
homework.prompt: I have a large volume of email to work through after a long weekend. Help me triage it by giving me a framework for sorting messages into: (1) respond today, (2) respond this week, (3) delegate, (4) archive without response. Then help me draft a short, professional reply to the following message: [paste one email].

2026-07-08.intro: This week's signals are converging on a single idea: powerful AI capabilities that used to be exclusive to enterprise budgets are now arriving at every price tier — making this one of the best moments in the AI era to level up your skills and your team's output.

trends.title: Powerful AI Agents Are Now Within Everyone's Reach
trends.body: A new wave of AI models is delivering multi-step, agentic performance — the ability to research, draft, and complete complex tasks in one pass — at dramatically lower prices. Claude Sonnet 5, launched in late June 2026, delivers near-flagship agentic capabilities at $2 per million input tokens, according to TechCrunch (June 30, 2026). Early testers report the model self-checks its own work and completes multi-step tasks where previous mid-tier models fell short — meaning full AI workflow automation is no longer just for enterprise budgets.

slants.strategy: The price-performance curve just reset — high-quality AI agents are no longer a premium line item, which means your team's AI capabilities can now scale without scaling your AI spend.
slants.operations: If your team has been putting off automating a multi-step workflow because the tools felt out of reach, the moment to act is now — capable AI agents at accessible prices mean your ops stack can punch well above its weight.
slants.pm: Multi-step agentic models handle research, summarization, and first drafts in a single request, which means your project documentation and status updates can practically write themselves without your judgment leaving the room.
slants.admin: Today's AI tools can take a briefing request and return a finished document — not a rough outline. You're no longer editing AI output; you're reviewing near-final work, which shifts your role from assistant to quality lead.

steps: Pick a task that usually takes you 20+ minutes and involves at least two steps — for example, research then write, or gather information then summarize.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "You are my expert assistant. Complete this task end-to-end: [describe your 2-step task]. First research and gather the key points, then organize them, then write the final output ready to share."
Review the output — note how close it is to what you'd produce manually, paying attention to structure, accuracy, and tone.
Refine with: "Revise the output with these specific changes: [your edits]. Then format the final version as [email / summary / one-pager]."
Save your two-prompt sequence as a reusable template so you can run this workflow again in under two minutes.

trends.title: Competition Is Bringing Better AI to Every Budget
trends.body: The competitive landscape between leading AI platforms is accelerating rapidly, and professionals are the direct beneficiaries. New model tiers are delivering flagship-level intelligence at mid-tier pricing — OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Terra variant is reported to match the performance of GPT-5.5 at roughly half the cost, according to Neowin and TechRadar (July 2026). With multiple AI platforms racing to offer the best price-to-performance ratio, the capabilities available to everyday knowledge workers are expanding at an unprecedented pace.

slants.strategy: A new performance-per-dollar benchmark is being set this month — this is the time to revisit your team's AI tool stack and see where you're overpaying for capability you don't need, or underinvesting in tools that could unlock real gains.
slants.operations: As AI model costs fall, the business case for automating more of your workflows becomes easier to make — the return on experimenting with AI-assisted operations is now higher than it has ever been.
slants.pm: Falling AI costs mean the tools that help you track, communicate, and plan projects are getting smarter and more accessible — now is an ideal moment to pilot an AI-assisted workflow on your next project.
slants.admin: More capable AI at lower price points means more AI assistance built into the tools you already use — features that once felt like premium add-ons will increasingly arrive as defaults.

steps: Think of one task you've been doing manually because the AI output wasn't quite there — a draft that needed heavy editing, or a summary that missed nuance.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "I'm going to give you a task I've tried before with AI and wasn't satisfied with the result. Here's what I need: [describe the task]. This time, ask me one clarifying question before you start."
Answer the clarifying question, then review the improved output.
If it's still not quite right, try: "The tone / structure / detail level needs to shift. Specifically: [one precise change]. Revise with that change only."
Note whether the output quality has improved since the last time you tried — the tools may have moved further than you think.

trends.title: AI Is Now Standard — and Your Expertise Sets You Apart
trends.body: AI in the workplace has moved from early adoption to expected infrastructure, and the professionals who invest in their AI skills now are the ones who will lead what comes next. 73% of U.S. companies now incorporate AI somewhere in their workflow, according to enterprise research compiled by coworker.ai (2026), and companies actively using enterprise AI complete 126% more projects per week compared to those using traditional methods alone. The proficiency gap between AI-fluent professionals and everyone else is widening — and that gap is your opportunity.

slants.strategy: The early adopter advantage window hasn't closed — it's just moved from using AI to using AI well. The leaders who can build thoughtful AI workflows in their teams are a tier above those who just have access to the tools.
slants.operations: With AI adoption nearly universal, what differentiates high-performing operations teams is no longer access to the tools — it's the quality of the prompts, workflows, and processes they've built around them.
slants.pm: The most in-demand PMs right now aren't just using AI — they're designing AI-assisted project workflows that make their whole team more effective. That's a skill you can start building today.
slants.admin: When the majority of companies are using AI, the admins and executive support professionals who deeply understand how to leverage it become essential to their organizations — not just helpful, but indispensable.

steps: Identify one workflow on your team that still runs mostly manually — a process where AI assistance hasn't been introduced yet.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "I want to design an AI-assisted version of this workflow: [describe it in 2-3 sentences]. Map out each step and suggest where AI could take over, speed up, or improve the output."
Review the AI's suggested workflow map and flag the one step that would have the highest impact if automated.
Refine by asking: "Focus on step [X]. Write a reusable prompt I could use to run that step with AI every time."
Share your reusable prompt with one teammate and invite them to test it — teaching someone else is the fastest way to cement the skill.

homework.title: Plan a weekend adventure with an AI co-pilot
homework.body: Whether it's a day trip, a movie marathon, or finally tackling a fun project you keep postponing — use AI to design a weekend plan that's 100% yours. Practice structured prompting and let the AI handle the logistics while you focus on what you actually want to do.
homework.prompt: I want to plan a fun, low-effort weekend that actually feels like a break. Before you suggest anything, ask me 3 questions about what sounds good right now — the vibe, where I am, and how much energy I want to spend. Then give me two options: one that requires zero planning, and one mini-adventure I might not have thought of.

2026-07-09.intro: Thursday. Midweek momentum. Three things happened in AI this week that have direct implications for how you work, plan, and build — whether or not you feel like it's an 'AI week' in the news.

trends.title: Perplexity Launches Enterprise Search With Direct Database Access
trends.body: Perplexity AI announced Perplexity Enterprise Pro this week, including direct integration with company knowledge bases, Confluence, Notion, and SharePoint. The feature allows employees to ask natural language questions and get answers sourced from internal documentation with citations. Early enterprise customers reported an 80% reduction in 'where do I find...' questions to IT and operations teams, with median response time to internal queries dropping from 4 hours to under 2 minutes (Perplexity, July 2026). Enterprise search is finally working the way it always should have.

slants.strategy: When employees can instantly find any internal knowledge via natural language, institutional knowledge stops being a bottleneck and becomes an asset — audit what's in your knowledge base and make sure it's complete.
slants.operations: An 80% reduction in 'where do I find' questions means your operations documentation becomes a force multiplier — invest in keeping it accurate and AI-searchable.
slants.pm: AI-powered search of your internal docs means your team can self-serve on specifications, decisions, and prior work — the PM who maintains the best documentation gets the most out of this.
slants.admin: Natural language search across SharePoint and Confluence means the 'ask your admin' layer for finding things is shifting — you can add more value by curating and organizing knowledge rather than being the search function.

steps: Identify one question your team asks repeatedly — a policy, a process, a location of a document.
Check whether the answer is documented clearly in your knowledge base (Confluence, Notion, SharePoint, or similar).
If it's not, document it now using your company-approved AI tool: "Help me write a clear, scannable knowledge base article that answers this common question: [describe the question and answer]"
Publish it to your team's knowledge base.
Share the article link and note how much time you estimate it will save over the next month.

trends.title: AI-Generated Presentations Are Becoming Indistinguishable From Human-Made
trends.body: Canva's Magic Design and Microsoft Copilot's PowerPoint features both received major updates this week, with reviewers noting that AI-generated slide decks now consistently pass for professional human designs in blind tests. A Gartner study found that 67% of senior executives could not reliably identify AI-generated presentation decks in a blind review, up from 31% one year ago (Gartner, July 2026). The bar for presentation quality is rising at every level.

slants.strategy: When executives can't distinguish AI-made from human-made decks, your competitive advantage comes from the thinking inside the deck, not the design — invest in better analysis and clearer narrative structure.
slants.operations: Operations decks, process documentation, and reporting packages can now be AI-drafted in a fraction of the time — if you're still building these from scratch, you're spending time you don't need to.
slants.pm: AI-generated decks save the most time on the documents PMs produce most often: sprint reviews, stakeholder updates, and roadmap presentations — build a library of AI prompt templates for each type.
slants.admin: Presentation preparation is one of the most time-intensive executive support tasks — AI-drafted decks that you edit and refine can save 2–3 hours per deliverable.

steps: Pick a presentation you need to create in the next two weeks.

Open your company-approved AI tool and describe the audience, goal, and key points: "Help me create an outline for a [10-slide / 5-minute] presentation for [audience] about [topic]. The goal is [what you want them to think, feel, or do after]."
Use the outline as a starting point rather than building the deck from scratch.
Note how much time the AI-generated structure saved you compared to your usual approach.
Share the outline (minus any confidential content) and ask for feedback on the structure.

trends.title: Voice AI Is Moving Into High-Stakes Professional Contexts
trends.body: This week, ElevenLabs announced partnerships with two major telemedicine platforms and a global HR services firm — all deploying voice AI for initial patient intake and employee benefits counseling. The AI systems are trained to recognize emotional cues, flag escalation scenarios, and seamlessly hand off to human professionals when needed. Pilot data showed a 94% user satisfaction rating for AI-handled interactions and a 40% reduction in human agent escalations versus phone-based intake (ElevenLabs, July 2026).

slants.strategy: Voice AI moving into healthcare and HR intake signals that AI can now handle emotionally complex, high-stakes conversations — the next frontier is not information retrieval but relationship and service delivery.
slants.operations: Any intake, triage, or initial screening process in your organization is a candidate for voice AI augmentation — map your customer or employee touchpoints against this new capability.
slants.pm: AI-handled first contact with 94% satisfaction opens up capacity for human agents to focus on complex cases — if your product has a support or intake component, rebuild your service tier model.
slants.admin: Voice AI handling routine employee inquiries means the HR admin, legal admin, or benefits admin role is shifting toward complex case management — position yourself as the escalation expert, not the first line.

steps: Think of a routine, repetitive interaction your team or organization handles at high volume — FAQs, appointment scheduling, status updates.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "Help me draft a script for an AI voice or chat assistant to handle [describe the interaction]. Include how it should greet users, gather needed information, and hand off to a human when needed."
Review the script for gaps — what does the AI miss that a human would catch?
Identify what the handoff trigger should be for your specific use case.
Share the interaction type and one thing about the AI script that surprised you.

homework.title: Build your AI meeting prep system
homework.body: One of the clearest time-return plays with AI is pre-meeting preparation. Instead of walking into meetings cold, you can use AI to brief yourself, anticipate questions, and clarify your own thinking in minutes rather than hours.
homework.prompt: I have a meeting tomorrow about [topic]. The attendees are [list names or roles]. My role is [what you're there to do]. Help me: (1) prepare a one-paragraph briefing on the topic, (2) anticipate the three most likely questions or objections, and (3) clarify what success looks like for this meeting.

2026-07-10.intro: Friday. End of a strong week. Three things that happened in AI this week that you'll want to carry into next week — and one homework prompt to close it well.

trends.title: OpenAI's o3 Reasoning Model Goes Wide — and Gets Faster
trends.body: OpenAI rolled out optimized inference for the o3 reasoning model this week, cutting response times by 60% while maintaining the same accuracy benchmarks. The model is now available to all Pro subscribers and via API. In independent benchmarks, o3's performance on multi-step reasoning tasks — including complex financial analysis, legal document review, and strategic planning scenarios — remained 15–20% above competing models (LMSYS Chatbot Arena, July 2026). Fast reasoning at scale changes what you can automate.

slants.strategy: Faster, accessible reasoning models mean complex analysis tasks that used to require senior-level human time — scenario planning, risk assessment, market sizing — can be automated and iterated on rapidly.
slants.operations: Multi-step operational analysis: root cause investigation, process failure post-mortems, capacity planning — all are now prime candidates for AI-first approaches with o3-class models.
slants.pm: Requirements analysis, user story generation, and trade-off evaluation are the PM tasks that benefit most from reasoning models — try a reasoning-first workflow on your next backlog refinement session.
slants.admin: Even if the advanced reasoning capabilities feel distant from your daily work, the downstream effect is that the tools you use every day — email, calendar, documents — will get much smarter in the next 12 months.

steps: Pick a decision or analysis you've been putting off because it feels too complex.
Open your company-approved AI tool and lay out the decision in full: context, options, constraints, and what a good outcome looks like.
Ask: "Walk me through a structured analysis of this decision. What information am I missing? What are the most important trade-offs? What would you recommend and why?"
Push back on one part of the recommendation: "What's the strongest argument against that recommendation?"
Share whether the AI's analysis changed your thinking and what it got right or wrong.

trends.title: AI Writing Tools Are Reshaping How Teams Communicate Internally
trends.body: A study of 500 organizations using Microsoft Copilot for internal communications found that Copilot-assisted messages were rated 31% clearer and 24% more action-oriented than unassisted messages by recipients — even when the sender was an experienced communicator. The biggest gains came in messages sent across seniority levels: when a junior employee used Copilot to communicate up, the quality gap with senior communicators almost disappeared (Microsoft Work Trend Index, July 2026).

slants.strategy: When AI-assisted communication across seniority levels levels the playing field, ideas rise based on substance, not polish — build a culture where AI-assisted writing is expected, not stigmatized.
slants.operations: Clearer, more action-oriented internal communication reduces re-work and follow-up — the ROI on AI writing assist tools is measurable in meeting time and task completion rates.
slants.pm: 31% clearer, 24% more action-oriented — those are the metrics your stakeholder communications should be hitting. Build AI writing review into your standard process for any message that goes up the chain.
slants.admin: AI-assisted communication closes the gap between junior and senior communicators — this is directly valuable for any admin supporting executives and needing to communicate across multiple levels.

steps: Find an internal message you sent in the last week — a status update, request, or summary.
Paste it into your company-approved AI tool with this prompt: "Review this internal message and rewrite it to be 20% clearer and more action-oriented. Flag what specifically made it less clear."
Compare the two versions and identify the pattern in what the AI changed.
Apply that pattern to your next message before you send it.
Share one edit pattern the AI consistently makes that you want to adopt going forward.

trends.title: AI Agents Are Handling Multi-Day Tasks Without Human Check-ins
trends.body: Anthropic published a case study this week featuring three enterprise customers running Claude-based agents on multi-day research and analysis tasks — with no human interaction until delivery. The tasks included competitive landscape analysis (3 days), regulatory compliance review (5 days), and vendor due diligence (4 days). All three customers reported output quality equivalent to a senior analyst's work, at roughly 1/10th the cost and 3–5x the speed (Anthropic, July 2026). The era of autonomous AI work is no longer theoretical.

slants.strategy: Multi-day autonomous AI work on research and analysis tasks means your strategy function can now run more investigations, scenario analyses, and due diligence processes simultaneously — replan your research capacity.
slants.operations: Regulatory compliance review and vendor due diligence — two of the most time-intensive ops tasks — are now candidates for AI-first execution. Map your next compliance cycle against this capability.
slants.pm: Competitive landscape analysis at 3–5x speed means product strategy cycles can compress significantly — AI-powered research should now be part of every major planning cycle.
slants.admin: Understanding that multi-day AI agent work is now enterprise-grade helps you frame AI's role accurately for your executive: not a drafting tool, but a junior analyst who can run long projects.

steps: Identify one research or analysis task that typically takes your team 2–5 days.
Break it into a sequence of steps and open your company-approved AI tool.

Start with: "I'm going to ask you to help me complete a multi-step analysis of [topic]. Start by giving me a research plan: what questions do we need to answer, in what order, and what information do we need for each?"
Work through the first step with the AI and note the quality.
Share whether the AI's research plan was better or worse than the one you'd have built manually.

homework.title: Design an AI agent for a task you do every week
homework.body: If AI can run multi-day enterprise projects, it can certainly handle your weekly recurring task. This weekend, design the briefing you'd give an AI agent to take over your most repetitive weekly work item — even if you can't automate it yet, the act of designing the process reveals exactly what could be.
homework.prompt: I want to design an AI agent to handle my weekly [task name]. Here's how I currently do it: [describe the steps]. The inputs are [describe what you start with] and the output is [describe the deliverable]. Help me write a detailed agent briefing — including step-by-step instructions, quality criteria, and how the agent should handle edge cases.

2026-07-11.intro: Today's throughline: the tech keeps getting easier, but the harder work is organizational — redesigning how teams operate, choosing tools that will still exist next quarter, and figuring out the new etiquette of talking about AI use out loud.

trends.title: The bottleneck isn't the AI anymore — it's your org chart
trends.body: Microsoft's 2026 Work Trend Index confirms what a lot of planners already suspect: handing people AI tools isn't the same as building an organization that can actually use them. Only 19% of AI users fall into the "Frontier" zone where individual skill and organizational readiness are both high — the rest are stuck, blocked, or still figuring it out (Microsoft Work Trend Index, May 2026). The tension is real: 65% of AI users fear falling behind if they don't adapt quickly, while 45% say it feels safer to just stick to their current workflow.

slants.strategy: Treat AI readiness as a structural project on your roadmap — audit where governance, incentives, and workflows still assume a pre-AI operating model, not just where headcount happens to use AI tools.
slants.operations: Map which processes have people using AI ad hoc versus which ones have actually been redesigned end-to-end around it — that gap is where inconsistency and rework hide.
slants.pm: Bake 'who reviews the AI's output and how' into project plans up front, instead of bolting it on after a rollout stalls.
slants.admin: If you've quietly gotten ahead of your team on AI, that's a signal worth surfacing — flag the gap between what you've figured out and what your team's official workflow supports.

steps: Pick one recurring task on your team that people already use AI for informally.

Ask your company-approved AI tool: "Here's a recurring task on my team: [describe task]. Write a simple three-step workflow showing where a human should review or approve the AI's output before it's used."
Compare that draft workflow to what actually happens today — is there a real review step, or does AI output go straight out the door?
Write down one gap between the ideal workflow and the current one.
Share your gap and the AI-drafted workflow in the group.

trends.title: AI tools are getting bought, buried, or both — plan around it
trends.body: The AI tools market just had its biggest shakeup yet: SpaceX's reported $60 billion acquisition of the coding tool Cursor was the largest startup acquisition ever recorded, part of a quarter where roughly 80% of venture investment went to AI startups (AI tools news roundup, July 2026). The steadier trend matters more for planners: 193 AI tools have already shut down or been acquired this year, and Cursor itself acquired a smaller rival just three weeks before being bought — proof that the tool your team builds a workflow around today may look totally different by next quarter.

slants.strategy: Build vendor-churn risk into your AI roadmap the way you'd plan for a key supplier being acquired — assume today's tool stack looks different in 12 months.
slants.operations: Before standardizing a process around any single AI tool, check whether your company-approved option has a stable enterprise agreement, not just a promising free tier.
slants.pm: Add a 'tool continuity' line to project risk logs for any initiative that leans heavily on one AI vendor.
slants.admin: If you've built a personal system around one free AI tool, keep a backup habit going with a second one — free tiers are shrinking fast across the board.

steps: List the AI tools you or your team currently rely on for any part of your workflow.

Ask your company-approved AI tool: "I rely on [tool name] for [task]. If this tool changed its pricing, got acquired, or shut down tomorrow, what's a backup approach using a different tool or a manual process?"
Review the answer and pick one backup you could realistically use.
Write the backup plan down in one sentence.
Share your primary tool and backup plan in the group.

trends.title: Being honest about using AI at work is quietly costing people
trends.body: New research from Atlassian's Teamwork Lab found something uncomfortable: even though 94% of knowledge workers use AI at work, disclosing it still carries a real penalty. In a controlled experiment, colleagues who admitted to using AI were rated 10x lazier and 24 points less likely to get recommended for a high-visibility project than peers who produced identical work without mentioning AI (Atlassian Teamwork Lab, June 2026). Framing your AI use as helping the team, rather than just saving yourself time, closed much of that gap.

slants.strategy: Set explicit team norms for how AI use gets discussed in planning documents and reviews — silence isn't a policy, it's a vacuum that culture will fill on its own.
slants.operations: Close the trust gap fastest by using AI visibly yourself and narrating it as a team efficiency win, not a personal shortcut.
slants.pm: Build 'AI-assisted' into status update templates as a normal field, so disclosing it stops feeling like a confession.
slants.admin: If you're already the AI power user on your team, you have a chance to model open, team-framed AI use before the culture defaults to secrecy.

steps: Think of one task you've used AI for recently but haven't mentioned to your manager or team.
Ask your company-approved AI tool: "Help me write a two-sentence note to my manager describing how I used AI to complete [task], framed around how it helped the team rather than just saving me time."
Read the draft and adjust it so it sounds like you.
Send it, or say it out loud in your next team check-in.
Share what you sent or said in the group.

homework.title: Let AI interview you before it plans your weekend
homework.body: Instead of dumping every trip detail into one giant prompt, try teaching the AI to ask you questions first — it's a technique that gets noticeably better results for any personal project, from trip planning to gift shopping. Use whichever free tool you like: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity.
homework.prompt: I want to plan a two-day weekend trip within driving distance. Before you suggest anything, ask me five questions about my budget, interests, and who's coming — then use my answers to give me three ranked options.

2026-07-12.intro: Sunday. A quieter day to catch up, reset, and prepare. This week's drop is lighter — one key development and a powerful use case to try at your own pace.

trends.title: AI Is Getting Dramatically Better at Understanding Your Documents
trends.body: Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google all updated their document understanding capabilities this month, with significant improvements in table extraction, cross-reference understanding, and multi-page reasoning. The practical effect: you can now drop a 100-page PDF into Claude or GPT-4o and ask it sophisticated questions that require reading across multiple sections simultaneously. Legal teams piloting these updated capabilities reported cutting document review time for contracts, compliance documents, and regulatory filings by 65–75% (LexisNexis, July 2026).

slants.strategy: Better document understanding means your AI can now analyze lengthy RFPs, annual reports, and strategic plans with the same accuracy as a trained analyst — incorporate this into your competitive intelligence and planning cycles.
slants.operations: Contracts, SOPs, compliance docs, and audit reports are all candidates for AI-first review — if you're still reading long documents linearly before extracting key points, you're spending time you don't need to.
slants.pm: AI that reads across a 100-page requirements document or technical specification to surface inconsistencies, gaps, and dependencies is now available to every PM — use it on your next spec review.
slants.admin: Board packs, legal agreements, and policy documents that used to require hours of careful reading can now be summarized and queried in minutes — this is one of the highest-leverage applications for executive support.

steps: Find a long document you've been meaning to read but haven't — a report, a policy, a contract.
Upload it to your company-approved AI tool (or paste the text).
Ask three questions that would normally require reading the entire document to answer.
Then ask: "What are the 5 most important things I need to know from this document, and what questions should I be asking that I haven't thought to ask yet?"
Share which question the AI's answer surprised you most on.

trends.title: The 'Human in the Loop' Standard Is Evolving
trends.body: The AI governance conversation shifted this week as the IEEE published new guidelines on human-AI oversight that distinguish between different categories of decisions based on reversibility and impact — rather than applying a blanket 'human must review' standard. The framework categorizes AI decisions into three tiers: fully autonomous (routine, low-impact, easily reversible), supervised autonomous (significant but recoverable), and human-required (high-stakes, hard to reverse) (IEEE Standards Association, July 2026). This is the governance model most enterprises are expected to adopt over the next 18 months.

slants.strategy: A tiered AI oversight framework is more pragmatic than blanket human review requirements — build your AI governance policy around reversibility and impact, not just 'did AI touch this?'
slants.operations: Mapping your AI-assisted workflows to this three-tier framework clarifies where you can run fully autonomous and where you need a human checkpoint — it also protects you in audits and compliance reviews.
slants.pm: Product features that include AI decision-making now have a clearer governance framework to design against — build your AI feature specs around which tier each decision falls into.
slants.admin: Understanding the tiered governance model helps you advise executives on AI risk: routine AI-assisted tasks are different from high-stakes AI decisions, and conflating the two leads to either over-caution or under-caution.

steps: List three ways you currently use AI in your work.
For each one, classify it using the IEEE's three-tier model: fully autonomous, supervised autonomous, or human-required.

Open your company-approved AI tool: "Based on this framework [describe the tiers], help me assess whether my use of AI for [task] is appropriately supervised or whether I should adjust my level of oversight."
Identify one AI task you're over-supervising (wasting time) and one you might be under-supervising (taking on risk).
Share your classification and whether the framework changed how you think about AI oversight.

trends.title: Sunday Prompt: Let AI Help You Plan the Week Ahead
trends.body: One of the most practical uses of AI is weekly planning — not just listing tasks, but thinking through priorities, blockers, and what 'success' actually looks like. Sunday is the ideal time to build this habit, and it only takes 10 minutes with the right prompt.

slants.strategy: Strategic planning at the weekly level is a compounding habit — spending 10 minutes on Sunday with AI to structure your week pays dividends every day that follows.
slants.operations: Weekly AI-assisted planning helps you identify resource conflicts, dependencies, and low-priority tasks that might crowd out high-impact work before the week starts.
slants.pm: A weekly AI planning session helps PMs stay out ahead of blockers, stakeholder communication needs, and sprint dependencies — try it as a standing Sunday evening routine.
slants.admin: Executive support requires anticipating what's needed before it's asked for — AI-assisted weekly planning helps you get ahead of your executive's needs rather than reacting to them.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool on Sunday evening.
Share your top 5 priorities for the week and any known constraints or blockers.
Ask: "Help me plan this week so the most important things actually get done. Suggest a day-by-day structure that protects time for deep work and builds in buffer for surprises."
Review the suggested plan and adjust it to your reality.
Check back at the end of the week: share whether the plan held and what you'd do differently.

homework.title: Create your AI planning ritual
homework.body: The most effective AI users aren't using it reactively — they have a small set of rituals that keep them ahead. A Sunday planning session is one of the most powerful. Try structuring yours with this prompt and see if it becomes a habit.
homework.prompt: I want to start using AI for weekly planning. Help me build a 10-minute Sunday ritual. Start by asking me about my upcoming week — my priorities, my meetings, my constraints, and my energy level. Then help me build a plan that maximizes my impact and protects my focus time.

2026-07-13.intro: Monday. New week. Three AI developments from last week that set the tone for what's coming — and one habit to build into this week's work.

trends.title: Salesforce Einstein Gets a Major Upgrade — AI Is Now Running Sales Cycles
trends.body: Salesforce announced Einstein Autopilot last week — a suite of AI agents that can manage lead follow-up, schedule meetings, draft proposals, and update CRM records autonomously. The system runs on Salesforce Data Cloud, meaning it has full context of every customer interaction. Early adopters in the beta reported a 45% increase in pipeline conversion rates and a 60% reduction in CRM data entry time for sales teams (Salesforce, July 2026). The AI sales assistant is now actually autonomous — not just a helper.

slants.strategy: AI running sales cycle tasks autonomously means your sales team can focus entirely on relationship and judgment work — restructure compensation and success metrics for a world where AI handles execution.
slants.operations: The 60% reduction in CRM data entry time is the operations number to watch — any workflow downstream of CRM (reporting, forecasting, customer success) gets faster when the data is more accurate and complete.
slants.pm: AI-managed sales cycles generate richer data about what works and what doesn't in the funnel — build your product intelligence on top of this data by connecting it to feature requests and churn analysis.
slants.admin: Autonomous scheduling, proposal drafting, and follow-up mean the administrative layer of the sales cycle is handled — executive admins supporting sales leaders can now focus on more complex coordination and stakeholder management.

steps: Identify one step in your team's sales, client, or customer process that is repetitive and data-dependent — follow-up emails, status updates, or scheduling.
Open your company-approved AI tool and paste the context for one real pending task in that step.
Ask: "Draft an action for this step as if you were an autonomous AI agent: what would you do, what information would you gather, and what would you send or update?"
Review the AI's draft action and note what it got right and what it missed.
Share one step in your workflow where full AI autonomy would save the most time.

trends.title: AI Is Now Drafting Regulatory Filings — and Regulators Are Noticing
trends.body: The SEC published guidance this week acknowledging that AI-drafted regulatory disclosures are becoming common, and clarifying that companies remain fully responsible for AI-generated content in filings regardless of how it was produced. Meanwhile, several law firms reported that AI-drafted 10-K sections are now passing first-round review without material changes. One mid-size firm's general counsel estimated AI cut their annual disclosure preparation time by 40%, from six weeks to three and a half (Bloomberg Law, July 2026).

slants.strategy: When AI handles regulatory drafting at the quality level of experienced counsel, the competitive advantage goes to companies that can move faster through compliance cycles — streamline your regulatory calendar.
slants.operations: Compliance documentation, audit reports, and regulatory submissions are all prime candidates for AI-first drafting with human review — calculate the hours saved and reinvest them in higher-value compliance work.
slants.pm: Privacy policies, terms of service, and product compliance documentation are the PM's regulatory burden — AI-first drafting with legal review is the right workflow for teams without full-time legal support.
slants.admin: Board resolutions, compliance filings, and regulatory submissions that cross an executive admin's desk are increasingly AI-drafted documents — build your review skills for AI-generated regulatory content.

steps: Identify one document your organization produces that follows a standard regulatory or compliance format.

Open your company-approved AI tool and ask: "Help me draft a [document type] for a [type of organization]. Here are the key facts: [list the key inputs]. Follow standard format for this document type."
Review the AI's draft against the actual requirements and note what it got right and what needed correction.
Identify what information the AI needed that you had to provide versus what it supplied from its training.
Share how close the AI draft was to what you'd produce manually.

trends.title: AI Tutoring Is Closing Educational Gaps at Scale
trends.body: Khan Academy's AI tutor Khanmigo reported this week that students who used the tool for 30+ minutes per week over the past academic year showed 1.8 grade levels of reading improvement on average — with the largest gains in students who started below grade level. Schools in under-resourced districts saw comparable gains to schools with full-time tutoring programs, at roughly 2% of the cost per student (Khan Academy Research, July 2026). Educational AI is delivering the equity case its proponents promised.

slants.strategy: AI that delivers 1.8 grade levels of improvement in a school year signals that personalized, AI-powered learning at scale is not future-state — it's happening now. Build your L&D strategy around this capability.
slants.operations: The cost-efficiency of AI tutoring ($X per student vs. $50X for equivalent human tutoring) maps directly to corporate L&D: AI-powered skill development is dramatically more accessible than traditional training.
slants.pm: User onboarding and skill development for complex products can be AI-tutored — the Khan Academy model (personalized, adaptive, patient) is exactly what enterprise product training should look like.
slants.admin: AI tutoring that closes skill gaps at scale means the 'I never had training on this' barrier is lower than ever — use AI tutoring tools to build skills your formal training doesn't cover.

steps: Identify a skill gap in your work that you've been meaning to close but haven't had time to address through formal training.

Open your company-approved AI tool and ask it to tutor you on that skill: "I want to improve my understanding of [topic]. Act as a patient tutor. Start by asking me what I already know, then teach me the most important concepts at my level."
Engage for 15 minutes — answer its questions, ask follow-ups, and let it adapt to your level.
At the end, ask: "What's the one thing you'd suggest I practice this week to reinforce what we covered?"
Share the skill you worked on and one thing the AI taught you that surprised you.

homework.title: Build your AI skill gap list
homework.body: AI tutoring works best when you're specific about what you want to learn. This week, use AI to help you map your own skill gaps — then commit to closing one of them using AI-assisted learning.
homework.prompt: I want to identify the skill gaps most likely to limit my career growth in the next two years. Here's my current role and responsibilities: [describe]. Here are the AI tools I use regularly: [list]. Ask me five questions to understand my current skill level, then give me a ranked list of the five skills I should develop most urgently — and a learning plan for the top one.

2026-07-14.intro: Tuesday. Three things that matter right now — one about the economics of AI, one about how it's changing decision-making, and one about a new capability most people haven't noticed yet.

trends.title: AI Infrastructure Costs Are Falling Faster Than Expected
trends.body: Morgan Stanley's latest AI infrastructure report (July 2026) revised its cost projection models after surveying 200 enterprise AI deployments. The cost per AI-assisted task has fallen 78% in 18 months, driven by model efficiency improvements, chip advances, and competitive pricing pressure — and projections now show another 50% reduction over the next 12 months (Morgan Stanley Research, July 2026). The implication: AI workflows that aren't economically viable today will be table stakes within a year.

slants.strategy: When AI task costs fall 78% in 18 months, the ROI threshold for AI investment moves from 'significant ROI' to 'nearly everything passes' — revisit every AI use case you've shelved on cost grounds.
slants.operations: Operational AI at scale is now economically viable for workflows that weren't worth automating 12 months ago — run the math on every high-volume process your team owns.
slants.pm: AI feature costs in your product are falling fast — features that were too expensive to include in your roadmap should be reconsidered as the cost structure shifts beneath you.
slants.admin: Falling AI costs mean the productivity tools you use professionally will continue to improve and get cheaper, not more expensive — the habit-building you do now compounds on increasingly capable infrastructure.

steps: Identify one AI use case you've shelved because the cost, time, or effort wasn't worth it.

Open your company-approved AI tool and revisit it: "I want to reconsider whether this is now worth building or automating: [describe the use case]. What would this take to implement today, and what's the ROI if it saves [time/money estimate]?"
Do a rough ROI calculation based on the AI's assessment.
Decide whether it's worth bringing back to the roadmap.
Share one use case you're reconsidering and why the economics have shifted.

trends.title: AI Is Changing How Executives Make Decisions — Not Just How Fast
trends.body: Deloitte's AI in the C-Suite survey (July 2026) found that 71% of executives who regularly use AI for decision support report changing the quality of their decisions, not just the speed. The most commonly cited changes: considering more options before deciding, identifying blind spots earlier, and stress-testing assumptions more thoroughly. Only 12% of executives said they were using AI primarily for drafting and communication — 88% said AI's primary value was analytical (Deloitte, July 2026). The highest-value executives use AI to think better, not just work faster.

slants.strategy: The executives getting the most from AI are using it as an analytical partner, not a writing assistant — the highest-value prompt is 'challenge my thinking on this,' not 'write this for me.'
slants.operations: More thorough assumption-testing and earlier blind spot identification are exactly what operations leaders need for complex system decisions — build AI into your pre-decision review process, not just your post-decision documentation.
slants.pm: PMs who use AI to stress-test their roadmap assumptions and identify blind spots will make better prioritization decisions — make AI-assisted devil's advocate review part of your planning cycle.
slants.admin: Understanding how executives use AI most effectively helps you frame AI tools better when introducing or recommending them — lead with analytical value, not drafting efficiency.

steps: Think of a decision you're currently working through — a recommendation, a priority call, or a strategic choice.
Open your company-approved AI tool and lay out your current thinking.
Ask: "Challenge my thinking on this. What assumptions am I making that could be wrong? What options haven't I considered? What would a smart critic say about this approach?"
Engage genuinely with the pushback — don't just dismiss it.
Share one assumption the AI challenged that you're going to investigate before deciding.

trends.title: Real-Time AI Fact-Checking Is Coming to Every Screen
trends.body: Google's Project Astra — its real-time visual AI — expanded to Android devices globally this week, enabling AI to analyze what's on your screen and provide context, corrections, and related information without being asked. Meanwhile, OpenAI confirmed that a similar capability is in development for iOS. In early user testing, real-time screen AI identified factual errors in news articles, highlighted outdated statistics in presentations, and flagged biased framing in news summaries — in real time as users read (Google Labs, July 2026).

slants.strategy: Real-time AI fact-checking on every screen changes the standard for accuracy in communications — assume that anything your organization publishes will be AI-reviewed by sophisticated readers.
slants.operations: Operational reports, data dashboards, and status communications that go external should be stress-tested against AI fact-checking tools before distribution — errors are easier to catch before publishing.
slants.pm: Real-time screen AI that flags outdated statistics and biased framing in presentations means your stakeholder decks will face a higher accuracy bar — build a fact-check step into your final review process.
slants.admin: Real-time AI on screen means the context behind any document — a news article, a policy, a report — is now just an AI query away. Use this to brief executives faster and more accurately.

steps: Find a recent document, article, or presentation you've read or produced.

Paste a section into your company-approved AI tool and ask: "Fact-check this passage. Identify any claims that should be verified, statistics that could be outdated, and assumptions that might be worth questioning."
Note what the AI flagged and whether you agree with the flags.
Apply the same review to one of your own recent communications.
Share what the AI caught that you hadn't noticed.

homework.title: Use AI to stress-test your most important current project
homework.body: The executives in Deloitte's survey are using AI to challenge their assumptions, not just execute on them. This week, try applying the same approach to your most important current project — give AI the full picture and ask it to find the holes.
homework.prompt: I'm working on [describe the project, goal, or decision]. Here's my current plan: [describe it]. Please act as a rigorous critic. What are the three most significant risks I'm not adequately addressing? What assumptions in my plan are most likely to be wrong? What would I need to know or change to be more confident this will succeed?

2026-07-15.intro: Wednesday. Midweek. The AI landscape is moving on multiple fronts simultaneously — productivity tooling, regulatory frameworks, and a new category of model capability that changes what's possible for individual contributors. Here's what matters.

trends.title: Anthropic Releases Claude 4 Opus — The Strongest Reasoning Model Yet
trends.body: Anthropic launched Claude Opus 4 this week, its most capable model to date, with dramatically improved performance on multi-step reasoning, coding, and extended context tasks. Available via API and Claude.ai, the model introduces 'extended thinking' mode — a visible chain-of-reasoning that lets users see how the model is working through a problem before delivering an answer. On standard academic benchmarks, Opus 4 scores above GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro on 14 of 17 categories, with particularly large gains in scientific reasoning and document analysis (Anthropic, July 2026). The reasoning gap between frontier and commodity models is widening.

slants.strategy: The best AI model for complex strategy work just got significantly better — if your team is still using basic prompting for strategic analysis, the gap between what you're getting and what's possible has grown.
slants.operations: Extended thinking mode is particularly valuable for operations work — seeing the reasoning chain helps you validate whether the AI is approaching a complex process problem correctly before it gives you a recommendation.
slants.pm: More capable reasoning on multi-step product problems means PMs can now use AI for more sophisticated trade-off analysis, dependency mapping, and requirements synthesis — rebuild your AI workflow assumptions.
slants.admin: The most capable AI to date is now available in tools you already use — the opportunity to uplevel your AI-assisted work is highest right now, before the techniques you develop become standard practice.

steps: Identify your most complex current work challenge — something with multiple variables, competing constraints, and no obvious answer.
Open your company-approved AI tool and present the full challenge with all its context.
Ask: "Think through this step by step before responding. Walk me through your reasoning as you work toward an answer, then give me your recommendation with confidence level."
Evaluate whether the reasoning chain revealed assumptions or gaps you hadn't considered.
Share one place where seeing the AI's reasoning changed whether you trusted the output.

trends.title: EU AI Act Compliance Deadline Creates a Rush — and an Opportunity
trends.body: The EU AI Act's first major compliance tier took effect this week for high-risk AI systems, requiring documented risk assessments, human oversight mechanisms, and audit trails for AI used in employment, credit, and healthcare decisions. A survey of 400 European companies found that only 34% were fully compliant as of the deadline, while 58% were in progress and 8% reported no preparation at all (PwC European AI Act Survey, July 2026). US companies with EU operations or customers are racing to understand their exposure.

slants.strategy: EU AI Act compliance is now a procurement criterion for European customers — companies with documented AI governance frameworks have a competitive advantage in European markets.
slants.operations: AI systems used in employment decisions, performance review, or HR workflows fall under high-risk categories — audit your AI use cases against the EU AI Act risk classification framework now.
slants.pm: If your product uses AI for recommendations, scoring, or decisions that affect users, your EU market access may depend on your compliance posture — add an AI Act impact assessment to your next product planning cycle.
slants.admin: AI governance documentation — audit trails, risk assessments, oversight logs — is becoming a standard operational requirement. Building these records now is far easier than reconstructing them after the fact.

steps: List three AI tools or AI-assisted processes your organization uses that touch employees, customers, or partners.

For each, ask your company-approved AI tool: "Under the EU AI Act risk classification framework, is this use case likely to be considered high-risk, limited-risk, or minimal-risk? Explain the key criteria."
Identify which of your AI use cases would most benefit from formal documentation.
Draft a one-paragraph description of one AI use case — its purpose, inputs, outputs, and the human oversight step — as a starting point for an AI use case register.
Share one AI use case in your organization that you think deserves more formal oversight.

trends.title: AI Is Now Writing and Running Its Own Code in Production
trends.body: GitHub Copilot Workspace — the agentic coding environment that generates, tests, and iterates on code with minimal human input — is now available to all GitHub Enterprise customers. In the first two weeks of broader availability, users completed over 1 million automated coding tasks, ranging from bug fixes to feature implementations. The median task completion time for a well-specified coding request was 4 minutes — versus 2.3 hours for a human developer tackling a comparable task from scratch (GitHub, July 2026). Agentic coding is no longer a research project.

slants.strategy: When agentic coding reduces development time by 97% for well-specified tasks, the strategic advantage shifts to organizations that can specify what they want clearly — invest in product and requirements quality.
slants.operations: Internal tools, workflow automations, and data pipelines that previously required developer time are now accessible to non-technical ops leads who can clearly articulate requirements — start building your list.
slants.pm: PMs who write tight specifications get 97% faster development turnaround from AI coding tools — the return on investment in requirements quality has never been higher.
slants.admin: Agentic coding completing 4-minute tasks means small software requests (a custom report, a simple integration, a data transformation) are now viable for non-technical teams to commission — know what to ask for.

steps: Think of one small software tool, automation, or report your team would find useful but has never been built because it's not a development priority.
Write a clear specification: what the tool does, what inputs it needs, what the output should look like, and who uses it.

Open your company-approved AI tool and share the specification: "Help me refine this software specification so it's clear enough for an AI coding agent to implement without ambiguity: [paste your spec]"
Note what the AI added, clarified, or questioned in the specification.
Share the refined specification and estimate how much time a working version of this tool would save per week.

homework.title: Map your AI skill gap against the year ahead
homework.body: You're halfway through 2026. The AI landscape has moved significantly since January — new models, new capabilities, new workflows. This is a good moment to assess where you are and where you want to be by the end of the year.
homework.prompt: It's mid-July 2026. I want to assess my AI skill level and set a goal for December 2026. Here's how I currently use AI: [describe your current usage]. Here's my role: [describe your role]. Ask me five questions to understand my skill level, then give me: (1) an honest assessment of where I am relative to professionals in my field, (2) the three skills or habits that would most accelerate my development, and (3) a specific 90-day plan to get there.

2026-07-17.intro: Today's stories all point to the same shift: AI is maturing from a technology question into a management one — how you pay for it, how you feed it, and which human skills it makes more valuable, not less.

trends.title: The real AI budget question isn't the model, it's the cleanup
trends.body: A McKinsey report out today reframes how leaders should think about agent costs: <cite index="30-1">Agentic AI tasks can use nearly 1,000 times more tokens than conventional code reasoning or chat-based AI tasks, the report said, "Per-token pricing has stopped being a useful measure for what enterprises actually pay for gen AI."</cite> The bigger surprise is where the money actually goes: <cite index="30-9">about 60 per cent an agentic task's costs, in fact, are tied to refining answers</cite>, not generating them. As McKinsey put it, <cite index="30-5">the decision to scale an agent is increasingly becoming a complex and fast-changing economics decision, not a technical one</cite>.

slants.strategy: When you build the AI business case next quarter, budget for revision cycles and retries, not just a per-seat license fee.
slants.operations: Before approving a new agent workflow, ask how much of its cost sits in verification and rework — that's the number that actually predicts your bill.
slants.pm: Bake cost variance into your AI-enabled project plans, since the same task can price out differently depending on how many times the agent has to try again.
slants.admin: The more back-and-forth you do polishing an AI draft, the more it's actually costing behind the scenes — tighter first requests save real money.

steps: Pick one recurring task you already hand to an AI assistant, like a weekly status summary or a meeting recap.
Run it once with a single, specific request instead of your usual back-and-forth: "Draft this in its final, polished form in one attempt — don't wait for me to ask for revisions."
Compare that one-shot result to how many rounds of editing you'd normally do to get the same quality.
Notice which part of the task — the first draft or the endless tweaking — actually took the most effort. That's the expensive part, for you and for the AI.
Share in the group: which task got cheaper (and faster) when you asked for the finished version up front?

trends.title: Your AI pilots are ready to scale — your data isn't
trends.body: McKinsey's tech insights team flagged a quieter constraint behind all the agentic AI headlines: <cite index="4-1">As companies push their AI pilots to scale, data is emerging as a constraint. Leaders are prioritizing data readiness</cite> before adding more automation. Separate industry research backs this up — <cite index="16-18">nearly 60% of AI leaders say legacy integration is a primary adoption challenge when implementing advanced AI like agentic AI</cite>. Translation: the tool isn't the hard part anymore. Getting clean, connected information into it is.

slants.strategy: Add "data readiness" as its own line item in your AI roadmap — it now predicts scale-up success more than the model choice does.
slants.operations: Before rolling an AI pilot out wider, audit whether the systems feeding it are consistent, not just whether the pilot worked in a clean test environment.
slants.pm: Build a data-quality checkpoint into your AI project timeline; assume the integration work takes longer than the AI setup itself.
slants.admin: If an AI tool gives you a confusing or incomplete answer, the problem is often messy source data upstream, not the tool — flag it instead of just re-prompting.

steps: Pick one workflow where you already lean on an AI tool — a report, a dataset, a status doc.
Ask your company-approved AI tool: "List the top 3 places in this workflow where you had to guess, or where the information you received was inconsistent or incomplete."
Read the output and see if any of those gaps are things you already suspected but hadn't named.
Pick one gap and flag it to whoever owns that data or process — a five-minute heads-up now saves a bigger headache later.
Share in the group what surprised you most about where the messiness lives.

trends.title: AI is making junior jobs demand senior judgment
trends.body: PwC's newest global jobs analysis found a real divide opening up in how AI reshapes careers. <cite index="24-1">Analysis of US data shows AI-exposed entry-level roles are seven times more likely to require traditionally senior-level skills such as judgement and leadership. These roles grew 35% since 2019, while other entry-level roles declined by 10%</cite>. As the report put it, <cite index="24-6,24-7">the traditional relationship between experience and expertise is changing. AI is removing some of the routine work that once acted as an apprenticeship, while increasing demand for judgement, leadership and adaptability much earlier in careers</cite>.
