slants.strategy: Rethink your talent pipeline assumptions — the old model of "years in seat before judgment calls" is compressing fast, and your planning cycles should account for it.
slants.operations: Look for the operational tasks AI has already absorbed on your team, then build in earlier, structured chances for junior staff to practice the judgment calls that remain.
slants.pm: When staffing projects, weigh a junior team member's decision-making instincts as heavily as their tool proficiency — that's the skill AI isn't replacing.
slants.admin: The routine parts of your role that AI now handles free up time for the parts that actually build your reputation: judgment, discretion, and knowing what matters.

steps: Pick one task in your role that AI now does quickly for you — drafting, summarizing, formatting, scheduling.
Ask your company-approved AI tool: "Given that AI now handles this task quickly, what judgment or leadership skill becomes more valuable for me to strengthen next?"
Read the suggestion and think of one real moment this week where that skill would have mattered.
Write down one small way to practice that skill in the next two weeks.
Share in the group what skill came up — you might spot a pattern across the team.

homework.title: Let AI plan your next weekend getaway
homework.body: Pick a free tool — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity — and use it to plan a short trip or day out you've been meaning to take. This time, instead of giving it all the details up front, make it work for the answer.
homework.prompt: Try this: "I want to plan a weekend trip but haven't picked a destination. Before you suggest anything, ask me questions one at a time about my budget, interests, and how much driving or flying I'm willing to do. Then give me your top 3 ranked recommendations with a one-line reason for each." Notice how asking it to question you first — instead of dumping everything at once — gets you a sharper, more personal answer.

2026-07-18.intro: Today's drop is about where AI decisions actually get made: which workflows leadership funds, which tools employees quietly reach for anyway, and which skills your team needs to protect on purpose.

trends.title: Companies are done crowdsourcing AI pilots — and starting to pick winners
trends.body: PwC's 2026 predictions call out a pattern most large companies fell into: letting every team run its own AI experiment and hoping something sticks. <cite index="41-6">Crowdsourcing AI efforts can create impressive adoption numbers, but it seldom produces meaningful business outcomes.</cite> The shift now is toward a smaller, sharper approach where <cite index="41-1,41-2">senior leadership picks the spots for focused AI investments, looking for a few key workflows or business processes where payoffs from AI can be big</cite> (PwC, 2026).

slants.strategy: This is your job now — picking the two or three workflows worth a real AI bet, and building the business case for why the rest wait.
slants.operations: Expect fewer scattered pilots landing on your desk and more concentrated, well-resourced rollouts with a clear ROI target attached.
slants.pm: You'll likely run one deep AI project instead of five shallow ones — plan for more scrutiny and higher stakes on the project you do get.
slants.admin: The 'try whatever tool you like' era may be winding down as your org standardizes around a chosen few — get familiar with the frontrunners early.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool.
Prompt it: "List the 3 recurring tasks on my team that eat the most time each week and have the clearest, most measurable outcome."
Pick the one that feels most winnable — not the flashiest, the most measurable.
Follow up with: "Write a 3-sentence pitch for why this task should be our team's one focused AI project this quarter."
Read the pitch, tighten anything that sounds off, and share it in the group.

trends.title: Employees trust their own AI judgment more than their company's rules
trends.body: A 2026 PagerDuty survey of 1,250 office professionals found <cite index="21-8">two-thirds (66%) of workers who have used AI say they did so even though they believed it was not permitted under company policy</cite>. Even more striking: <cite index="21-1">a majority of office professionals (72%) believe they understand how to use AI for their job better than the team responsible for managing AI at their company</cite> (PagerDuty, June 2026).

slants.strategy: If two-thirds of your workforce is quietly using unapproved tools, your AI budget conversations are missing a huge piece of real usage data.
slants.operations: The workflow shortcuts your team found using personal AI tools are free signal — they show exactly where the approved tools fall short.
slants.pm: If your project plans assume everyone sticks to sanctioned tools only, you may be underestimating both your team's real capacity and its real risk.
slants.admin: Whatever time you're quietly saving with a personal AI tool is worth surfacing to your manager or IT — better to name it than hide it.

steps: Jot down 2-3 AI tools you personally use for work tasks, whether officially approved or not.
Open your company-approved AI tool and prompt: "Here are tasks I do weekly: [list your tasks]. Which of these could I realistically move to an approved tool instead of a personal one?"
Read the suggestions honestly — don't dismiss them just because switching feels inconvenient.
Note one task where you'd still reach for another tool, and ask yourself if that's a real capability gap or just habit.
Share your honest answer in the group — this works best when people are candid, not defensive.

trends.title: Half of executives already see their teams' thinking skills slipping
trends.body: BCG's June 2026 research names a real organizational risk: <cite index="31-20">in a global study of 70 C-suite leaders and senior executives across multiple industries, we found that half are already observing de-skilling in their organizations, and more than 60% believe that de-skilling will pose a material threat within the next three to five years.</cite> One fix already in motion: <cite index="31-1">at CNIL, France's data protection authority, managers are responsible for assessing employees' ability to challenge AI outputs — not just to use them</cite>, making that judgment a visible, evaluated part of the job.

slants.strategy: Build skill-preservation checkpoints into your AI rollout plans now — the gap shows up later as a bad forecast nobody caught in time.
slants.operations: Map which of your processes now depend so heavily on AI that no one on the team could run them manually if the system went down.
slants.pm: Add a human-only checkpoint to at least one project phase per cycle so your team's judgment gets exercised, not just outsourced.
slants.admin: Keep practicing your own drafting and proofreading instincts on at least a few tasks a week — don't let AI polish become your only quality check.

steps: Pick one recurring task you now complete almost entirely with AI help.
Do it once this week without AI, and time yourself.
Open your company-approved AI tool and prompt: "Ask me questions before answering: help me spot 2 judgment calls in [describe the task] where I should double-check an AI's output before trusting it."
Compare your unaided attempt to the AI's usual output — note where your instincts were sharper or shakier than you expected.
Share one honest takeaway in the group.

homework.title: Plan a weekend getaway without doing all the legwork yourself
homework.body: Pick a place you've been meaning to visit and use ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity to help you plan it — but make the tool work for the details, not just hand you a generic list.
homework.prompt: Try this: "I want to plan a 2-day trip to [destination] on a budget of [amount]. Before you suggest anything, ask me questions about my travel style, food preferences, and pace so your plan actually fits me." Notice how the questions the AI asks change the quality of what it gives you back — that's the habit worth keeping for bigger prompts later.

2026-07-19.intro: Today's throughline: as agentic AI moves from pitch deck to production, the winners are the ones who can tell real capability from relabeled automation, spot where agents are quietly touching routine buying decisions, and close the training gap before confidence collapses.

trends.title: Not every 'AI agent' is actually an agent — Gartner says stop assuming otherwise
trends.body: Gartner is telling planning leaders to stop taking agentic AI pitches at face value. At its Supply Chain Symposium, the firm warned that hype and "agent washing" are creating real risks for organizations under pressure to deliver results, and separately estimates that of the thousands of vendors now claiming agentic AI capability, only about 130 are building genuinely autonomous systems (Gartner, May 2026).

slants.strategy: Before you greenlight budget for an 'agentic' platform, require the vendor to show what it does that scripted automation couldn't already do.
slants.operations: Run any pilot on your messiest, most unpredictable real cases — not the vendor's clean demo — to see if it's a true agent or automation in a costume.
slants.pm: Add a vendor-evaluation checkpoint to your intake process so 'agentic' claims get tested against project requirements, not just marketing language.
slants.admin: When you're helping schedule or scope a new tool demo, ask the presenter directly what happens when the system hits something it's never seen before.

steps: Pick one AI tool or 'agentic' feature your team currently uses or is evaluating.

Open your company-approved AI assistant and ask it: "I'm evaluating a tool marketed as an 'AI agent' for [type of task]. Give me 5 specific questions I should ask the vendor to tell whether this is genuinely autonomous versus repackaged automation."
Compare the answers against what you already know about the tool and flag any gaps.
Share your checklist in the group so teammates can reuse it before their next vendor call.

trends.title: AI agents are quietly starting to do your reordering, renewing, and invoice-paying
trends.body: Away from the consumer shopping headlines, enterprise-side agents are already handling real recurring work: enterprise-side agents (Microsoft Copilot, Salesforce Agentforce, custom internal agents) reorder office supplies, renew SaaS subscriptions, and pay invoices on behalf of a company. The consumer version of this is moving more cautiously — OpenAI recently paused its Instant Checkout feature, a signal that even the biggest players think the infrastructure and trust layers aren't fully ready yet.

slants.strategy: Get ahead of spend visibility now — if agents start making micro-purchasing decisions, your forecasting model needs a line item for it.
slants.operations: Audit your recurring purchase and renewal workflows to identify which ones are low-risk enough to delegate to an agent with human approval built in.
slants.pm: Treat a first agentic-procurement pilot like any other project: define scope, approval checkpoints, and a rollback plan before it touches real spend.
slants.admin: You're well-positioned to own this shift — start learning how approval workflows for agent-initiated purchases actually work, since someone will need to monitor them.

steps: List three recurring purchase or renewal tasks your team handles manually (software renewals, supply reorders, invoice approvals).

Ask your company-approved AI assistant: "Here are three recurring purchasing tasks on my team: [list them]. Which, if any, would be safe to delegate to an AI agent with human approval built in, and what guardrails should I put in place first?"
Pick the safest candidate and sketch what a one-step human approval checkpoint would look like.
Share your idea in the group chat.

trends.title: Companies are training their leaders on AI — and leaving everyone else to figure it out alone
trends.body: New research is putting a number on something a lot of people feel but rarely see measured: 78% of organizational decision-makers feel confident using AI at work, versus just 43% of the workers below them. The report also finds that 36% of employees report self-teaching as their primary route to AI skills, compared to just 23% who received any formal employer training (TrustedTech, July 2026).

slants.strategy: Build training investment into the AI roadmap itself, not as an afterthought — the confidence gap is a business risk, not just an HR issue.
slants.operations: Identify which frontline teams are navigating AI tools alone and pair them with structured guidance instead of assuming they'll self-teach.
slants.pm: Add an AI-literacy check-in to project kickoffs so every team member — not just the lead — has a baseline before the work starts.
slants.admin: If formal training hasn't reached you yet, don't wait — a short, structured self-practice routine can close a lot of that gap on your own timeline.

steps: Think of one AI skill you've picked up mostly on your own, with little or no formal training.

Ask your company-approved AI assistant: "Act as a mentor helping me get better at using AI at work. Ask me three questions about how I currently use AI tools, then give me a simple two-week practice plan to build one specific skill."
Try one of the suggested exercises today.
Share your two-week plan in the group and invite a teammate to try it alongside you.

homework.title: Let AI plan your next low-key weekend — but make it ask you first
homework.body: This one's just for you: pick a free tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity) and use it to plan a small weekend trip or day trip, but with a twist — you're going to make it interview you before it gives any answers.
homework.prompt: "I want to plan a low-key weekend trip within driving distance. Before you suggest anything, ask me at least five questions about my budget, interests, and who's coming — then give me three ranked options with a one-line reason for each."

2026-07-26.intro: Today's three stories all land on the same idea from different directions: the real AI advantage goes to people who rethink how work gets done, not just the ones who click generate.

trends.title: Adopting AI isn't the same as redesigning around it
trends.body: McKinsey's newest global survey makes the value gap explicit: companies that redesigned workflows were 5.3 times more likely to report enterprise value capture than those that just layered AI onto the old process. Yet only 11% of business leaders say their organization has actually reached that redesign stage — most are still stuck handing out tools and hoping.

slants.strategy: This is your opening to make workflow redesign — not tool selection — the actual agenda item in AI planning conversations.
slants.operations: Audit one standard operating procedure this quarter for steps that could be rebuilt around AI entirely, not just sped up.
slants.pm: Add 'workflow redesign' as a real deliverable in your next AI-related project charter, separate from the tool rollout itself.
slants.admin: Notice the routing and scheduling tasks you do the same way every time — those are exactly the steps ripe for a redesign conversation.

steps: Pick one process you touch weekly, like status reporting, budget rollups, or intake requests.

Open your company-approved AI tool and ask: "Here's how this process works today: [describe the steps in a few sentences]. Which of these steps could be redesigned around AI instead of just assisted by it?"
Read the response and circle one step it flagged that you hadn't considered changing.
Write a one-line note on what would need to change to make that happen — a rule, an approval, a habit.
Share your one-line idea in the group.

trends.title: Meeting notes just became AI's biggest foot in the door
trends.body: Three out of four professionals now use an AI note-taker in their work meetings, making meeting capture the single largest entry point for AI in the enterprise. But adoption drops sharply at the top — large companies with 5,000+ employees sit at just 43%, versus 78-81% at small businesses, and the holdup isn't the technology at all — it's procurement, legal review, and shadow-app risk.

slants.strategy: If your org is one of the laggards, the fix isn't a better tool — it's a faster, clearer governance policy so teams stop going around IT.
slants.operations: Pilot connecting notetaker output directly into your existing trackers so action items stop requiring manual re-entry.
slants.pm: Structured meeting output can auto-populate your status reports — worth testing before you write another recap by hand.
slants.admin: Your role shifts from writing the minutes to reviewing the AI's draft and catching what it missed — a faster, still essential job.

steps: Grab a recent meeting recap you wrote yourself — a general summary is fine, nothing confidential.
Paste it into your company-approved AI tool and ask: "Turn this into three sections: decisions made, who owns what, and open questions."
Compare the structured output to your original notes — what did it catch that you didn't?
Decide if this format could replace how you write meeting recaps going forward.
Share your before-and-after in the group.

trends.title: The new cost of AI shortcuts has a name: knowledge decay
trends.body: A June 2026 Harvard Business Review essay names the organization-level version of AI's quality problem: polished-but-empty AI output that quietly degrades the accuracy of everything built on top of it. The research behind it found 40% of workers had received this so-called 'workslop' in a single month, with each incident costing close to two hours to sort out.

slants.strategy: Build a quality checkpoint into any workflow where AI output becomes the record other teams rely on — before it becomes the record.
slants.operations: Track rework hours alongside AI usage stats; that hidden time is where your productivity gains are quietly disappearing.
slants.pm: Bake review time into your timeline for AI-assisted deliverables instead of assuming 'AI-generated' means 'done.'
slants.admin: If something crosses your desk that reads polished but says nothing, flag it back to the sender instead of quietly fixing it yourself.

steps: Find a recent AI-assisted piece of work you or a teammate produced — a report, email, or deck section.
Ask your AI tool: "Review this like a skeptical reader — where does it sound confident but actually say very little?"
Mark the spots it flags as filler.
Rewrite just one of those spots with a concrete detail, number, or example.
Share the before-and-after in the group.

homework.title: Let AI plan your next weekend getaway — properly this time
homework.body: Pick a place you've been wanting to visit, even just for a weekend, and let ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity help you plan it. This week's technique: make the AI ask you questions before it gives you a plan, so the result actually fits your budget, pace, and mood instead of a generic itinerary.
homework.prompt: I want to plan a weekend trip to [destination, or 'somewhere new within driving distance']. Before you suggest anything, ask me 5 questions about my budget, pace, food preferences, and what kind of weekend I actually need right now. Then give me two different itinerary options based on my answers.

2026-07-27.intro: Today's throughline: the money, the tools, and the people around AI are all quietly renegotiating the same question — is this actually working, or does it just look like it is?

trends.title: AI spending jumped 63% — now it has to prove itself
trends.body: Worldwide spending on AI models and platforms is projected to hit $64 billion in 2026, up 63.4% year over year, but Gartner says the easy-money phase is ending. Enterprise AI budgets are coming under greater scrutiny, with increased focus on usage efficiency, cost control and measurable outcomes, and dollars are moving toward vendors who can prove their tools actually deliver (Gartner, July 2026).

slants.strategy: When you build the business case for the next AI tool, lead with a measurable before/after number, not a feature list — that's what budget owners are asking for now.
slants.operations: Expect renewals and procurement reviews to start asking for usage data and cost-per-task math instead of just a signed contract.
slants.pm: Build a simple 'did it work' checkpoint into any project that adopts a new AI tool, so you have evidence ready when someone asks if it earned its keep.
slants.admin: If you're requesting a new AI tool or license, bring one concrete example of time it would save you — that framing lands better than 'everyone else has it.'

steps: Pick one task you already do with your company-approved AI tool at least weekly.

Do the task once with the tool, timing yourself, then ask it: "Help me write a two-sentence summary comparing how long this task used to take me manually versus using you, in language I could show my manager."
Read the output and edit anything that overstates the benefit — accuracy builds more trust than enthusiasm.
Share your before/after summary in the group chat so others can borrow the framing.

trends.title: One AI helper is becoming a small team of them
trends.body: Forrester and Gartner both point to 2026 as the year multi-agent setups — where several specialized AI agents split up a task and hand off work to each other — become the norm instead of a single all-purpose assistant handling everything alone. Anthropic's own research found its multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on complex research tasks, but the company is also candid that this only pays off for the right kind of work.

slants.strategy: Start mapping which of your team's multi-step processes have natural 'handoff points' — those are exactly where a coordinated agent workflow could replace several separate tool requests.
slants.operations: Document your process handoffs clearly and in order; that sequence is the blueprint an orchestrated AI workflow will eventually follow.
slants.pm: Think of upcoming AI tooling less like one assistant and more like a small subcontractor team — assign clear swim lanes the same way you would to human contributors.
slants.admin: Watch for scheduling, inbox triage, and follow-ups to start moving through one connected system instead of separate one-off AI requests — knowing the handoff order will make you the person who understands how it works.

steps: Pick one process at work that currently requires you to hand information from one step to another (like drafting something, then reviewing it, then sending it).

Describe that process in general terms to your company-approved AI tool and ask: "If two AI agents were working together on this instead of me doing every step, how would you split the work between them?"
Compare its suggested split to how you actually do it today — note anywhere it caught a handoff you hadn't thought about.
Share the split it proposed in the group chat, especially if it surprised you.

trends.title: Employees are already building their own AI workaround
trends.body: A Gartner survey of over 12,000 employees found 88% of employees with enterprise AI access also use personal AI tools for business tasks, often because the sanctioned tool is clunkier or slower than the one on their phone. Only 27% of executives say they have a comprehensive AI strategy, which is part of why Gartner predicts half of companies without one will lose their best AI talent to competitors by 2027 (Gartner, May 2026).

slants.strategy: If people on your team are quietly using personal AI tools instead of the company one, treat that as free user-experience feedback and route it to whoever owns your AI roadmap.
slants.operations: Audit whether your approved tool is actually easy to open and use inside daily workflows — friction, not policy gaps, is usually what drives people to their own apps.
slants.pm: Check in with your project team about whether the sanctioned AI tool fits their day-to-day tasks; a tool nobody opens doesn't show up as a risk until it's already a habit.
slants.admin: If you've caught yourself reaching for a personal chatbot instead of the work-approved one, that's useful information — mention it to your manager instead of just working around it quietly.

steps: Think honestly about whether you've used a personal AI app for a work task in the last month, even something small.
If so, ask any AI assistant: "I use [personal AI tool] instead of my company's approved AI tool for [task]. What are three reasons that might be happening, and what would fix each one?"
Pick the reason that feels most true and jot it down in one sentence.
Share that one sentence in the group — patterns across the team are worth more than any single answer.

homework.title: Let AI plan something just for you this week
homework.body: Pick something personal you've been putting off — planning a trip, meal-prepping a week of dinners, or drafting a tough text to a friend — and try it in ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity, all free to use.
homework.prompt: Before you tell it what to do, try this prompting technique: "I want your help with [your personal task]. Before you give me any suggestions, ask me 5 questions to understand my situation better." Answer its questions, then see how much sharper its actual suggestions get compared to just asking it directly.

2026-07-28.intro: Tuesday. Momentum keeps building: assistants that handle busywork on their own, faster models doing more per dollar, and fresh data showing AI is becoming a normal part of how you work.

trends.title: Your assistant can now handle the busywork itself
trends.body: A new kind of assistant just arrived: Microsoft's Autopilots, led by an agent called Scout, quietly handle scheduling, prep, and deadline tracking across your everyday apps without waiting to be asked. It's early proof of a shift that's working in your favor — 39% of employees already report noticeable productivity gains from AI over the past year (DHR Global), and hands-free help only widens that lead.

slants.strategy: Agents that act on their own turn AI from a tool your team opens into help that's always running, so leaders who map out where hands-free support fits will pull ahead first.
slants.leaders: The shift to hands-free coordination changes what you delegate — not just to people, but to systems. Leaders who define now which decisions stay human and which get handed to agents will set the pace before the default gets set for them.
slants.operations: Let an assistant own the repetitive coordination — scheduling, reminders, follow-ups — and you reclaim hours for the higher-value work that actually needs you.
slants.pm: An agent tracking deadlines and prep in the background means fewer status chases and more room for you to steer the work, expanding what one person can shepherd.
slants.admin: When an assistant handles the calendar-wrangling and document prep, you're free to focus on the judgment calls and relationships that make your support irreplaceable.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and list the three recurring coordination tasks that eat the most of your week.
Paste this prompt: "Here are three recurring tasks I handle every week: [list them]. For each, describe how an AI assistant could take the first pass so I only review and approve."
Pick the task with the clearest, most repeatable steps and try handing its first draft to AI today.
Paste this follow-up: "Turn the best approach into a simple checklist I can reuse each week to run this task with AI."
Share with the group the one recurring task you'd most like to hand off to an assistant.

trends.title: A faster model that does more per dollar
trends.body: The models behind your daily tools keep getting leaner and quicker. Google's new Gemini 3.6 Flash runs 17% more token-efficient than the version it replaces, with computer-use built in (Google), meaning faster answers and more capability for the same spend. When the engine improves, everything you build on top of it gets easier.

slants.strategy: More capability per dollar means the experiments you shelved as too costly are suddenly worth revisiting, so leaders who reassess now capture the upside early.
slants.leaders: Efficiency gains in the underlying models translate directly into budget flexibility and faster iteration cycles. Revisit AI investments you shelved on cost or speed grounds — the economics have shifted enough to reopen the conversation.
slants.operations: A faster, cheaper model means the AI steps in your workflow run quicker and stretch further, letting you automate more of the day without a bigger budget.
slants.pm: Leaner models let you fold AI into more parts of a project without the cost conversation, simplifying work that used to need extra hands.
slants.admin: Quicker, more affordable AI makes the drafting and organizing you do faster and easier to justify, keeping you at the front of every new capability.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and pick one task where speed matters most in your day.
Paste this prompt: "I want to speed up this task: [describe it]. Show me the fastest way to get a strong first result, and what details to give you up front."
Run the task with the AI's suggested approach and time how long it takes compared to your usual way.
Paste this follow-up: "Now make this repeatable: give me a short prompt template I can reuse to get this result every time."
Share with the group the task where AI saved you the most time this week.

trends.title: AI skills are quickly becoming everyday skills
trends.body: Using AI at work is shifting from novelty to norm, and getting comfortable now puts you ahead of the curve. A new SHRM survey of nearly 5,900 U.S. workers finds 41% already use AI for their jobs (SHRM), climbing sharply as the tools land in more roles. The people who build the habit early become the ones everyone else turns to.

slants.strategy: As AI fluency becomes a baseline expectation, leaders who help their teams build it now turn a rising tide into a genuine competitive advantage.
slants.leaders: With 41% of workers already using AI daily, the leadership question has shifted from adoption to direction. The teams with an advantage aren't just using AI — they have someone setting standards for how.
slants.operations: Every bit of AI skill you build compounds, making the workflows you own smoother and marking you as the person who knows how to get results.
slants.pm: As more of your team adopts AI, coordinating how it's used well becomes a natural extension of your role — and a highly visible one.
slants.admin: Being early and fluent with AI positions you as the go-to resource in your office, turning a growing trend into real visibility for your value.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and think about one skill you'd like to be known for on your team.
Paste this prompt: "I want to get noticeably better at using AI for [name the skill or task]. Give me a simple week-long practice plan with one small exercise per day."
Do today's exercise and save the result somewhere you can revisit it.
Paste this follow-up: "Based on how that went, suggest one way I could share what I learned with a colleague this week."
Share with the group one AI skill you're committing to building this week.

homework.title: Turn a pile of leftovers into dinner
homework.body: This practices role prompting: you assign the AI a specific persona so its answer comes back sharper and more useful than a generic reply. Giving it a role focuses its expertise on exactly what you need.
homework.prompt: Act as a resourceful home cook who hates food waste. Suggest three simple dinners I can make tonight using only what I already have, with quick steps for each. Here's what's in my fridge and pantry: [paste your ingredients here].

2026-07-29.intro: Today's stories all point to the same shift: AI is redrawing the org chart, exposing the gap between deploying a tool and actually getting value from it, and turning the job search itself into an AI-versus-AI contest.

trends.title: The layer between strategy and execution is getting thinner
trends.body: <cite index="1-2">Gartner projects that by the end of 2026, 1 in 5 organizations will eliminate more than half of their middle management positions</cite>, and <cite index="2-1">AI has given companies the justification to cut back, and middle management is feeling the squeeze</cite> (Newsweek, July 2026). The roles surviving the cut aren't the ones relaying status updates — they're the ones translating strategy into decisions and coaching people through change, since <cite index="2-8">McKinsey's November 2025 report found demand for AI fluency grew sevenfold in job postings between 2023 and 2025</cite>.

slants.strategy: This is your cue to model workforce and succession plans around fewer layers now, before a reorg forces the redesign on someone else's timeline.
slants.leaders: This is your cue to model workforce and succession plans around fewer layers now, before a reorg forces the redesign on someone else's timeline.
slants.operations: Coordination work that used to sit with a manager is landing on ops teams directly, so build the handoffs before the layer disappears.
slants.pm: With fewer middle managers to translate priorities, PMs are becoming the de facto bridge between leadership intent and team execution — worth naming out loud in your next status update.
slants.admin: The tasks most at risk are scheduling, reporting, and status relay, so the fastest way to stay essential is to own the judgment calls those tasks used to hide.

steps: Look at your last week's calendar and tag each meeting or task as either 'coordination/reporting' or 'judgment/decision-making.'
Pick one recurring coordination task — like a status update or scheduling thread — and open your company-approved AI tool.
Use this prompt: "Draft a reusable template for a weekly status update that highlights blockers, decisions needed, and next steps, based on a project with [general topic, no confidential details]."
Review the draft and adjust it to match how your team actually communicates.
Share the template in the group and ask who else wants to reclaim time from status reporting.

trends.title: Companies deployed the AI. Most still haven't unlocked it.
trends.body: A new global survey of 639 enterprise AI leaders found that <cite index="11-3">the share of enterprises whose ROI fails to outpace their investment has held at 57% since 2025, even as enterprise AI production capability continues to climb</cite> (Domino Data Lab, July 2026). The report calls this a <cite index="13-4">last-mile gap between AI models in production and the business users who need to unlock their value</cite> — the tools are live, but most people never got shown how to use them.

slants.strategy: Deployment metrics look great in a board deck, but the real KPI is adoption — push for that number in every AI initiative review.
slants.leaders: Deployment metrics look great in a board deck, but the real KPI is adoption — push for that number in every AI initiative review.
slants.operations: The last-mile gap is an enablement problem, which means ops teams that build simple training loops will out-earn teams that just wait for usage to happen.
slants.pm: Add 'adoption rate 30 days post-launch' as a real project milestone instead of letting 'go-live' count as done.
slants.admin: You likely already have access to a tool nobody walked you through — closing that gap for yourself is a fast, personal win this week.

steps: Pick one AI tool your company already licenses that you haven't fully explored.
Choose one task you do weekly that feels tedious — sorting, summarizing, or drafting.
Use this prompt: "Walk me through how to use this tool for [task type], step by step, as if I've never tried it before."
Try the workflow once on a real (non-confidential) task and time how long it takes versus doing it manually.
Share what you learned in the group so someone else can skip the trial-and-error.

trends.title: Hiring just became AI arguing with AI
trends.body: <cite index="24-4">HireVue's 2026 report noted that almost three in four candidates now use AI to create resumes</cite>, and companies have responded with their own screening tools — yet <cite index="24-7">only a mere 41% of hiring teams fully trust AI</cite> (Forbes, July 2026). Both sides are automating the same funnel, which means the humans who show real specificity are the ones actually getting through.

slants.strategy: Workforce planning now has to account for a hiring funnel that's noisier and slower even though it's more automated — factor that into headcount timelines.
slants.leaders: Workforce planning now has to account for a hiring funnel that's noisier and slower even though it's more automated — factor that into headcount timelines.
slants.operations: Time-to-hire is stretching despite more AI in the process, so it's worth auditing whether your screening stack is actually filtering or just adding steps.
slants.pm: When staffing a project team fast, remember that a polished AI-written resume tells you less than one specific, verifiable example of past work.
slants.admin: If you coordinate interviews or first-pass resume review, a quick verification step — one direct follow-up question — catches more than another filter ever will.

steps: Open a document with your own resume or LinkedIn summary — something personal, not a company file.
Paste one or two bullet points into your company-approved AI tool or any AI assistant.
Use this prompt: "Review this resume bullet and tell me if it reads like generic AI filler. Then suggest a version with one specific, concrete detail only I could know."
Compare the two versions and pick the one that sounds like an actual person did the work.
Share your before-and-after in the group — it's a fun way to spot the difference together.

homework.title: Let AI plan something you've been putting off
homework.body: Pick a personal project you keep meaning to start — a trip, a big cooking project, or a tricky message you need to send someone. Use ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity, all free, and try a technique that makes AI far more useful: asking it to interview you before it gives you an answer.
homework.prompt: "I want your help with [your personal project]. Before you give me any suggestions, ask me five questions to understand what I actually need and what constraints I'm working with. Then give me your recommendation."

2026-07-31.intro: Today's throughline: the gap between what leaders believe about AI and what they've actually built for it, whether that's office space, your calendar, or your next brainstorm.

trends.title: Leaders bet on AI growing headcount, not cutting it
trends.body: A new JLL survey of over 2,200 C-suite and real estate leaders found 60% expect their workforces to grow, not shrink, because of AI, with the most AI-advanced organizations actually hiring more full-time staff and entry-level talent. But there's a catch: only 31% are actively preparing spaces and systems for human-AI collaboration, even though 78% expect AI to reshape their real estate strategy (JLL, July 2026).

slants.strategy: If your workforce plan assumes growth but your operating model hasn't changed, you're planning for a future you haven't actually built yet.
slants.leaders: If your workforce plan assumes growth but your operating model hasn't changed, you're planning for a future you haven't actually built yet.
slants.operations: Optimism about AI headcount doesn't fix the process gaps — 36% of leaders still cite skills gaps as the top barrier to making it real.
slants.pm: Build "redesign the workflow" into your project charter, not just "roll out the tool," or you'll hit this same execution gap mid-project.
slants.admin: You may be the first to notice when scheduling, space, or supply systems haven't caught up to leadership's AI ambitions — flag it early.

steps: Pick one task or process on your team that already uses AI in some form.

Open your company-approved AI tool and ask: "Here's a task I do with AI: [describe it]. What would need to change in my role, process, or team setup for this to actually work better — not just faster?"
Read the suggestions and circle one you could realistically try this month.
Share that one idea in the group, with a note on whether you'll test it.

trends.title: AI saves you time, then quietly asks for some of it back
trends.body: Glean's Work AI Institute surveyed 6,000 digital workers and found 87% use AI at work and say it saves 11 hours a week — but only 13% say their organization is actually performing better because of it. The reason: workers spend an average of 6.4 hours a week "botsitting" — feeding AI context, checking its output, and cleaning up mistakes (Glean Work AI Institute, June 2026).

slants.strategy: When you build the business case for AI ROI, count the babysitting hours, not just the adoption rate — that's where the real return lives or dies.
slants.leaders: When you build the business case for AI ROI, count the babysitting hours, not just the adoption rate — that's where the real return lives or dies.
slants.operations: Treat AI output review as a formal step in your process, not an invisible extra task nobody accounts for.
slants.pm: Add a line item for verification and cleanup time when you estimate how long an AI-assisted task will actually take.
slants.admin: If you're switching between several AI tools daily, the context you re-explain each time is exactly the hidden labor this report is describing.

steps: For one workday, jot down every time you have to fix, recheck, or re-explain something to AI.
At day's end, add up roughly how many minutes that took.
Ask your company-approved AI tool: "Here's a list of things I had to redo or fix after using you today: [list]. What's one change to how I prompt you that would cut this cleanup time?"
Try the suggestion tomorrow and see if the list gets shorter.
Share your before-and-after time in the group.

trends.title: Your brainstorm needs a head start before AI joins it
trends.body: A new MIT Sloan Management Review synthesis of four separate studies found that AI assistance consistently improved individual output quality but narrowed the collective diversity of ideas across groups, from short stories to circular-economy solutions. The fix researchers identified is simple: having people generate their own ideas first, then bring in AI, preserves nearly as much variety as fully human brainstorming (MIT Sloan Management Review, July 2026).

slants.strategy: For scenario planning or options analysis, generate your own list before opening AI, or every plan across the org starts converging on the same few ideas.
slants.leaders: For scenario planning or options analysis, generate your own list before opening AI, or every plan across the org starts converging on the same few ideas.
slants.operations: Process-improvement workshops should start with a human-only round of ideas before anyone opens a chatbot.
slants.pm: Risk registers and mitigation plans benefit from this too — brainstorm your own risks first so AI expands the list instead of narrowing it.
slants.admin: Even something like event themes or agenda ideas gets better when you scribble your own three options before asking AI for more.

steps: Next time you need fresh ideas for anything — a plan, a process, an agenda — spend 5 minutes writing your own list first, no AI involved.
Then ask your company-approved AI tool: "Here are my initial ideas: [list them]. Give me 5 more that are genuinely different from these, not just variations."
Compare the two lists and notice how many of AI's ideas overlap with yours versus how many are new.
Share which round — yours or AI's — produced your best idea.

homework.title: Let AI plan your next weekend off — but make it interview you first
homework.body: Pick a free tool — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity — and use it to plan a low-key weekend getaway or a day trip you'd actually enjoy. The trick is a prompting technique called "ask me questions first," where you make the AI gather information before it gives advice, so you get an itinerary that fits you instead of a generic list.
homework.prompt: I want to plan a relaxing weekend trip within 3 hours of where I live. Before you suggest anything, ask me 5 questions about my budget, interests, and energy level. Then give me 3 ranked options based on my answers.

2026-08-01.intro: Today's stories are about three different kinds of accounting: what your AI spend actually buys you, what AI quietly takes off your plate, and what you owe your future leaders if you skip the entry-level rungs on the way there.

trends.title: AI spend just became a forecasting problem, not a shopping list
trends.body: As companies move from simple copilots to full agentic workflows, McKinsey finds that organizations with high forecasting maturity save 10 percent more on AI spend than their peers on average, yet most haven't built that muscle yet — only 20–25 percent of companies have mature AI FinOps practices in place (McKinsey, July 2026). Guessing at AI usage the way teams used to guess at cloud bills is starting to cost real money.

slants.strategy: Build AI demand forecasting into your next planning cycle the same way you'd forecast headcount or capital spend — it's now a strategy input, not an IT afterthought.
slants.leaders: Build AI demand forecasting into your next planning cycle the same way you'd forecast headcount or capital spend — it's now a strategy input, not an IT afterthought.
slants.operations: Track which processes are actually driving AI usage and cost so you can flag runaway spend before finance does.
slants.pm: Add a line for AI tool usage to your project budgets — assuming it's free or negligible is how projects quietly overrun.
slants.admin: If you manage software licenses or expense approvals, expect more questions about which AI tools are actually earning their keep.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and pull up your calendar or task list from the past week.
List every task where you used AI — drafting, summarizing, research, formatting, etc.
Ask it: "Here's a list of tasks I used AI for this week. Which ones likely delivered the most time savings, and which ones probably weren't worth the effort? Help me spot the pattern."
Compare the answer to your own gut sense — does it match where you actually felt AI helped most?
Share in the group: one task where AI clearly paid off, and one where it didn't.

trends.title: Your CRM notes just got an AI co-writer
trends.body: Microsoft's Sales Agent and Service Agent are now generally available inside Microsoft 365 Copilot, Outlook, Teams, and Dynamics 365 (CX Today, July 2026), letting sellers capture key takeaways, objections, priorities, and follow-up commitments, then add those notes to CRM or update opportunity fields without breaking their flow. It's a real signal of where enterprise tooling is headed: less switching between apps, more AI quietly doing the paperwork inside the tools you already use.

slants.strategy: Watch this as a preview of what 'AI embedded in the flow of work' will look like for planning and reporting tools, not just sales and service.
slants.leaders: Watch this as a preview of what 'AI embedded in the flow of work' will look like for planning and reporting tools, not just sales and service.
slants.operations: Service teams get automatic case context and history at the start of the day instead of digging for it — that's hours back for actual problem-solving.
slants.pm: If your projects touch CRM data, expect status updates and stakeholder notes to arrive more current and less stale, since reps are logging them in real time.
slants.admin: Some of the meeting-recap and data-entry work you currently own may start showing up pre-drafted — your value shifts to catching what the AI missed.

steps: Pick one recurring task in your week that feels like pure busywork — updating a tracker, compiling a status recap, logging notes after a call.
Open your company-approved AI tool and describe the task in detail.

Ask: "Here's a recurring task I do every week: [describe it]. Draft a simple way I could hand the first pass of this to an AI assistant, and tell me exactly where a human still needs to check the work."
Read the output and mark which steps you'd actually trust an AI tool with today versus which need your eyes.
Share your one biggest hand-off opportunity in the group.

trends.title: Cutting entry-level jobs quietly borrows against your future leaders
trends.body: A widely discussed HBR piece this summer names a cost most companies haven't put on a spreadsheet: the entry-level job pipeline is thinning globally, and the consequences of eliminating these types of roles in favor of AI are compounding (Harvard Business Review, June 2026). The logic is blunt — eliminate entry-level roles, and you reduce the headcount that justifies mid-level managers; reduce mid-level managers, and you shrink the pool feeding director and VP pipelines, a bill that won't come due for years.

slants.strategy: Factor 'leadership pipeline health' into any workforce plan that leans on automating junior work — it's a multi-year risk, not a quarterly savings line.
slants.leaders: Factor 'leadership pipeline health' into any workforce plan that leans on automating junior work — it's a multi-year risk, not a quarterly savings line.
slants.operations: If AI is absorbing the routine tasks juniors used to learn on, build a deliberate way for them to still get hands-on reps — don't let training happen by accident.
slants.pm: Look for ways to give junior team members real ownership on a project phase instead of only having them review AI-generated drafts.
slants.admin: If you're early in your career, seek out stretch assignments now — the traditional 'learn by doing the grunt work' path is narrowing, so you'll need to ask for exposure directly.

steps: Think of one junior colleague or new hire you currently work with.

Open your company-approved AI tool and ask: "I want to help a junior teammate build real judgment, not just review AI output. Give me three specific ways I could involve them in a project this month so they get hands-on experience."
Pick the one idea that feels most realistic for you to actually do this month.
Share it in the group — and tag the colleague if it feels right.

homework.title: Plan a weekend that isn't just another to-do list
homework.body: Pick a trip, a day out, or even a big cook-off you've been putting off, and use ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity to plan it — but this time, make the AI work for the details instead of just spitting out a generic itinerary.
homework.prompt: "I want to plan a [weekend trip / dinner party / day out] focused on [relaxation / adventure / trying something new]. Before you suggest anything, ask me questions about my budget, pace, and what I want to feel like by the end of it — then use my answers to build the plan."

2026-08-03.intro: Today's stories are about the gap between what AI can do and what your organization is actually ready for — in governance, in prompting, and in hiring.

trends.title: Companies are running AI agents faster than they can govern them
trends.body: McKinsey's 2026 AI Trust Maturity Survey gathered responses from approximately 500 organizations already deploying agentic AI, and found that only about one-third of them report a mature level of strategy, governance, and controls for the autonomous systems they've already turned on (McKinsey, 2026). That gap matters because once an agent acts on its own, the decision is already made before anyone reviews it.

slants.strategy: This is your cue to build the governance roadmap now, before agent rollout outpaces your ability to explain what they did and why.
slants.leaders: This is your cue to build the governance roadmap now, before agent rollout outpaces your ability to explain what they did and why.
slants.operations: Before letting any agent touch a live process, confirm there's a documented, fast 'off switch' someone can actually pull.
slants.pm: Add a governance checkpoint to any project plan that includes AI agents — treat it like a milestone, not an afterthought.
slants.admin: If you're using an AI scheduling or inbox agent, it's worth asking IT what data it can see and who's accountable if it gets something wrong.

steps: Pick one task where you or your team already lets AI act with minimal review (drafting, scheduling, data lookups).
Open your company-approved AI tool and ask: "Help me write a 5-line checklist to review before I let AI act automatically on this kind of task, covering what could go wrong and who should sign off."
Read the checklist and cut anything that doesn't apply to your actual workflow — keep it to 5 lines or fewer.
Share your checklist in the group chat and ask if anyone else's team has already built something similar.

trends.title: The smartest prompt in the world still fails without the right context
trends.body: Datadog's 2026 State of AI Engineering report found that context quality — not volume — is now the limiting factor for AI agents, since most teams don't even use the full context window their models allow. The lesson for anyone typing into a chat box: a clever prompt on a blank slate still produces a generic answer.

slants.strategy: Before asking AI for a forecast or plan, feed it your actual assumptions, targets, and constraints — not just the question.
slants.leaders: Before asking AI for a forecast or plan, feed it your actual assumptions, targets, and constraints — not just the question.
slants.operations: Build a reusable 'context pack' of your team's SOPs and process docs so every AI request starts from the same baseline, not from zero.
slants.pm: Paste in the project's real status, risks, and timeline before asking AI to summarize or flag issues — generic prompts get generic project updates.
slants.admin: Give AI the specific names, dates, and formats you use daily instead of a bare-bones request — it cuts editing time in half.

steps: Pick a task you'd normally hand AI with a short, bare prompt (like 'write a status update' or 'summarize this').
First, ask it with almost no context: "Write a short project status update." Save that output.

Now try it with real (non-confidential) detail: "Write a short project status update for a team of 5, currently on track but 2 days behind on one deliverable, audience is my manager who prefers bullet points."
Compare the two outputs side by side — notice how much more usable the second one is with almost no extra effort.
Share both versions in the group to show the difference context makes.

trends.title: AI fluency just moved from 'nice to have' to a baseline job requirement
trends.body: NACE's spring 2026 survey found that more than one-third of entry-level jobs now require AI skills, nearly triple what employers reported just six months earlier. That mirrors a bigger shift McKinsey flagged last year: demand for AI fluency in job postings has jumped nearly sevenfold in two years, faster than any other skill tracked.

slants.strategy: Workforce planning models need an 'AI fluency' line item now, the same way they track technical or language skills.
slants.leaders: Workforce planning models need an 'AI fluency' line item now, the same way they track technical or language skills.
slants.operations: Look at which frontline roles are being paired with AI training versus which are just being asked to 'figure it out' — that gap becomes a retention risk.
slants.pm: Add AI fluency to your team's skills matrix when staffing projects — it's becoming as relevant as tool experience or domain knowledge.
slants.admin: Documenting the AI tools you already use well is now a legitimate resume line, not just a footnote.

steps: Think of one task where you've already used AI successfully in the past month (drafting, summarizing, brainstorming, scheduling).
Open any AI assistant and ask: "Help me turn this into one strong resume or self-review bullet point: I used AI to [describe your task] and it helped me [describe the result]."
Review the draft and tighten it to one sentence that sounds like you, not a template.
Share your bullet point in the group — it's a low-key way to see how differently everyone is already using AI.

homework.title: Let AI help you plan something just for you this week
homework.body: Pick something personal you've been putting off — a trip, a tricky email to a friend or family member, or figuring out a confusing bill — and try it with a free tool like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity.
homework.prompt: "Before you help me with [your task], ask me 3 questions first so you understand what I actually need — then give me your suggestion."

2026-08-05.intro: Today's stories all point to the same quiet shift: AI isn't replacing the humans in the middle, the tools building it are getting radically easier to use, and the biggest blocker left is how honest we're willing to be about the time it saves.

trends.title: Managers aren't getting replaced by AI — they're getting redefined
trends.body: Gartner once predicted that AI would flatten hierarchies, with <cite index="16-1">20% of organizations using AI to flatten their structure, eliminating more than half of current middle management positions</cite> by the end of this year. New Salesforce research says the opposite is happening on the ground: <cite index="17-1">AI is making the middle manager even more important, and raising the stakes for companies to get their enablement right for the AI era</cite>. Harvard Business Review has even named the emerging version of the job — <cite index="16-10">Harvard Business Review published "To Thrive in the AI Era, Companies Need Agent Managers" in February 2026</cite> — the person who defines tasks for AI agents, reviews their output, and handles the exceptions that agents can't.

slants.strategy: Start mapping which roles on your org chart are shifting from 'coordinator' to 'agent supervisor' — that's the headcount conversation you'll be asked about next planning cycle.
slants.leaders: Use your positional influence now to claim the 'agent manager' framing for your own role before someone else defines it for you.
slants.operations: Audit which status-update and reporting tasks eat your team's week, since those are exactly what agents are already absorbing.
slants.pm: Redesign your status-reporting workflow so an agent drafts the update and you spend that reclaimed time on the judgment calls stakeholders actually need from you.
slants.admin: The coordination and scheduling skills you've built are shifting toward oversight work, not disappearing — that's worth naming in your next review.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool.
List the five most common status-update or reporting tasks you do in a typical week.

Prompt: "Here are five recurring status-update or reporting tasks I do each week: [list them]. For each one, tell me whether an AI agent could draft a first version, and what human judgment step should stay with me."
Review the response and pick one task to test handing the first draft to AI next week.
Share in the group: post the one task you're testing and why.

trends.title: You no longer need to know what a 'trigger' is to build an automation
trends.body: <cite index="30-1">After an extended beta, Zapier's AI agent layer hit general availability in July</cite>, and the bigger deal isn't the launch — it's what changed underneath it: <cite index="30-2">it lets you build multi-step agents using natural language prompts rather than drag-and-drop Zap construction</cite>. Describing an outcome in plain English is now enough to build the workflow behind it.

slants.strategy: Factor this into vendor and budget conversations — 'ease of building' is no longer a reason to greenlight a big consulting spend on automation.
slants.leaders: Encourage your team to try building one small automation themselves this week; it's a low-risk way to build AI confidence without a formal training program.
slants.operations: Look at your most repetitive multi-step handoffs — the ones that used to need an IT ticket — and see if you can describe them into existence instead.
slants.pm: Consider automating recurring project admin like status collection or file routing by simply describing the steps, no build sprint required.
slants.admin: This is the tool category where admin professionals often become the fastest experts in the building — plain-language building plays to skills you already have.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool (or an approved automation platform if you have one).
Pick one repetitive task with clear steps, like summarizing weekly updates or routing a recurring request.
Prompt: "I want to automate this task: [describe the task in plain language]. Break it into the exact steps an agent would need, including where a human should review before it goes out."
Review the steps it gives you and note where you'd want a human check before trusting it fully.
Share in the group: post the task you'd automate first and why.

trends.title: The time AI saves you might be the thing you're hiding
trends.body: A new Forbes analysis of workplace survey data found that <cite index="36-1">66% of employees fake productivity, staying online or slowing down, with 73% of managers admitting similar behavior</cite>. The root cause isn't laziness — <cite index="36-7">companies demand AI transformation but reward employees for appearing constantly busy</cite>, so workers quietly hide the very time savings leadership says it wants to see.

slants.strategy: Build 'what did AI free up, and what did we do with it' into your next planning review, or you'll never see the real capacity you've gained.
slants.leaders: Say out loud, in your next team meeting, that reclaimed time from AI is safe to report — your team is watching for permission, not asking for it.
slants.operations: If your team measures activity instead of output, that metric is quietly training people to hide their AI gains — worth flagging to whoever owns the dashboard.
slants.pm: Reframe status updates to track deliverables hit, not hours logged, so AI-driven speed shows up as a win instead of a risk to report.
slants.admin: If AI is cutting your task time, document it as freed-up capacity for higher-value work rather than something to quietly absorb into busywork.

steps: Think of one task this week where AI genuinely saved you time.
Prompt: "I saved about [X] minutes this week using AI on [task]. Help me write two or three sentences framing this as freed-up capacity for higher-value work, not something to downplay."
Read the draft back and edit it until it sounds like you, not a press release.
Decide if you'd feel comfortable saying that sentence to your own manager this week — no pressure either way.
Share in the group: post the framing sentence you landed on.

homework.title: Let AI plan something you've been putting off
homework.body: Pick a personal task you've been avoiding — planning a trip, writing a tough text to a friend, or decoding a confusing bill — and try it in ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity (all free to use).
homework.prompt: Before you answer, ask me at least three clarifying questions about what I actually need. Then give me two or three ranked options, not just one answer, and tell me the tradeoffs of each. Here's my situation: [describe your task].

2026-06-11.intro: Thursday's drop: the most expensive AI subscription is the one nobody uses. Three things to think about — plus something small for tonight.

trends.title: Half of you have AI access. Most of you aren't using it.
trends.body: Deloitte's January 2026 enterprise report flagged something blunt: under 60% of employees with access to AI tools actually use those tools in their daily workflows — nearly the same as last year. The takeaway: licenses don't create habits. People do.

slants.strategy: Your AI ROI calculations probably assume usage you're not getting. Audit actual adoption before you defend the spend.
slants.leaders: Your AI ROI calculations probably assume usage you're not getting. Audit actual adoption before you defend the spend.
slants.operations: Find one tool your team has access to but doesn't open. Pick the friction point — login, integration, training — and fix that one.
slants.pm: Use sprints to make AI usage explicit: 'This week, try X tool for stand-ups.' Habit beats capability.
slants.admin: If you've got AI access through your role and aren't using it, you're not alone. Pick the smallest possible first try.

steps: List every AI tool you currently have access to through work — even free ones. (Copilot? Gemini at Workspace? An enterprise Claude account?)
Mark each: "Use weekly," "Use rarely," or "Don't use."
Pick one from the 'Don't use' list and open it now.
Ask it one real question you would normally Google or ask a colleague.
Share which tool surprised you most in the group — good or bad.

trends.title: Hours saved are real — but unevenly distributed
trends.body: Recent enterprise studies converge on a number: employees who use AI well save 2–3 hours per day on routine activities. The catch: the gains skew heavily toward people who've crossed the 'I actually trust this' threshold. Trust is the throttle.

slants.strategy: Your AI ROI model is missing a variable: time-to-trust. Plan for it explicitly.
slants.leaders: Your AI ROI model is missing a variable: time-to-trust. Plan for it explicitly.
slants.operations: Track time saved on a single workflow for two weeks. You'll find your real ROI faster than any vendor case study.
slants.pm: Time savings on individual tasks don't always show up in team velocity. The bottleneck moves — find where.
slants.admin: If you're saving 30 minutes a day, that's 2.5 hours a week. Don't fill it with more tasks — use some for learning.

steps: Pick one daily task that takes 15+ minutes (drafting an email, summarizing a doc, formatting notes).
Time yourself doing it the old way today.
Tomorrow, do the same task with AI as the first draft, then edit.
Time it again. Note the actual difference, and the quality difference.
Share your before/after in the group — let's see which tasks are worth the swap.

trends.title: The Chief AI Officer is officially a thing
trends.body: 61% of enterprises now have a Chief AI Officer or equivalent role, per recent enterprise surveys. That signals something: AI strategy moved out of IT pilots and into the boardroom. Companies with dedicated AI leadership are more likely to see measurable productivity gains.

slants.strategy: If your org has a CAIO, find them. If it doesn't, identify who's filling that gap unofficially — it's often someone in ops or strategy.
slants.leaders: If your org has a CAIO, find them. If it doesn't, identify who's filling that gap unofficially — it's often someone in ops or strategy.
slants.operations: AI governance is going to land on someone in your org. Volunteer before it's volunteered for you.
slants.pm: AI program management is becoming its own specialty. If you like coordinating across functions, this is your lane.
slants.admin: Whoever owns AI at your company needs an org-savvy partner. Admins frequently end up in that role.

steps: Search your company's intranet or internal news for 'AI strategy' or 'AI governance.'
Find the name of the person leading it (CAIO, VP of AI, or de facto owner).
Open your company-approved AI tool and ask: "Help me draft a 3-sentence intro email to a [their role] explaining one thing I've learned about AI in my role and one thing I'd like to learn from them."
Save the draft. Don't send it yet — sit with it.
Share whether you found a clear AI leader in your org, or if it's still ambiguous.

homework.title: Use AI to plan a tiny weekend win.
homework.body: It's almost Friday. Pick one small thing you want to feel good about by Sunday night — finishing a book, organizing a drawer, calling a friend, trying a new recipe — and let AI help you plan it.
homework.prompt:
"I want to [the small thing] this weekend. Help me figure out the smallest version that still counts. Ask me 2 questions about what would make it actually happen."

The smallest version that still counts framing kills perfectionism. Try it on bigger things later.

2026-06-12.intro: Friday: the gap between feeling more productive and your org becoming more productive. Three things to think about — and a weekend mindset for tonight.

trends.title: 5× faster individually, 29% ROI organizationally
trends.body: Writer's 2026 enterprise survey put a sharp number on the AI productivity paradox: individual productivity gains of 5×, but only 29% of organizations see significant ROI from generative AI. The gap isn't capability — it's that personal gains aren't compounding into shipped outcomes.

slants.strategy: Don't celebrate individual AI gains as org wins. The work is in the handoffs between people, not the work itself.
slants.leaders: Don't celebrate individual AI gains as org wins. The work is in the handoffs between people, not the work itself.
slants.operations: Look for places where someone's AI-assisted output bottlenecks on someone else's old process. That's where the leak is.
slants.pm: If devs ship 2× faster but reviews and QA didn't scale, throughput didn't move. Find the new bottleneck.
slants.admin: When AI lets one person do twice as much, the system isn't faster — it just looks faster until it hits the next gate.

steps: Think of one workflow at your job that involves more than one person — a proposal, a sign-off, a content review.
On paper, list the steps and who owns each one.
Next to each step, mark: "This person uses AI here," "They don't," or "Not sure."
Look at the pattern. Where does an AI-fast step hand off to a non-AI step? That's the bottleneck.
Share the bottleneck you spotted in the group — without naming names.

trends.title: Synthesis is the new senior skill
trends.body: As more team members produce AI-drafted work, the new bottleneck becomes synthesizing across multiple AI outputs into a single coherent direction. Anyone can generate; few can synthesize. The synthesis skill is what separates the AI-savvy operator from the AI-flooded one.

slants.strategy: Synthesis across multiple analysts' AI-assisted briefs is the new senior-strategist skill. Practice it deliberately.
slants.leaders: Synthesis across multiple analysts' AI-assisted briefs is the new senior-strategist skill. Practice it deliberately.
slants.operations: When three people send you AI-drafted summaries, your job is to find the contradictions, not to paste them together.
slants.pm: Two AI-generated status updates that say the same thing differently are a warning sign, not redundancy. Look for what's missing.
slants.admin: You see drafts before anyone else. Spot the assumptions repeated across them — that's where the team's blind spot is.

steps: Find two AI-generated outputs you have access to — both yours, or one yours and one from a colleague (with permission, no confidential data).
Open your company-approved AI tool.
Paste both in and add: "What do these two outputs agree on, what do they disagree on, and what does neither one address?"
Read the response carefully. The 'neither one addresses' part is usually the gold.
Share one blind spot you found in the group.

trends.title: The 11.5% productivity bump nobody's bragging about
trends.body: Buried in ManpowerGroup's 2026 data: enterprises reported an average 11.5% increase in net productivity over the past 12 months, partly from AI and partly from broader efficiency work. Real, modest, hard-won. Not the 10× headlines — but compounding year over year, this is what changes how companies actually run.

slants.strategy: Plan for compounding, not breakthroughs. 11% per year is over 50% in five — and it's exactly where good operators add value.
slants.leaders: Plan for compounding, not breakthroughs. 11% per year is over 50% in five — and it's exactly where good operators add value.
slants.operations: Steady process improvements are back in fashion. Pair each AI experiment with a measurable old-school KPI.
slants.pm: Velocity charts should track sustained gains, not spikes. A 10% rolling improvement is the win.
slants.admin: Small efficiencies you find — better templates, smarter folders, AI-assisted scheduling — add up faster than they look.

steps: Write down three things you do this week that take noticeably less time than they did a year ago.
For each, note what changed (tool, habit, skill, team).
Pick the one with the biggest gain.
Open your AI tool and ask: "Here's something I do faster now: [describe]. What's the next improvement I could make to compound the gain?"
Share your top time-saver — and the next improvement AI suggested — in the group.

homework.title: End-of-week mindset reset.
homework.body: Fridays are good for closing tabs — literal and mental. Tonight, use AI to help you actually finish your week.
homework.prompt:
"I'm trying to end this week feeling like I closed it well. Ask me 3 questions to help me decide what's worth carrying into next week and what I should let go of."

The trick is making AI a reflection prompt, not an answer machine. The 'let go' question is the one that matters.

2026-06-13.intro: Saturday's drop is lighter on purpose. Three angles on how AI can teach you something this weekend — no work allowed.

trends.title: AI tutors got weirdly good in 2026
trends.body: One of AI's most underrated uses this year — quietly bigger than enterprise pilots in many people's daily lives — is personalized tutoring. Patient, infinite, judgment-free explainers for whatever you've been meaning to learn. The barrier was never finding an explanation; it was finding one that matched your level.

slants.strategy: Learning to learn faster is a leadership skill. AI tutoring is the cheapest way to compound it.
slants.leaders: Learning to learn faster is a leadership skill. AI tutoring is the cheapest way to compound it.
slants.operations: Pick one process at your company you don't fully understand. Ask AI to explain it from scratch.
slants.pm: Quietly studying a domain through AI before a project lands is the new prep work. Free and invisible.
slants.admin: If you've ever felt 'I should know this by now,' AI is the no-judgment teacher you deserved years ago.

steps: Pick one thing you've quietly been meaning to understand — a finance concept, a piece of tech, a historical event, anything.
Open a free AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity).
Use this prompt: "Teach me [topic] like I'm a curious adult with no background. Use a metaphor I'd recognize from everyday life. Then ask me one question to check if I got it."
Answer the check-in question honestly.
Share what you learned in the group — and whether the metaphor actually helped.

trends.title: Reading AI critically is the real skill
trends.body: Plenty of people can ask AI questions. The smaller, more valuable group can spot when the answer is wrong. That muscle isn't built by using AI more — it's built by deliberately challenging it.

slants.strategy: Skeptical readers of AI output make better strategic decisions. Train the muscle in low-stakes settings.
slants.leaders: Skeptical readers of AI output make better strategic decisions. Train the muscle in low-stakes settings.
slants.operations: The first answer is rarely the best one. Make 'ask twice with different framing' a habit.
slants.pm: Verification beats generation. The job is increasingly to check what AI claims, not to ask it more things.
slants.admin: You already double-check exec emails before they go. Same instinct, new collaborator.

steps: Pick a topic you actually know well — a hobby, a former job, a specialty.
Open AI and ask: "Give me 5 facts about [your area of expertise]."
Read carefully. Find at least one fact that's wrong, misleading, or oversimplified.
Reply: "Fact #X is wrong because [your correction]. What else might you have gotten wrong?"
Share in the group what AI got wrong about something you know.

trends.title: Hobby AI is the easiest practice ground
trends.body: There's a pattern across communities like this one: members who use AI on something they genuinely love — a recipe, a fantasy league, a garden, a creative project — build prompting skill faster than members who only use it at work. The reason: they don't tolerate bad answers when it's something they care about.

slants.strategy: Your weekend AI practice sharpens your weekday judgment. Don't treat them as separate.
slants.leaders: Your weekend AI practice sharpens your weekday judgment. Don't treat them as separate.
slants.operations: The instincts you develop fighting AI on a personal project transfer directly to fighting it on a work problem.
slants.pm: Project-managing a fun side project with AI teaches scope creep faster than any pro training.
slants.admin: Using AI on something personal builds the taste that work AI doesn't earn from you.

steps: Pick one hobby, interest, or personal project you'd love to spend an hour on this weekend.
Open a free AI tool.
Ask: "Help me get one hour of meaningful progress on [thing] this weekend. Ask me 3 questions first, then give me a 3-step plan."
Do at least one of the steps.
Share what you actually did in the group — even if it's tiny.

homework.title: Teach AI something this weekend.
homework.body: Flip the script. AI usually teaches you. Tonight, teach it. The act of explaining clarifies your own thinking — that's the real win.
homework.prompt:
"I want to teach you something I know well: [topic]. I'll explain it in my own words. After I do, ask me 2 questions that would help you understand it better."

The 'ask me questions to deepen your understanding' framing turns AI into a curious student. Surprisingly clarifying.

2026-06-14.intro: Three things worth thinking about today — and one for you to try at home.

trends.title: The strategic memo is being rebuilt — fast
trends.body: Microsoft's 2026 Work Trend Index just landed. 49% of Copilot conversations now support cognitive work — analysis, problem-solving, strategic thinking — and 58% of AI users say they're producing work they couldn't have done a year ago. The work isn't disappearing. It's being promoted.

slants.strategy: You're shifting from writer to editor + pressure-tester.
slants.leaders: You're shifting from writer to editor + pressure-tester.
slants.operations: Synthesis across systems is now a 30-min job, not a 3-day one.
slants.pm: Status reports get auto-drafted; framing the right questions is the new value-add.
slants.admin: Your judgment on tone, context, and 'what the exec actually meant' becomes the premium skill.

steps: Pick a document you wrote last quarter — a recommendation, memo, or proposal. Make sure it doesn't contain confidential client or customer information.
Open your company-approved AI tool (Copilot, Gemini Enterprise, Claude for Work — whatever's blessed at your company).
Paste the document in, then add this prompt: "Argue against this from the perspective of a skeptical executive. Be specific about the weakest assumptions."
Read the response carefully and identify one point you hadn't considered before.
Share that insight in the group — what surprised you most?

trends.title: The Transformation Paradox
trends.body: Deloitte's 2026 enterprise report puts it plainly: companies are layering AI onto legacy processes instead of redesigning work holistically. The investment isn't compounding because the workflow underneath is still pre-AI.
