slants.strategy: The QBR was built for a pre-AI world. Rethink the inputs and outputs.
slants.leaders: The QBR was built for a pre-AI world. Rethink the inputs and outputs.
slants.operations: Your SOPs probably encode 2019 assumptions.
slants.pm: "Weekly check-ins" exist because info moved slowly. Does it still?
slants.admin: Calendar-and-email triage workflows are ripe for a clean-slate redesign.

steps: Pick ONE recurring meeting or process you own — the QBR, a weekly check-in, a status report.
Open a notes app or grab a piece of paper.
Write at the top: "If AI were a teammate from minute one, this would [...]"
Finish the sentence. Don't overthink it — the first instinct is usually the most honest one.
Share your one-sentence answer in the group.

trends.title: AI fluency is the new literacy
trends.body: Stanford HAI's 2026 AI Index: AI-related skills now appear in 2.5% of all U.S. job postings — a 297% increase over a decade. This isn't "learn to code." It's learn to direct, evaluate, and trust-but-verify AI output.

slants.strategy: Prompting is problem-framing. The clearer your ask, the sharper your strategy.
slants.leaders: Prompting is problem-framing. The clearer your ask, the sharper your strategy.
slants.operations: Knowing when AI is wrong saves more time than AI being right.
slants.pm: Agent orchestration is the next PM specialty.
slants.admin: You already know how things actually work here. AI doesn't.

steps: Open a blank document or note.
List your top 3 weekly recurring tasks — the things you do every week without fail.
Next to each task, write one of three labels: "AI could draft this", "AI could review my work on this", or "Only I can do this."
Look at your split. Pick one task you didn't realize AI could help with.
Share your split in the group, and call out that one surprise task.

homework.title: Brand new to AI? Start with something personal tonight.
homework.body: The fastest way to lose the fear: use AI on something where there's no security policy and no judgment. Try one of these in your free tool of choice (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity all have free web versions):
homework.prompt:
"I'm trying to [plan a weekend / write a tough message / figure out a recipe from what's in my fridge / understand a confusing bill]. Ask me 3 questions before you help, so your answer actually fits."

That last line — ask me questions first — is the single most useful prompting habit you'll ever learn.

2026-06-15.intro: Welcome to a fresh week. Three things to think about — and one small thing to try tonight.

trends.title: Using AI more, feeling less sure about it
trends.body: ManpowerGroup's 2026 Global Talent Barometer caught something unexpected: regular AI usage jumped 13 points to 45% of workers, while confidence in using technology fell 18 points. The gap between doing it and feeling good about it is real — and it's exactly why peer communities like this one exist.

slants.strategy: Confidence comes from frameworks. Pick one decision lens and apply it to AI's output, not the other way around.
slants.leaders: Confidence comes from frameworks. Pick one decision lens and apply it to AI's output, not the other way around.
slants.operations: If you're using AI but quietly second-guessing every output, you're in the majority. Compare notes with someone before redoing the work.
slants.pm: Your team likely feels this too. Make AI use a normal topic in retros — not a separate AI-only conversation.
slants.admin: Trust your judgment. AI doesn't know context the way you do, and 'this doesn't sound right' is almost always worth flagging.

steps: Open any AI tool you've used recently (work-approved or personal).
Find one piece of AI output from the last week that left you a little unsure.
Paste it back into the AI with this prompt: "Critique this. What might be wrong, missing, or weaker than it sounds?"
Read the self-critique. Notice how it changes your confidence in the original.
Share what you found in the group — was the self-critique useful or hand-wavy?

trends.title: Assistants are becoming agents
trends.body: McKinsey found 62% of organizations are already experimenting with agentic AI, and Gartner expects 40% of enterprise applications to feature embedded task-specific agents by 2026 — up from under 5% in 2025. The shift: from "answer my question" to "run this multi-step task and report back."

slants.strategy: If your strategy assumes humans coordinate every step, it's already aging. Plan for agents that own short workflows.
slants.leaders: If your strategy assumes humans coordinate every step, it's already aging. Plan for agents that own short workflows.
slants.operations: The new ops bottleneck won't be doing the work — it'll be defining the work clearly enough for an agent to run it.
slants.pm: Directing agents is a project management skill. You already manage humans who need clear briefs and check-ins. Same muscle.
slants.admin: Routine scheduling, reminders, follow-ups — agents handle these first. Your value moves to context and judgment calls.

steps: Pick one task you do every week that has clear steps — booking a meeting, summarizing a thread, formatting a doc.
Open your company-approved AI tool.
Write out the steps in plain English, as if briefing a new teammate. Be specific about inputs and what 'done' looks like.
Paste your brief in and ask: "If you were an agent doing this task, what would you need from me that I haven't given you?"
Share one gap you discovered in the group — that's your starter playbook for working with agents.

trends.title: New AI roles, no coding required
trends.body: A wave of new positions is opening up around agent orchestration, AI governance, and human-AI workflow design. The encouraging part for operators: many of these roles value process thinking, communication, governance, and strategic skills as much as coding ability. Your operations background is more relevant than you think.

slants.strategy: Whoever defines how AI fits into the strategic planning cycle owns a new center of gravity. That can be you.
slants.leaders: Whoever defines how AI fits into the strategic planning cycle owns a new center of gravity. That can be you.
slants.operations: Workflow design is operations work — just with a new collaborator (the agent) in the workflow.
slants.pm: Multi-agent coordination is project management with non-human teammates. Same coordination logic, broader toolkit.
slants.admin: You already manage information flow, scheduling, and exec needs. Agent governance is a natural extension.

steps: Open a doc or note.
Write down one part of your current job that you genuinely enjoy — the thinking part, not the typing part.
Open an AI tool and ask: "What's an emerging 2026 role that builds on someone who is good at [that thing]?"
Read the response with curiosity, not pressure. Note one role title that intrigues you.
Share the role with the group — let's see what shows up across the community.

homework.title: Tonight, ask AI for help with one thing on your personal to-do list.
homework.body: Monday-night habit-builder: pick something small from your personal list and let AI take a swing. The point isn't the answer — it's noticing how it feels to ask.
homework.prompt:
"Here's something I'm trying to figure out: [name it — a gift idea, a tough text, a recipe, a budget question]. Ask me 2 questions to understand my situation, then give me 3 options ranked by [whatever matters most]."

The ranked-by trick is the move. Make AI commit to an opinion, not just list possibilities.

2026-06-16.intro: Tuesday: what separates the orgs winning with AI from the ones still pitching it. Plus something small for you to try tonight.

trends.title: The 25% gap
trends.body: Hackett Group's 2026 Enterprise Key Issues Study found that the organizations getting transformational AI results — 25%+ improvements across customer experience, employee experience, and productivity — aren't the ones deploying the most tools. They're the ones reimagining their operating model. The lever is structural, not technological.

slants.strategy: If your AI roadmap is a tool list, you're losing to orgs whose AI roadmap is an operating-model redesign.
slants.leaders: If your AI roadmap is a tool list, you're losing to orgs whose AI roadmap is an operating-model redesign.
slants.operations: The most underrated AI question right now: "Which of our standard processes deserve to exist at all?"
slants.pm: Project portfolios are still designed around human cadence. The next wave reshapes the portfolio itself, not just the projects in it.
slants.admin: If you've been told to 'make existing workflows faster,' push back. The question is whether the workflow should look the same at all.

steps: Pick a single workflow you own end-to-end (intake to delivery).
On paper or in a doc, draw it as 5–7 steps from start to finish.
For each step, mark one of three labels: "Required for value," "Habit, not value," or "Worth questioning."
Look at the 'Habit' and 'Worth questioning' labels — that's your AI-redesign opportunity list.
Share your most surprising 'Habit, not value' step in the group.

trends.title: The 'strategy theater' gap
trends.body: Writer's 2026 enterprise survey landed a hard finding: 75% of executives admit their company's AI strategy is "more for show" than actual guidance, with 39% lacking any formal revenue plan tied to AI. There's a vacuum at the strategy layer — and operators who can connect strategy to measurable outcomes just became more valuable.

slants.strategy: If you're in strategy and your AI deck is real, you're rarer than you think. Lean into outcome metrics, not capability lists.
slants.leaders: If you're in strategy and your AI deck is real, you're rarer than you think. Lean into outcome metrics, not capability lists.
slants.operations: When leadership's strategy is unclear, ops becomes the de facto translator. Document the gap, then propose the bridge.
slants.pm: 'Connect strategy to delivery' has always been a PM superpower. AI just made it 10× more visible.
slants.admin: If you can summarize what's actually being asked (vs. what's being announced), that clarity is a leadership skill in disguise.

steps: Find your company's most recent AI announcement or strategy doc that's safe to share with an AI tool.
Open your company-approved AI tool.
Paste in the doc and add this prompt: "Pull out every specific, measurable outcome promised here. If there are none, say so."
Look at the list. Notice the ratio of concrete outcomes to aspirational language.
Share one observation in the group — was the strategy specific, or mostly directional?

trends.title: Knowing which AI mode to use is the new skill
trends.body: Microsoft's 2026 Copilot update introduced "Quick Response" and "Think Deeper" modes — two different reasoning depths for two different kinds of questions. The skill isn't using the tool; it's knowing which mode for which question. Expect every major AI tool to follow this pattern.

slants.strategy: Quick Response for status, Think Deeper for trade-off decisions. Mixing them up wastes either time or quality.
slants.leaders: Quick Response for status, Think Deeper for trade-off decisions. Mixing them up wastes either time or quality.
slants.operations: Most ops questions are quick lookups; a few are real analysis. Match the mode to the task and your team's output improves.
slants.pm: Use Quick Response for stand-up summaries. Use Think Deeper for risk assessment and dependency mapping.
slants.admin: Drafting an email? Quick. Resolving a calendar conflict that affects three execs? Deeper. Trust the difference.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool that offers different reasoning modes (Copilot, Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT all have variations).
Pick the SAME work question and ask it twice — once in fast mode, once in slow/deep mode.
Compare the answers. Was the slower one actually better, or just longer?
Decide your own rule of thumb: "For [type of question], I'll use [mode]."
Share your rule of thumb in the group — we'll learn from each other's defaults.

homework.title: Use AI to win an argument with yourself tonight.
homework.body: Most of us have one small decision we've been putting off — a purchase, a route change, a routine swap. Tonight, let AI play both sides.
homework.prompt:
"I'm trying to decide whether to [the thing]. Steelman the case for doing it. Then steelman the case against. Don't give me a recommendation — I'll decide."

The trick is asking for both sides, no recommendation. You'll think more clearly than if you'd asked for advice.

2026-07-16.intro: Thursday. Three data points this week that share a thread: the organizations pulling ahead on AI aren't doing more — they're thinking differently about what AI is for.

trends.title: Most of AI's economic value is going to a small group — and spending isn't what separates them
trends.body: PwC's 2026 AI Performance Study surveyed 1,217 executives across 25 sectors. The headline: 74% of AI's economic value is being captured by just 20% of organizations. The top performers aren't outspending everyone else — they're using AI differently. Companies generating the most value are 2–3 times more likely to use AI for growth and business reinvention than for cost-cutting. The result: a 7.2x ROI gap and operating margins four points higher.

slants.strategy: If your AI business case starts and ends with "reduce costs," you're optimizing for the smaller prize. The top performers are asking where AI creates new revenue — not just where it trims existing spend.
slants.leaders: If your AI business case starts and ends with "reduce costs," you're optimizing for the smaller prize. The top performers are asking where AI creates new revenue — not just where it trims existing spend.
slants.operations: Ops leaders in the top 20% aren't automating the same old processes faster. They're asking which workflows to redesign entirely now that AI is a factor.
slants.pm: If every AI project in your portfolio is a cost-reduction play, the portfolio itself may need rebalancing. Growth-focused AI projects are showing a stronger track record.
slants.admin: The companies getting the most from AI aren't the ones with the most tools — they're the ones with the clearest strategy. That matters when your leadership is still shopping for the next shiny thing.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool.

Paste this prompt: "My organization is investing in AI. Help me brainstorm 3 ways AI could create new value in my department — not by cutting costs or reducing headcount, but by enabling something we couldn't do before. My department does [describe your team's work]."
Read the three ideas. Pick the one that feels most realistic for your team this quarter.
Share that idea in the group — and whether 'growth' or 'cost-cutting' is the dominant AI conversation at your organization right now.

trends.title: More knowledge workers are going independent — and AI is the catalyst
trends.body: Upwork's 2026 Future Workforce Index, released this week, surveyed 2,400 U.S. knowledge workers. The finding: 38% of skilled knowledge workers now freelance, up from 28% a year ago. And 58% of full-time employees say they're considering it, up from 36%. AI is the accelerant — freelancers who integrate AI into complex professional work earn 34% more per hour. Upwork calls the emerging archetype the "AI Orchestrator": someone who connects AI tools to domain expertise and takes accountability for the output.

slants.strategy: The rise of skilled freelancing changes how you source expertise. The best analyst for your next initiative won't always be on your payroll — and doesn't need to be.
slants.leaders: The rise of skilled freelancing changes how you source expertise. The best analyst for your next initiative won't always be on your payroll — and doesn't need to be.
slants.operations: If 38% of knowledge workers are freelancing, your vendor onboarding, compliance workflows, and access provisioning need to keep pace. Prepare the systems before the demand arrives.
slants.pm: Project staffing is shifting. Knowing how to scope work for a blended team — internal staff plus AI-fluent freelancers — is becoming a core PM skill.
slants.admin: The admin infrastructure around freelancers — contracts, access provisioning, communication channels — is growing. If your organization isn't ready for a larger freelance bench, that gap lands on you first.

steps: Think about the last time your team brought in outside help — a consultant, contractor, or freelancer.

Open your company-approved AI tool and try this prompt: "I work in [your department]. If I could bring in a freelance AI specialist for 10 hours this month, what's the highest-value project I could hand them? Assume they're skilled at using AI for analysis, drafting, and process design."
Read the suggestion. Does it describe work someone on your team is doing slowly — or work nobody has time to start?
Share the project idea and your reaction in the group.

trends.title: AI saves you hours on email — but it can't touch your meeting problem
trends.body: A Harvard Business School AI Institute study tracked 7,000 workers across 66 companies in a randomized controlled trial. Workers with access to AI assistants spent 3.6 fewer hours per week on email — a 31% reduction. Collaborative documents got completed 25% faster. But meetings? No change at all. Same number, same duration, same attendance. The researchers' explanation: email is individual, so one person with AI can change their own habits. Meetings are collective — changing them requires coordination that no individual tool can provide.

slants.strategy: If your AI rollout is saving individuals hours but the meeting calendar hasn't budged, you're reclaiming personal time and losing it again in collective time. The net gain may be smaller than it looks.
slants.leaders: If your AI rollout is saving individuals hours but the meeting calendar hasn't budged, you're reclaiming personal time and losing it again in collective time. The net gain may be smaller than it looks.
slants.operations: This study gives you a clean argument for the meeting audit your team probably needs: AI freed up time, and meetings absorbed it.
slants.pm: You own the meeting cadence. If AI is giving people back 3 hours of email time and that time is vanishing into status syncs, the fix is a project management decision — not a technology one.
slants.admin: You see it before anyone else: calendars haven't gotten lighter, even though inboxes have. If you manage schedules, you have the data to start the conversation.

steps: Look at your calendar for last week. Count the total hours you spent in meetings.
Now estimate how much time you spent on email — and whether that number has changed since AI tools arrived at your organization.

Open your company-approved AI tool and try: "I spent approximately [X] hours in meetings and [Y] hours on email last week. Based on workplace research, which of those is more likely to be reduced by AI tools, and what's one structural change I could propose to reduce the other?"
Share your meeting-to-email ratio and the most useful suggestion in the group.

homework.title: Tonight, let AI help you think through a purchase you've been mulling over.
homework.body: Everyone has one — a new mattress, a different phone plan, a kitchen gadget, a subscription you're not sure about. Instead of reading 47 reviews, try this in any free AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity):
homework.prompt:
"I'm thinking about buying [the thing]. Before you recommend anything, ask me 5 questions about what matters most to me — budget, features, how I'll use it, deal-breakers. Then give me 3 options ranked by how well they fit my answers."

The technique — having AI interview you before it advises — produces far better answers than dumping your question cold. It works for any decision, personal or professional.

2026-07-20.intro: A Monday reset: what the skills gap is actually costing, why most AI training misses the mark, and the policy problem hiding in plain sight.

trends.title: The AI skills gap isn't a hiring problem — it's a $5.5 trillion drag on the economy
trends.body: IDC estimates that AI and digital skills shortages will cost the global economy up to $5.5 trillion in 2026 — not in vague lost potential, but in concrete damage: delayed transformations, quality problems, and missed revenue. Over 90% of enterprises face critical shortages, and nearly two-thirds report that the gap has already pushed back their digital transformation timelines by an average of 10 months.

slants.strategy: When your AI roadmap says '12 months to value,' add 10 for the skills bottleneck nobody budgeted for.
slants.leaders: When your AI roadmap says '12 months to value,' add 10 for the skills bottleneck nobody budgeted for.
slants.operations: Those delays aren't theoretical — they're the gap between 'we bought the tool' and 'someone can actually run it.'
slants.pm: Skills readiness belongs on the RAID log right next to budget and timeline — it's the risk that quietly kills AI projects.
slants.admin: If you've been self-teaching AI on your own time, you're ahead of most. That capability has real value — name it.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool.

Paste this prompt: "I work in [your role]. List three AI-adjacent skills that would make me most valuable over the next 12 months — not coding skills, but judgment and workflow skills. For each one, suggest one free resource I could start with this week."
Pick the skill that surprises you most and bookmark the resource.
Share your top pick in the group — and whether the AI's suggestion matched what you expected.

trends.title: 85% of employees say their AI training doesn't help them do their actual jobs
trends.body: Docebo's 2026 AI Readiness Gap report found that 85% of employees say the AI training they receive doesn't help them in their actual role. The reasons are structural: 78% say training happens in systems completely disconnected from the tools where they work, and 56% are so buried in pre-AI manual tasks they can't find time to learn at all.

slants.strategy: If your team's AI training isn't tied to specific workflows, you're producing certificates — not capability.
slants.leaders: If your team's AI training isn't tied to specific workflows, you're producing certificates — not capability.
slants.operations: Ten minutes applying AI to a real task teaches more than an hour of courseware. Push for practice over modules.
slants.pm: Before adding 'AI training' to the project plan, ask: training on what, specifically, and will they use it this week?
slants.admin: If your training felt useless, it probably was. The fix isn't more hours — it's training that starts from your actual tasks.

steps: Think of one task you did last week that took longer than it should have.

Open your company-approved AI tool and try this: "I spent [time] on [describe the task] last week. Show me how I could use AI to cut that time in half — step by step, using tools I likely already have access to."
Try the first step right now — even a quick five-minute test counts.
Share what you tried in the group — and whether it actually helped.

trends.title: Nearly half of workers say their company's AI policy is blocking them from learning
trends.body: SHRM's 2026 workplace survey of nearly 6,000 U.S. workers found that 46% feel their organization's AI policies block them from experimenting with new tools. Among companies that do have policies, only 25% of HR professionals consider them clear and future-proof — and 54% say their rules are too restrictive, written around specific tools that are already evolving past what the policy covers.

slants.strategy: A policy that blocks experimentation doesn't reduce risk — it pushes AI use underground where you can't see it.
slants.leaders: A policy that blocks experimentation doesn't reduce risk — it pushes AI use underground where you can't see it.
slants.operations: If your team is quietly using AI around the policy, the policy is the vulnerability — not the tool.
slants.pm: When kicking off an AI-involved project, check whether the policy even covers what you're planning. There's a good chance it doesn't.
slants.admin: You're often the first to notice when a policy doesn't match how people actually work. That observation is worth raising.

steps: Find your organization's AI use policy — or confirm that one doesn't exist yet (that's a finding too).

Summarize the key rules in a few bullet points, then open your company-approved AI tool and try: "Here are the key points of my company's AI use policy: [paste your summary]. What's missing, what's too vague to follow, and what might already be outdated? Give me three specific suggestions."
Pick the suggestion that felt most obvious and write it down.
Share your takeaway in the group — especially if the answer was 'we don't have one.'

homework.title: Let AI build you a reading list tonight — but make it earn every pick.
homework.body: Forget browsing bestseller lists or Amazon recommendations. Use any free AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity) to get a reading list that actually fits you — and learn a prompting trick along the way.
homework.prompt:
"I'm looking for my next great read. I recently enjoyed [name a book or two you liked]. I'm in the mood for something [describe the vibe — e.g., thought-provoking, escapist, funny, short]. Don't give me 10 options — give me exactly 3. For each one, tell me in one sentence why it fits what I just told you, not just why it's a good book. Then pick the single best one to start with and tell me why."

The technique here — constraining the output and demanding personalized reasoning — stops AI from giving you a generic list. It works for any recommendation: restaurants, podcasts, movies, gifts.

2026-07-30.intro: Thursday. This week's throughline is momentum: AI is widening what any one person can do, while the money and tooling race to keep pace — every signal an opening you can step into.

trends.title: Your role just got bigger, in the best way
trends.body: AI is quietly widening what one person can take on. A new OpenAI study of more than 800,000 workplace ChatGPT messages found that 43.5% of job-specific AI requests involve tasks that traditionally belong to a different role (OpenAI) — designers running analysis, marketers drafting code, support staff shaping policy. The skills next to yours are suddenly within reach.

slants.strategy: The advantage now belongs to people who stretch across boundaries, so map where your team's adjacent skills overlap and encourage the crossover before your competitors formalize it.
slants.leaders: Your team can suddenly reach into work that used to require a specialist, so your edge is deciding which cross-role moves to encourage and pairing people to learn faster together.
slants.operations: You can now own more of a workflow end to end instead of waiting on a handoff, turning what used to be a queue into something you finish yourself.
slants.pm: Reaching confidently into design, analysis, or copy means fewer dependencies to chase and more of the project you can move forward single-handedly, expanding your influence.
slants.admin: The adjacent skills you pick up — a quick analysis, a polished draft, a sharp summary — make you visibly more valuable across every team you support.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and name one task you usually hand off to a specialist, like a data cut or a design tweak.
Paste this prompt: "I want to try doing this myself with your help: [describe the task]. Walk me through it step by step and produce a first version I can refine."
Review what it produces and note the one part that felt genuinely new to you.
Paste this follow-up: "Explain the reasoning behind that step so I can do it confidently on my own next time, and give me a short checklist."
Share with the group one skill you reached into this week that used to feel outside your lane.

trends.title: The engine behind your AI tools just scaled up
trends.body: The infrastructure powering everyday AI is expanding fast. Meta and BlackRock just formed a venture to build a $14 billion, 1-gigawatt AI data center campus in El Paso, set to come online in 2028 (CNBC). Translation: the assistants you already rely on are on track to get faster, cheaper, and more capable, with the raw capacity to back it up.

slants.strategy: Capacity at this scale means AI costs keep falling, so plan now for what becomes affordable to automate next year rather than budgeting only for today's prices.
slants.leaders: Cheaper, more capable AI is coming whether or not you plan for it, so the leaders who sketch out what their team will do with that headroom get to shape the upside first.
slants.operations: As compute gets cheaper, the tasks too slow or costly to automate today open up, so keep a running list of what you'd hand off the moment it becomes practical.
slants.pm: More capacity means the AI features baked into your tools keep improving mid-project, so revisit what's newly possible before you scope your next plan.
slants.admin: The tools you use daily will keep getting quicker and smarter on the same subscription, quietly compounding the time you save every week.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and pick one task you skipped automating before because it felt too slow or clunky.
Paste this prompt: "Here is a task I do regularly: [describe it]. Show me the fastest way to do it with you today, start to finish."
Run through the steps it suggests and time how long the task now takes.
Paste this follow-up: "Now turn this into a repeatable routine I can reuse each time, with the exact prompts to paste."
Share the reusable routine with your group so someone else can reclaim the same time.

trends.title: AI teammates are showing up inside your software
trends.body: You won't have to go hunting for AI — it's arriving inside the apps you already open. 80% of enterprise applications shipped or updated in early 2026 now embed at least one AI agent, up from 33% in 2024 (Digital Applied). Every tool on your screen is quietly gaining a capable teammate, no new login required.

slants.strategy: When agents ship as a standard feature of software you already own, the win goes to leaders who inventory those built-in capabilities and put them to work before the next budget cycle.
slants.leaders: You can expand what AI does for your team using tools you've already paid for, so make it a habit to ask what new agent features each app added this quarter.
slants.operations: Agents living inside your existing apps mean automation without a migration, so try the built-in helper on your most repetitive task this week.
slants.pm: Embedded agents can take on status nudges, summaries, and follow-ups, freeing you to run more threads at once without dropping any of them.
slants.admin: The software you already navigate better than anyone is gaining assistants you can master first, making you the go-to person when the rest of the team catches up.

steps: Pick one app you use daily and open your company-approved AI tool alongside it.
Paste this prompt: "I use [name the app] every day for [task]. What AI or agent features does it likely have now, and how would I start using them?"
Explore the app's menus and settings to find the built-in AI feature it points you to.
Paste this follow-up: "Give me three specific ways to use that built-in feature to save time on my weekly work, with an example for each."
Share with the group which hidden feature you found and what it now does for you.

homework.title: Plan a weekend outing without the back-and-forth
homework.body: This one practices structured output — telling the AI the exact format you want back so you get a usable answer instead of a wall of text. When you specify the columns, order, and detail up front, the response comes ready to act on:
homework.prompt:
"Plan a relaxed one-day outing for me. Return it as a simple hour-by-hour schedule with three columns: time, activity, and a one-line why. Keep it to a single day and assume a budget-friendly pace. Here are the details: [paste your city, who's coming, and what you enjoy here]."

The technique — specifying the exact format you want back — turns a vague answer into something you can act on immediately. Try adding "return it as a table with these columns" to your next request and watch how much more usable the response gets.

2026-08-02.intro: Sunday. Three signals heading into next week: AI anxiety just showed up in the data, learners are outpacing their employers, and access without readiness is the gap most companies haven't closed.

trends.title: Employee wellbeing just dropped below pandemic levels — and AI anxiety is a driver most leaders aren't seeing
trends.body: Mercer's Global Talent Trends 2026, surveying nearly 12,000 executives, HR leaders, and employees worldwide, found a number that should stop every strategy leader cold: only 44% of employees report they are thriving at work — down from 66% in 2024, and below pandemic-era levels. A significant driver is what Mercer calls "FOBO" — fear of becoming obsolete. Employee concern about AI-related job loss jumped from 28% to 40% in two years. And the disconnect runs deep: 62% of employees say their leaders underestimate AI's emotional impact, yet only 19% of HR leaders factor that into their digital rollout plans.

slants.strategy: If your AI roadmap doesn't have a line item for what this does to people's confidence, you're planning for deployment but not for adoption.
slants.leaders: Your team's silence on AI anxiety isn't agreement — it's avoidance. Ask the question directly and you'll learn more in five minutes than a dozen adoption dashboards will tell you.
slants.operations: A team running on anxiety doesn't troubleshoot well, doesn't adopt new tools well, and doesn't flag problems early. Name the concern before it names itself.
slants.pm: Project adoption metrics miss the emotional layer entirely. Add a 'how confident are you with this tool?' check to your next retro — the honest answers will tell you more than login counts.
slants.admin: If you're feeling uneasy about AI, you're in the majority — 40% of the workforce shares that concern. Naming it is the first step to moving past it.

steps: Think about your team's most recent AI tool rollout. Did anyone ask how people felt about it — not whether they logged in, but how they felt?

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste this prompt: "I manage a team that recently adopted new AI tools. Draft five specific, non-generic questions I could ask in a quick pulse check to understand how my team feels about AI — not just whether they're using it, but whether they're anxious, confident, or somewhere in between."
Read the questions and pick the two that feel most honest and useful for your team.
Ask those two questions this week — in a 1:1, a team chat, or an anonymous form.
Share in the group what you learned. The answers will likely surprise you.

trends.title: AI learners are surging at 14 enrollments per minute — and they're teaching themselves the hard skills too
trends.body: Coursera's 2026 Job Skills Report, drawn from over 6 million enterprise learners across nearly 7,000 organizations, shows AI learning isn't slowing down — it's accelerating. GenAI enrollments rose 234% year-over-year, hitting 14 enrollments per minute — the most in-demand skill in Coursera's history. But the surprise is what people are learning alongside it: Critical Thinking enrollments surged 185% among GenAI learners, suggesting the sharpest AI adopters already know that using the tool well means thinking well without it.

slants.strategy: The demand signal is clear — people want to learn. If your org isn't offering structured AI learning paths, your most motivated people are building their own anyway.
slants.leaders: Your team is already investing personal time in AI skills — meet them halfway with structured learning time and they'll compound the investment for you.
slants.operations: Ops teams that pair AI fluency with critical thinking will outperform those that just automate — because someone still has to catch what the automation misses.
slants.pm: When 234% more people are actively building AI skills, the talent bench for AI-enhanced projects is deeper than you think. Look for it.
slants.admin: If you've been learning AI on your own time, you're part of the fastest-growing skill movement in Coursera's history. That initiative is worth naming on your resume.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and think of one skill you use daily that still feels manual — summarizing, analyzing, formatting, scheduling.

Paste this prompt: "I want to get better at using AI for [describe the skill]. Give me a 15-minute learning plan: what to try first, one technique to practice, and one common mistake to avoid. Keep it practical."
Try the technique it suggests on a real, non-confidential task right now.
Paste this follow-up: "Now give me a short checklist I can use to critically evaluate the output — what should I look for before I trust it?"
Share your 15-minute learning plan with the group — someone else wants to learn the same thing.

trends.title: Access to AI doubled in a year — readiness didn't follow
trends.body: Deloitte's eighth annual State of AI in the Enterprise, surveying 3,235 senior leaders across 24 countries, shows a lopsided expansion: workforce access to AI grew by 50% in a single year, reaching roughly 60% of workers equipped with sanctioned tools. But the readiness scores tell a different story. Talent readiness sits at just 20%, governance at 30%, and only one in four organizations has moved even 40% of its AI pilots into production. Companies got the tools into people's hands. They didn't get the training, the guardrails, or the redesigned workflows into place alongside them.

slants.strategy: Access without enablement is an unfunded promise. If your team has tools but no training plan, close that gap before the next budget review asks what the tools actually delivered.
slants.leaders: You expanded access — now fund the readiness. A 20% talent readiness score means 80% of your team is guessing, and that's a liability you can fix with intention.
slants.operations: You're likely sitting on AI tools right now that nobody walked you through. Closing your own readiness gap — even informally — puts you ahead of most of the organization.
slants.pm: Add 'team AI readiness' as a real project dependency. A tool nobody knows how to use well is a risk, not an asset.
slants.admin: If you feel like you were handed a new tool with no instructions, you're in the majority. Ask for the training — or find it yourself and become the person who helps others.

steps: List the AI tools your team currently has access to — including any built into apps like Copilot, Gemini, or embedded assistants.
For each tool, honestly rate your team's readiness on a 1–5 scale: 1 means 'we have it but nobody uses it,' 5 means 'we use it daily and trust the output.'

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "My team has access to these AI tools: [list them] with these readiness levels: [list your ratings]. For the lowest-rated tool, give me a 3-step onboarding plan I could run in a single team meeting."
Pick the most practical suggestion and block 30 minutes on your calendar to try it.
Share your readiness ratings and your onboarding plan with the group — this is a problem that gets easier when teams compare notes.

homework.title: Build a reading list that actually fits your life right now.
homework.body: Sunday night is a good time to queue up something worth reading. But most book recommendations are generic because the request is generic. Tonight, try a technique that fixes that: tell AI to rank its picks by a criterion that matters to you. Use any free AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity):
homework.prompt:
"I want to read more but I have about [X] minutes a day. Here's what I'm in the mood for: [describe it — e.g., 'something that changes how I think about work,' 'a novel I can't put down,' 'nonfiction that's practical, not preachy']. Give me 5 book recommendations, ranked by which one I'll actually finish given my time and mood. For each, tell me in one sentence why it fits and roughly how long it takes to read at my pace."

The technique — asking AI to rank by a criterion that matters to you — works far better than a plain 'recommend me books.' Try adding 'ranked by [what matters most to me]' to any recommendation request and you'll get answers shaped to your real life, not someone else's list.

2026-08-04.intro: Tuesday. Three patterns worth noticing: the hidden cost of using AI on everything, what your team's tool choices are telling you, and the one question that separates useful AI from noise.

trends.title: The teams getting real value from AI are using it on fewer things, not more
trends.body: Gartner's 2026 Future of Work Trends report found that the highest-performing teams aren't the ones using AI on everything — they're the ones being selective. When AI is applied broadly without quality checks, the result is what Gartner calls workslop: output that looks polished but needs fixing downstream. 40% of workers encountered it in a single month, with each case taking nearly two hours to sort out. The teams pulling ahead are the ones choosing where AI adds real value — and skipping the rest.

slants.strategy: The question isn't 'can AI do this?' — it's 'does the output need to be right on the first pass?' Treat quality gates as a planning input, not an afterthought.
slants.leaders: If your team is spending hours cleaning up AI output, the tool is creating work, not saving it. Ask where quality actually matters and protect those tasks from autopilot.
slants.operations: Every AI draft that needs two hours of repair is a net loss. Keep a short list of tasks where AI's first pass is genuinely good enough — and use it there.
slants.pm: Add a quality-check step to any workflow where AI generates deliverables. The time saved on drafting disappears if nobody reviews before sending.
slants.admin: If you've been fixing AI-generated documents that landed on your desk half-done, you're not imagining the extra work. Name it and push back.

steps: Think of one task where you or a teammate recently used AI to produce a deliverable — a draft, a summary, a report, a presentation.
Honestly assess: did the output go straight to its audience, or did someone have to rework it? Estimate how long the rework took.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "Here is a task I regularly use AI for: [describe it]. What are the three most common quality problems AI output has for this kind of work, and how can I check for each one in under five minutes?"
Try the quality-check routine on your next AI-generated draft and note whether it catches anything.
Share your quick-check routine in the group — others are dealing with the same cleanup problem and will save time from your approach.

trends.title: Your team already found their own AI tools — and that's a signal worth reading
trends.body: Gartner's 2026 Global Labor Market Survey, covering 12,004 employees across 40 countries, surfaced a number that should start a conversation: 88% of employees with access to enterprise AI tools are also using personal AI tools for business tasks. These hybrid users are 1.7 times more likely to report significant time savings. But 73% of the most productive AI users are managers and executives — individual contributors, the people doing the most automatable work, are the least supported.

slants.strategy: If 88% of your workforce is supplementing enterprise AI with personal tools, that's a product-experience signal about your current tooling — not an employee behavior problem.
slants.leaders: Your team isn't going rogue — they're working around a gap. Ask what they're using and why. You'll learn more about your AI strategy's blind spots than any usage dashboard will show you.
slants.operations: The people closest to the repetitive work are the ones finding their own tools. That's useful intelligence — capture what they've figured out and share it across the team.
slants.pm: If project team members are using personal AI tools to get work done faster, the risk isn't the tools — it's not knowing what data is flowing through them. A quick inventory closes that gap.
slants.admin: If you've found a personal AI tool that handles a task better than the approved one, you're not doing something wrong. Share what you've found with your team lead — it might improve the toolkit for everyone.

steps: List the AI tools you currently use for work — both the ones your company provides and any personal ones you've tried on your own.
For each personal tool, note what it does that the enterprise tool doesn't — or doesn't do well enough.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "I've been using [name the personal tool] for [task] because [reason the enterprise tool fell short]. What features or prompt techniques should I try in my enterprise AI tool to get the same result without using a personal tool?"
Try the suggestion on a real, non-confidential task and see if it closes the gap.
Share what you learned in the group — the pattern of what's missing from enterprise tools is useful for everyone, and your workaround might help someone else.

trends.title: The best AI use cases aren't the fast ones — they're the painful ones
trends.body: A finding from the same Gartner report that flips the usual productivity narrative: optimizing individual employees' use of AI tools, on its own, does not lead to growth or cost reduction. What does work is applying AI selectively to the tasks that create the most friction — the ones that drain energy, require excessive coordination, or demand tedious formatting with no judgment involved. Gartner's recommendation: effort, not time saved, is the most reliable indicator of where AI should reshape work.

slants.strategy: Audit your team's work by effort, not hours. The tasks that drain the most energy for the least strategic value are where AI delivers the most meaningful return.
slants.leaders: Ask your team one question this week: 'What's the most draining part of your regular work?' The answer is where AI should go first — not the tasks that are merely slow.
slants.operations: The biggest wins aren't shaving five minutes off an email. They're eliminating the 90-minute formatting exercise nobody wants to do.
slants.pm: When prioritizing AI use cases for a project, rank candidates by effort required, not time consumed. The tasks people avoid are the ones with the best adoption potential.
slants.admin: Think about the task you dread most each week. That's your best candidate for AI — not because it's the longest, but because it takes the most out of you.

steps: Open a blank note and list your five most effort-intensive tasks from this past week — not the longest ones, but the most draining.
Rank them from most to least draining. Be honest about which ones you avoid or procrastinate on.

Pick the top one and open your company-approved AI tool. Paste: "This is a task I find very draining: [describe it in detail, without confidential info]. Show me how to use AI to handle the most tedious part of it, step by step. Focus on the piece that takes the most effort, not just the piece that takes the most time."
Try the approach on a real, non-confidential version of the task this week.
Share your top effort-drainer and how you tackled it in the group — the most draining tasks tend to be the same across roles, and your solution will save someone else real energy.

homework.title: Practice the conversation you've been putting off.
homework.body: Everyone has one — a conversation you keep delaying because you're not sure how to start, what they'll say, or how you'll handle it. Tonight, try something that makes AI surprisingly useful: have it play the other person. Use any free AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity):
homework.prompt:
"I need to have a conversation with [someone — a family member, friend, neighbor, partner] about [topic]. I'm nervous because [what worries you about it]. Play their role and respond the way they realistically would. I'll say my opening line and you react — then coach me on what landed well and what I could say differently."

The technique — having AI simulate the other person's responses — lets you rehearse without the stakes. You hear how your words might land, spot the weak points in your approach, and walk into the real conversation calmer. Try it on anything you've been avoiding — the practice round takes the edge off.

2026-08-06.intro: Thursday. Three pieces of good news hiding in the data: the skills that matter most in an AI economy are the ones you already have, there's a clear pattern behind the AI projects that actually succeed, and the next big operational redesign at your company needs the people who know how things really work.

trends.title: Your best skills just became more valuable
trends.body: McKinsey Global Institute mapped roughly 10,500 skills by how much automation reshapes them — and the results are encouraging. The skills with the lowest automation exposure? Leadership, coaching, negotiation, and empathy. The ones most affected are narrow technical tasks like SQL queries and invoice processing. More than 70% of skills employers seek today are used in both automatable and non-automatable work, which means most skills aren't going away — they're being upgraded. Problem-solving becomes problem-framing. Your experience gets more valuable, not less.

slants.strategy: Your ability to frame the right question is becoming more valuable than running the analysis — that's a skill worth investing in across your team.
slants.leaders: The skills your team built over years — coaching, negotiating, reading a room — are the ones AI reinforces, not replaces. Name that value and build on it.
slants.operations: Your deep knowledge of how processes actually work is what makes you the best person to shape where AI fits. That expertise is appreciating, not depreciating.
slants.pm: Problem-framing is your wheelhouse — scoping, prioritizing, and asking the right questions is what PMs already do. AI just makes that skill more central.
slants.admin: The judgment calls you make every day — tone, timing, context, what the executive actually needs — are in the most durable skill category. That's your strength.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and pick one skill you use daily — summarizing, scheduling, reviewing, analyzing, coordinating.

Paste this prompt: "Here is a skill I use regularly at work: [describe it]. How is AI changing how this skill is applied — not whether it's needed, but how the best practitioners use it differently now? Give me one specific way the skill is shifting and one example of what 'upgraded' looks like."
Read the response and compare it to your own experience — does the shift it describes match what you're already seeing?
Paste this follow-up: "Now give me a 2-step exercise I can do this week to practice the upgraded version of this skill, using AI as a tool rather than a replacement."
Share your skill shift with the group — what's changing about how you apply it, and what stayed the same?

trends.title: Successful AI projects share one simple habit
trends.body: Gartner surveyed more than 3,400 organizations investing in agentic AI and found a clear pattern: the projects that succeed are the ones that start with defined goals, cost guardrails, and a governance plan. Over 40% of agentic AI projects are expected to be cut by end of 2027 — not because the technology doesn't work, but because nobody set a clear target for what success looks like. The good news? That's entirely within your control. The teams that scope AI the way they'd scope any strategic initiative are the ones seeing real returns.

slants.strategy: Define what success looks like in measurable terms before your next AI initiative kicks off — the clearest targets produce the strongest results.
slants.leaders: The most valuable thing you can do for an AI pilot right now is give it a clear mission — what does it need to deliver, by when, and how will you know it's working?
slants.operations: Build in a 90-day checkpoint with clear criteria: is this saving time, reducing errors, or improving quality? A simple check-in keeps good projects on track.
slants.pm: Scope agentic AI the way you'd scope any project — goals, budget, timeline, and success criteria. That discipline is exactly why the best AI projects have a PM behind them.
slants.admin: Your feedback on whether an AI tool is actually saving time is one of the most valuable signals a pilot can get. Speak up — it helps the whole team invest wisely.

steps: Think about an AI tool or feature your team adopted in the last six months. Has anyone measured whether it's delivering real value?

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "My team adopted [name the tool or feature] for [describe the task]. We haven't formally measured its impact. Help me design a simple 3-question evaluation: one question about time saved, one about output quality, and one about whether it created any new work or problems. Keep it something I could answer in 5 minutes."
Answer the three questions honestly based on your own experience with the tool.
Paste the results back and ask: "Based on these answers, should we double down on this tool, adjust how we use it, or consider dropping it? Give me a one-sentence recommendation."
Share your evaluation with the group — the honest assessments help everyone make better decisions about which tools earn their keep.

trends.title: The next big redesign needs you in the room
trends.body: Gartner surveyed 469 CEOs and found that 80% are actively rethinking how their operations work in an AI-assisted world. Today, 54% say automation only touches specific tasks. By 2028, most expect to expand into AI-assisted decision-making and smarter workflows. That means how work gets done at your company is about to be redesigned — and the people who understand how it actually works today, not just how it's drawn on a slide, are exactly who that redesign needs most.

slants.strategy: The best operational redesigns start with the people who run the current operation. Get their perspective into the planning room early — it's the highest-value input you have.
slants.leaders: This is your team's moment to shape what comes next. The operational knowledge your people carry is the design input that makes the difference between a plan that works and one that doesn't.
slants.operations: You know where the workarounds live, where the handoffs work, and where the process on paper doesn't match reality. That knowledge is your seat at the table — claim it.
slants.pm: Operational redesigns are multi-quarter programs, and PM skills are what keep them from stalling at the whiteboard. If scoping hasn't started, this is your opening.
slants.admin: The workflows you manage are being rethought. The people who can document how things actually work — not how they're supposed to — will have the most influence on what comes next.

steps: Pick one operational process you're involved in — approvals, reporting, scheduling, procurement, onboarding — anything that follows a repeatable pattern.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "Here's an operational process I'm part of: [describe it in detail, without confidential info]. Map out the current workflow step by step, then identify which steps could be enhanced by AI and which ones require human judgment. Be specific about why each judgment step needs a person."
Compare the AI's map to how the process actually works in practice. Note where it's accurate and where it misses the informal steps, workarounds, or judgment calls only an insider would know.

Paste this follow-up: "Here's what your map missed: [list the informal steps or workarounds]. Redraft the workflow including these realities. Which steps are the best candidates for AI now, and which ones need a human even more than before?"
Share your process map with the group — the gap between how a process is designed and how it actually works is where the most valuable redesign insights live.

homework.title: Build your perfect weekend movie marathon — without scrolling for an hour.
homework.body: The irony of having every streaming service: you spend more time choosing than watching. Tonight, try something different — instead of telling AI a genre, describe the mood you're going for. Use any free AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity):
homework.prompt:
"I want to set up a movie or TV marathon for this weekend. Instead of a genre, here's the mood I'm going for: [describe it — e.g., 'something that makes me feel like anything is possible,' 'cozy and low-stakes,' 'smart and gripping but not stressful,' 'nostalgic without being cheesy']. I have about [X] hours. Build me a marathon — 3 to 5 picks, in the order I should watch them, with a one-line reason each one fits the mood. Include at least one I probably haven't seen."

The technique — describing the mood you want instead of naming a category — works for more than movies. Try it next time you ask AI for music, books, recipes, or even meeting formats. 'I want to feel energized' gets sharper results than 'give me something upbeat.'

2026-08-07.intro: Friday. Three patterns to carry into the weekend: how to spot the candidates who actually know how to work with AI, the biggest productivity drain at work already has a fix, and the institutional knowledge in your head is worth more than you think.

trends.title: Hiring is about to test for two things at once — and you need to know what to look for
trends.body: Gartner's strategic predictions paint a dual picture of where hiring is headed. By 2027, 75% of hiring processes will include formal testing for AI proficiency — not just for technical roles, but across marketing, finance, operations, and HR. But here's the twist: in the same timeframe, 50% of organizations will also require "AI-free" assessments to verify that candidates can think, reason, and solve problems without AI assistance. If you're involved in hiring, you now need to evaluate for both — and the candidates who can do both are the ones worth fighting for.

slants.strategy: Build both checks into your hiring criteria now. The candidates who can use AI effectively and reason independently are the ones who'll strengthen your team's strategic capacity.
slants.leaders: When you're interviewing, ask candidates to walk through a problem twice — once describing how they'd use AI, and once describing how they'd solve it without it. The contrast tells you more than either answer alone.
slants.operations: The best ops hires will be the ones who know when to lean on AI and when to trust their own troubleshooting instincts. Test for both in your interview process.
slants.pm: When evaluating candidates, look for people who can use AI to accelerate their work but can also scope, prioritize, and make trade-offs on their own. That combination is becoming the bar.
slants.admin: If you're part of the hiring process — screening resumes, scheduling interviews, sitting on panels — knowing what AI proficiency looks like in practice helps you spot the strongest candidates.

steps: Think about the last person you interviewed or helped evaluate for a role on your team. Did the process test for any AI-related skills?

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "I'm involved in hiring for [describe the role or team]. Help me design two short interview questions: one that tests whether a candidate can use AI effectively for this type of work, and one that tests whether they can think critically and solve problems without AI. Each question should take 5 minutes to answer and reveal genuine skill, not rehearsed buzzwords."
Review the questions and adjust them based on what you know about the role — the AI gives you a starting structure, but your context makes it real.
Share your two-question approach in the group — building a library of AI-aware interview questions helps everyone hire stronger.

trends.title: Your meetings aren't unproductive — they're undocumented
trends.body: Metrigy's AI for Business Success study of 1,100 companies found that 42% are planning to roll out AI meeting assistants in the next year, and nearly 40% have already deployed them. The reason is hard to argue with: the average knowledge worker now spends over 21 hours a week in meetings, 71% of which senior managers call unproductive, and nearly half of all action items discussed are never captured. That's not a meeting problem — it's a systems problem. AI meeting assistants handle the capture layer so people can focus on the thinking layer.

slants.strategy: If your strategy depends on meetings to align people, and half the action items vanish afterward, AI capture isn't a nice-to-have — it's a reliability upgrade for your operating rhythm.
slants.leaders: Ask your team a simple question: "After our last three meetings, could you find every action item without digging through your notes?" The answer tells you whether meeting capture is worth prioritizing.
slants.operations: Every handoff that depends on someone remembering what was said in a meeting is a failure point. AI meeting tools turn verbal agreements into trackable commitments.
slants.pm: Half your project risks live in meeting notes nobody wrote down. AI meeting capture is the cheapest risk-reduction tool available right now.
slants.admin: If you've ever spent 30 minutes reconstructing what was decided in a meeting so you could act on it, you already know the problem. AI meeting tools solve exactly this.

steps: Count your meetings from this past week. Estimate how many hours total — include the prep time and follow-up, not just the calendar blocks.
Pick one meeting from the week where something important was decided or assigned. Can you find the specific action items right now, without digging through notes or asking someone?

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "I spent approximately [X] hours in meetings this week. Here's a list of my recurring meetings and their purposes: [list them]. Help me identify which meetings could benefit most from AI-assisted note capture and action-item tracking, and which ones might not need to be meetings at all."
Try the suggestion on one meeting next week — either add AI capture or convert the meeting to a different format.
Share your meeting audit results in the group — the total hours and the 'this didn't need to be a meeting' list tend to surprise people.

trends.title: The knowledge in your head is worth trillions — and most companies aren't capturing it
trends.body: A joint Deloitte and eGain report puts a number on what's being lost: more than 30 million Americans will turn 65 in the next four years, representing $6.9 to $9.6 trillion in institutional knowledge at risk. And 92% of organizations aren't effectively capturing it. The knowledge that matters most — why a process was designed that way, which vendor workaround actually works, how to read the room in a client meeting — lives in people's heads, not in documentation. If you're one of those people, your expertise just became a strategic asset.

slants.strategy: The institutional knowledge walking out your door isn't in your documentation — it's in the judgment calls, the workarounds, and the context nobody wrote down. Build a capture plan before the retirement wave hits your team.
slants.leaders: Identify the three people on your team whose departure would cause the most knowledge loss. Start structured knowledge capture with them this quarter — not as an exit task, but as a current one.
slants.operations: The workarounds, tribal knowledge, and 'it works this way because of that one time' context you carry is irreplaceable. Documenting it now makes it durable — and makes you indispensable in a different way.
slants.pm: Every project has institutional context that isn't in the project plan — the stakeholder preferences, the historical decisions, the unofficial dependencies. Capturing it is a PM value-add that compounds over time.
slants.admin: You know things nobody else knows — how the approval chain actually works, who needs to be CC'd, which process on paper doesn't match reality. That knowledge is genuinely valuable. Start writing it down.

steps: Think about one thing you know at work that isn't written down anywhere — a process quirk, a vendor relationship, a historical decision that still affects how things are done.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "I have institutional knowledge about [describe the topic] that isn't documented anywhere. Interview me about it — ask me 5 specific questions to extract the most important details, the 'why' behind the decisions, and the context a new person would need to understand it. Then turn my answers into a short knowledge document someone else could use."
Review the document and fill in anything the AI missed — especially the judgment calls and the reasons behind them.
Save the document somewhere your team can find it, and share your experience in the group — what did you know that you didn't realize was undocumented?

homework.title: Plan a game night that actually fits your group — not just the internet's top 10.
homework.body: Generic game recommendations assume you have a group of enthusiastic adults who all love the same things. Real life is messier: mixed ages, different energy levels, someone who hates competition, someone who gets bored easily. Tonight, try a technique that fixes that. Use any free AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity):
homework.prompt:
"I want to plan a game night for [number] people. Here's who's coming: [describe the group — ages, personalities, what they enjoy, any landmines to avoid like 'my cousin hates trivia' or 'two people are super competitive']. Recommend 3 games we could play, in the order we should play them, with a one-line reason each one fits this specific group. Include one game none of us have probably tried before."

The technique — describing the people, not just the activity — works any time you ask AI for recommendations. 'Plan a dinner for 6' gets generic. 'Plan a dinner for 6 where two are vegetarian, one is adventurous, and the host hates cooking under pressure' gets useful.

2026-08-08.intro: Saturday. Three patterns hiding in plain sight: where your AI budget is actually going, how AI is shaping customer decisions before your sales team picks up the phone, and a quiet accountability gap forming between employees and the AI they're asked to stand behind.

trends.title: Speed is the easy AI win — the harder one is worth twice as much
trends.body: A Gartner survey of 204 finance leaders reveals a misalignment that explains a lot of AI frustration: 45% of CFOs say their AI investments lean toward productivity, while only 20% lean toward decision quality. The gap matters because organizations investing in AI that changes decisions — not just speeds up tasks — are more than twice as likely to report significant value (Gartner, July 2026).

slants.strategy: If your AI portfolio is concentrated on making things faster, you're optimizing a curve that flattens. The compounding value comes from AI that changes which decisions get made and how.
slants.leaders: Ask your team a simple question: 'Which of our AI projects changes a decision, not just a task?' If nobody can name one, your investment mix needs rebalancing.
slants.operations: Productivity AI hits a ceiling once a workflow is automated. The next step is feeding those efficiency gains into better business decisions upstream.
slants.pm: When prioritizing AI initiatives, weight decision-quality outcomes higher than time-saved metrics. The projects that change decisions deliver more durable value than the ones that speed up tasks.
slants.admin: The admin tasks most likely to grow in value are the ones that involve judgment and context — the decision-quality layer, not the speed layer.

steps: List the AI tools or features you use (or your team uses) at work this week. Next to each, write whether it primarily saves time or improves a decision.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "I work in [your role]. Here are the AI tools and features I use: [list them]. For each one, help me identify whether it's primarily saving time (productivity) or improving a decision (decision quality). Then suggest one way I could shift one productivity use toward a decision-quality use."
Review the suggestion. Does it point to a decision in your workflow that could be sharper, not just faster?
Share your productivity-vs-decision split in the group — the pattern across roles is usually eye-opening.

trends.title: AI is describing your business to customers before you get the chance
trends.body: Harvard Business Review profiles three companies that discovered AI tools were shaping customer perceptions before any human conversation happened. A manufacturer improved sales by screening AI-generated inquiries; a hotel learned to monitor how AI described its property; a software company replaced periodic reviews with continuous monitoring of AI-generated market perceptions. The vendor shortlist is narrowing — average B2B shortlists have shrunk from 3.2 to roughly 2.5 as AI pre-filters options before a sales team even gets a pitch (HBR, July 2026).

slants.strategy: AI is a new channel you can't control but can influence. If you're not auditing how ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Copilot describe your products, you're invisible in a growing share of buying decisions.
slants.leaders: Ask someone on your team to query three AI tools about your company's product or service. What comes back is what your next customer sees first — and it's worth knowing before they do.
slants.operations: Your public-facing content now serves two audiences: humans and AI. Structured, clear, factual content performs better in both channels.
slants.pm: If your project involves any customer-facing deliverable, add a step: 'How would an AI tool summarize this?' The answer shapes perception before your launch does.
slants.admin: If you maintain public-facing content — websites, directories, FAQs — know that AI tools are pulling from it to answer customer questions. Accuracy and clarity matter more than ever.

steps: Pick a product, service, or team you work with that has a public presence.
Open a free AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity) and ask: "What can you tell me about [your company/product/service]? What are its strengths and weaknesses compared to alternatives?"
Read the response carefully. Is it accurate? Is anything outdated, missing, or misleading? Note the gaps.
Now ask a follow-up: "Where are you getting this information? What sources are you drawing from?"
Share what you found in the group — the gap between what AI says about your organization and what's actually true is usually surprising.

trends.title: Ask your team to explain an AI decision — the pause tells you everything
trends.body: A multi-year field study across banking, recruitment, and biotech found that when AI is embedded in core decisions, frontline workers quietly mask, reinterpret, and substitute their own explanations for AI outputs to preserve professional credibility. At one bank, loan officers cited common expert reasons for AI-driven rejections even when those weren't the model's actual reasoning — and customers noticed. The one organization that avoided this built an interpretive layer: access to underlying data, developer feedback loops, and shared language around the model's logic (HBR, July 2026).

slants.strategy: If your strategy depends on AI-driven decisions at the front line, the interpretive layer between model and customer is a strategic requirement — not a training afterthought.
slants.leaders: Employees won't raise their hand to say 'I don't understand the AI's decision' if they feel they're expected to own it. Create space for that honesty before it costs you a customer.
slants.operations: Process design must include how employees explain AI outputs, not just how they receive them. If the explanation step isn't designed, employees will improvise — and that becomes unmanaged risk.
slants.pm: When scoping AI deployments, budget for the last mile: documentation, feedback loops, and training that let the people delivering AI decisions actually understand them.
slants.admin: You're often the person between the system and the person asking 'why did this happen?' Making that interpretive role visible — and supported — is valuable.

steps: Think about a decision or recommendation at work that's influenced by AI or an automated system — it could be a report, a score, a suggestion, or an approval.
Ask yourself honestly: could you explain to a colleague or customer exactly why the system produced that output? Not what it said — but why.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "I work in [your role] and we use AI or automated systems for [describe the decision]. Help me write three plain-language questions I should be able to answer about any AI-generated decision before I communicate it to someone else. Focus on questions that build genuine understanding, not just talking points."
Try answering those three questions for a recent AI-assisted decision. Note where you're confident and where you're guessing.
Share your three questions in the group — building a shared explainability checklist helps everyone communicate AI decisions more honestly.

homework.title: Pick a cuisine you've never cooked and let AI walk you through the first dish.
homework.body: You don't need to be a cook to try this — you just need a kitchen and some curiosity. Open any free AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity):
homework.prompt:
"I want to try cooking [a cuisine you've always been curious about — Thai, Ethiopian, Japanese, Peruvian, whatever draws you]. I'm a [beginner/decent/confident] cook. I have about an hour and a regular grocery store nearby. Recommend one dish that's a good entry point, explain why it's a good first dish for this cuisine, and give me a step-by-step recipe with exactly what I need to buy. If any ingredient might be hard to find, suggest a substitute."

The technique — giving your skill level and constraints upfront — stops AI from recommending something impressive but impractical. It works any time you're asking for advice in unfamiliar territory.

2026-08-09.intro: Sunday. Three patterns to sit with before the week starts: the gap between using AI and actually being changed by it, a compliance deadline that just landed this month with most companies unprepared, and a clarity gap between the C-suite and the people who actually execute AI strategy.

trends.title: Most companies have adopted AI — very few have actually changed
trends.body: Publicis Sapient surveyed 1,550 AI decision-makers for its 2026 Global Enterprise AI Report and found a gap that explains a lot of AI frustration: 73% of enterprises say AI is used regularly across most business processes, but only 10% say it's core to how their business actually operates. The disconnect isn't about tools — it's about operating models. 42% say their organizations aren't set up to capture AI's value, and 22% identify the way their organization operates as the primary barrier to AI success.

slants.strategy: The strategic question isn't 'are we using AI?' — it's 'has anything we do actually changed because of it?' Adoption without integration means you're paying for capability your operating model can't absorb.
slants.leaders: Ask your team: 'Name one workflow that's fundamentally different because of AI — not faster, different.' If the answer takes too long, you're in the 73%, not the 10%.
slants.operations: If your AI tools are accelerating legacy workflows rather than replacing them, you're compounding efficiency on a process that may not need to exist in its current form.
slants.pm: Tag each AI initiative in your portfolio: 'bolt-on' (speeds up an existing process) vs. 'redesign' (changes the process itself). The ratio tells you where the value ceiling is.
slants.admin: If AI automates one step in your workflow but everything else stays the same, the process wasn't redesigned — it was patched. The real efficiency comes from rethinking the full flow.

steps: Pick one process or workflow you manage or contribute to regularly — something you do every week.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "I have a recurring workflow that goes like this: [describe the process — steps, tools, handoffs, approvals]. Right now, AI helps with [describe any AI involvement, or say 'none yet']. Tell me honestly: is AI bolted on to an old process, or has the process actually changed because of it? If it's a bolt-on, suggest one way the workflow itself could be redesigned with AI as a core part — not just a speed boost."
Read the suggestion and ask yourself: would that redesigned workflow be better, or does the current process exist for a reason the AI doesn't see?
Share your bolt-on vs. redesign assessment in the group — the pattern across roles is usually revealing.

trends.title: The biggest AI compliance deadline of the year just landed — and most companies weren't ready
trends.body: August 2, 2026 was the binding enforcement date for the EU AI Act's high-risk AI system obligations — and most companies missed it unprepared. The Cloud Security Alliance reports that 78% of enterprises had not taken meaningful steps toward compliance, and over half lacked even a systematic inventory of AI systems in production. Fines can reach €35 million or 7% of global annual turnover. Whether or not your company operates in Europe, the governance patterns being set now are shaping AI accountability everywhere.

slants.strategy: Regulatory compliance is downstream of good governance. If you don't know what AI systems you're running and what decisions they influence, the compliance gap is a symptom of a bigger strategic blind spot.
slants.leaders: Ask your team: 'Can we list every AI system we use and what decisions it affects?' If the answer involves spreadsheets and guesswork, that's the gap to close — regulation or not.
slants.operations: Over half of enterprises lack a systematic AI inventory. If your ops team can't enumerate AI systems in production, that's risk management 101 — compliance deadline or not.
slants.pm: Compliance deadlines create clear requirements and hard dates — which makes them projects. If your organization hasn't scoped this one yet, the PM who steps up will be doing leadership a favor.
slants.admin: If you track systems, licenses, or vendor contracts, you may already know more about what AI tools are actually in use than the compliance team does. That knowledge has new value.

steps: Think about the AI tools and automated systems you interact with at work — Copilot, chatbots, recommendation engines, scoring models, anything that uses AI or machine learning.
Make a quick list: tool name, what it does, and what decisions or outputs it influences.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "I've listed the AI systems I interact with at work: [paste your list]. For each one, help me categorize it: does it make or influence decisions about people (hiring, performance, access), safety, or legal/financial outcomes? Those are the categories most likely to attract regulatory scrutiny under frameworks like the EU AI Act."
Review the categorization. Were any systems in higher-risk categories than you expected?
