Help me break down exactly what AI made possible that wasn't before — was it speed, quality, scope, or a combination? Then suggest two adjacent tasks in my role where the same approach could unlock similar results."
Review the suggestions. Pick the one that feels most immediately useful and try it this week.
Share your 'couldn't have made this a year ago' example in the group — the range of answers will surprise you.

trends.title: AI-related learning just surged fivefold — and the fastest-growing skill isn't technical
trends.body: Udemy's 2026 Global Learning & Skills Trends Report, drawn from data across 17,000+ enterprise customers, shows AI-related enrollments surpassing 11 million globally — a fivefold increase in one year. The surprise is where the growth is landing. Technical AI courses are surging (Microsoft Copilot content up 3,400% year-over-year), but adaptive skills are keeping pace: critical thinking rose 37% and decision-making rose 38%. The companies getting it right are treating AI fluency as a company-wide operating system, not a technical silo (Udemy, 2026).

slants.strategy: The learning data says your people want to grow — and the fastest-rising skills are judgment and critical thinking, not just prompting. Build your upskilling plan around both.
slants.leaders: When 11 million people enroll voluntarily, the appetite is real. Your job is to channel it — connect the learning to actual workflows so the skills stick.
slants.operations: Decision-making skill demand is up 38%. That tracks: as AI handles more routine analysis, the human role shifts toward better judgment calls on messier problems.
slants.pm: Critical thinking is now a skill people are actively building, not just listing on resumes. Factor that into how you staff projects — the people investing in it are becoming your strongest contributors.
slants.admin: The learning surge includes you. If you've been building AI skills on your own time, you're part of the fastest-growing professional development wave in a decade — and it shows in your work.

steps: Rate yourself honestly on two scales, 1–5: (a) your comfort using AI tools at work, and (b) your confidence making judgment calls when AI gives you conflicting or incomplete answers.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "I rated my AI tool comfort at [a] out of 5 and my judgment confidence with AI at [b] out of 5. Based on these scores, suggest three specific learning priorities for me — one technical AI skill, one critical thinking exercise, and one decision-making practice. Keep each suggestion to something I can start this week in under 30 minutes."
Pick one of the three suggestions and block 20 minutes on your calendar this week to try it.
Share your two ratings and your chosen learning priority in the group — the pattern across the team will show where to invest together.

trends.title: The workers building the strongest AI habits know exactly when to think for themselves
trends.body: GoTo's Pulse of Work 2026, surveying 2,500 employees and IT leaders globally, surfaced a striking moment of self-awareness across the workforce: 50% of workers say they rely on AI too much, and 39% say that reliance is making them less intelligent. Among Gen Z, that number climbs to 46%. The positive read: workers who can name the dependency can manage it. The ones who deliberately choose when to think independently — and when to let AI handle the routine — are building the most durable professional advantage.

slants.strategy: The strategist who uses AI for research but does the synthesis solo is building a different kind of muscle than the one who outsources both. Choose which thinking you keep sharp.
slants.leaders: Normalize this conversation on your team: 'Where does AI make your work better, and where does it make your thinking lazier?' The teams that answer honestly are the ones improving fastest.
slants.operations: If you can troubleshoot a process failure without reaching for AI first, that's a skill worth maintaining — and it's one that fewer people will have next year.
slants.pm: Before defaulting to AI for your next project plan or risk assessment, try drafting the first version yourself. The gap between your instinct and AI's output teaches you where your judgment is strongest.
slants.admin: Your ability to read a situation, catch a tone problem, or know the right person to loop in — those are skills AI can't build for you. Keep exercising them.

steps: Think about your last full workday. List the three tasks where you used AI the most — drafting, researching, analyzing, summarizing, anything.
For each task, honestly label it: "AI made this better", "AI made this faster but not better", or "I could have done this just as well without AI."

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "Here are three tasks I used AI for recently: [list them with your labels]. Based on these, help me build a personal decision tree: when should I use AI, when should I use AI as a second opinion only, and when should I do the work independently? Make it specific to my role and these tasks."
Save your decision tree somewhere visible — a sticky note, a pinned note, wherever you'll actually see it.
Share your split and one surprise in the group — the patterns across roles are worth comparing.

homework.title: Got a bill you've been meaning to negotiate? Let AI coach you through the call.
homework.body: Cable, internet, insurance, gym membership — there's almost always room to negotiate, and the hardest part is knowing what to say. Tonight, pick one recurring bill you suspect you're overpaying and use any free AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity) to prep the call:
homework.prompt:
"I pay $[amount] per month for [service] with [provider]. I've been a customer for [how long]. Help me prepare to negotiate a lower rate: What's a realistic target price? What should I say when I call? What will they likely counter with, and how should I respond? Role-play the conversation with me — you be the retention agent, and I'll practice my side."

The technique — having AI play the other side of a conversation before you have it for real — is one of the most practical uses you'll find. It works for salary negotiations, tough conversations with a landlord, even preparing for a difficult talk with a family member. The rehearsal builds confidence, and the script gives you a starting point you can adapt in the moment.

2026-08-21.intro: Friday. Three things to carry into the weekend: the companies getting the most from AI are aiming it somewhere most aren't, the readiness gap has a fix that's simpler than you'd think, and the teams pulling ahead are designing something most haven't started yet.

trends.title: The companies capturing the most AI value are aiming it at growth
trends.body: PwC's 2026 AI Performance Study surveyed 1,217 senior executives across 25 sectors and found a clear pattern: the top 20% of AI-performing companies capture 74% of AI's total economic value, earning roughly 7.2 times the financial gains of their peers with operating margins four points higher. The difference isn't budget or tools — it's aim. Leaders pointed AI at new revenue and business model reinvention, while the rest focused primarily on cutting costs (PwC, 2026).

slants.strategy: The biggest AI returns are going to organizations that aim AI at growth — new revenue, new offerings, new ways to serve. If your AI business case starts with growth, the efficiency gains follow.
slants.leaders: The leaders in PwC's top 20% directed AI at growth opportunities, not just cost reduction. Your highest-leverage move is shaping where AI gets aimed — toward what your team can build and deliver next.
slants.operations: The operational teams generating the most AI value are the ones connected to revenue outcomes. Look at where AI currently saves time in your processes and ask what it could help create instead.
slants.pm: Projects framed around AI-enabled growth — new capabilities, faster time-to-market, better customer outcomes — are the ones seeing 7x returns. Frame your next AI initiative around what it builds.
slants.admin: The AI value story is shifting from 'do the same work faster' to 'do work that wasn't possible before.' The skills you're building now position you for the growth side of that equation.

steps: Pick one task or process in your role where AI currently saves you time — drafting, scheduling, analyzing, researching, anything.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "I currently use AI to [describe the task], and it mostly saves me time. Help me reimagine this same area for growth instead of efficiency. What could I create, offer, or deliver that wasn't possible before AI? Give me 3 specific ideas I could pitch to my team this month."
Review the three ideas. Which one would create the most value for your team or organization?
Share your best growth idea in the group — the shift from 'save time' to 'create value' opens up a different conversation.

trends.title: The AI readiness gap has a surprisingly simple fix
trends.body: Skillsoft's 2026 Workforce Readiness Report surveyed 2,000 workers across North America, the UK, and Germany and found a perception gap worth naming: 77% of leaders believe they've set employees up for AI success, but only 24% of individual contributors agree. That's a 53-point gap. Only 11% of individual contributors have had any formal AI skills assessment. The tools shipped — the preparation didn't.

slants.strategy: Before planning the next AI initiative, close the perception gap. A five-question readiness survey costs nothing and tells you whether your rollout is landing or just launching.
slants.leaders: If you believe your team is ready, ask them — directly and anonymously. The 53-point gap in this report suggests most leaders are surprised by the answers.
slants.operations: When only 11% of workers have had a formal skills assessment, you're running new tools on untested foundations. A lightweight self-assessment before rollout shifts the conversation from assumption to evidence.
slants.pm: Project timelines built on the assumption that the team is AI-ready are optimistic. A quick skills check before kickoff saves you from discovering the gap mid-sprint.
slants.admin: If you feel underprepared for AI despite using it every day, you're in the majority — and that's a training gap, not a personal one. Ask for the structured learning your role deserves.

steps: Rate your own AI readiness on a scale of 1–5, where 1 is 'I barely know where to start' and 5 is 'I'm confident and effective with AI tools.'
Now rate what you think your leadership believes your readiness level is.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "I work as a [your role]. I rated my AI readiness at [your score] out of 5, but I think my leadership would rate me at [their assumed score]. Help me identify the 3 specific skills or knowledge areas that would move my actual readiness up by one point. For each one, give me one concrete action I can take this week — no courses, no certifications, just something I can do in 20 minutes."
Pick one action and try it before the weekend. Share your readiness gap — your score versus what you think leadership assumes — in the group. The pattern tells a story.

trends.title: Teams that design clear human-AI handoffs are pulling ahead
trends.body: Deloitte's 2026 Global Human Capital Trends report, drawn from 9,000 leaders across 76 countries, names the step most organizations skip: only 6% of leaders say they are making progress in designing how humans and AI actually work together. Not deploying AI — designing the handoff. Who leads, who checks, how the two improve each other over time. Deloitte calls the result the "human advantage": the multiplier that emerges when human judgment is intentionally paired with AI's speed and scale.

slants.strategy: The next competitive edge isn't having AI — everyone does. It's designing the human-AI handoff for each workflow so the combination produces something neither could alone.
slants.leaders: If your team has AI tools but no clear agreement on who does what with the output, you're in the 94%. Start with one workflow: map where AI leads, where the human leads, and where they check each other.
slants.operations: Process documentation that says 'use AI for step 3' does 10% of the work. Documentation that says 'AI drafts, human validates against these criteria, then routes to this person' does 90%.
slants.pm: Add a human-AI handoff column to your project task list. For each AI-assisted task, name who starts it, who finishes it, and what the quality check looks like. That clarity prevents rework.
slants.admin: You're already designing handoffs every day — deciding what AI handles, what you fix, and when to start from scratch. That instinct is exactly what organizations need to formalize.

steps: Pick one workflow you do regularly that involves AI — drafting, summarizing, researching, scheduling, analyzing, anything.
Map it on paper or in a note: what does AI do, what do you do, and where does the handoff happen? Is there a clear quality check, or do you just eyeball it?

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "I have a workflow where I [describe the task]. Currently, AI handles [what AI does] and I handle [what you do]. Help me design a better handoff: where should AI lead, where should I lead, and what's the quality checkpoint at each transition? Give me a clear, step-by-step workflow I can follow."

Try the redesigned workflow once this week and note what changed. Share your before-and-after handoff design in the group — seeing how different roles structure these is where the real learning happens.

homework.title: It's Friday — plan your perfect end-of-summer getaway in 10 minutes.
homework.body: Labor Day is around the corner, summer is winding down, and whether you've got a long weekend or just a free Saturday, a quick trip is worth planning. Tonight, use any free AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity):
homework.prompt:
"I have [timeframe — a long weekend / one free day / a Saturday afternoon] and want to get away before summer ends. My budget is roughly $[amount]. I'm near [your city or region]. I like [what you enjoy — hiking, food, history, beaches, small towns, whatever]. Give me 3 trip options ranked by how much relaxation I'll get per dollar spent. For each one, include: where to go, one thing I shouldn't miss, and a rough cost breakdown."

The technique — asking AI to rank options by a specific criterion you care about — works for any decision with multiple good answers. Ranked by cost-per-value, by effort-to-impact, by time-to-enjoyment — the ranking forces the AI to evaluate tradeoffs instead of just listing options, and it forces you to name what actually matters to you.

2026-08-22.intro: Three patterns worth your attention: the AI investment that actually pays off targets expertise bottlenecks most teams overlook, a new approach to scaling professional knowledge just landed in production, and the barrier that kept sensitive work away from AI is falling fast.

trends.title: Your middle office is AI's biggest untapped opportunity
trends.body: HBR examined why heavy AI investment isn't translating to results and found a clear answer: most companies are overlooking expertise-heavy processes like contract review, compliance, and risk management. Research linking AI adoption surveys to payroll data found that the effect on earnings and hours after two years of broad AI rollouts was statistically indistinguishable from zero. The fix: target processes where difficult cases still get handed to specialists, build AI that learns from those experts as they work, and redirect freed time to higher-value decisions (HBR, August 2026).

slants.strategy: The biggest AI ROI sits in expertise bottlenecks — processes where tough calls queue up for specialists. Map those before greenlighting another chatbot rollout.
slants.leaders: Direct your next AI investment toward where your best people spend time on routine escalations. The leverage is freeing their judgment for harder problems, not replacing it.
slants.operations: Audit where difficult cases pile up waiting for an expert. Those queues are your highest-value AI targets — far more impactful than speeding up tasks that were already fast.
slants.pm: Scope your next AI project around measurable escalation reduction rather than time-saved. That framing connects AI output to business results leaders actually fund.
slants.admin: The expertise you've built — knowing which cases are routine and which need a specialist — is exactly the judgment AI needs to learn from. That pattern recognition makes you central to how AI gets deployed well.

steps: Think about your work over the past two weeks. Identify one process where a difficult case had to be escalated to someone more senior or specialized.
Write down what made it difficult — ambiguity, risk, unusual circumstances, missing information, or something else?

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "In my role as a [your role], we regularly escalate [type of case] to specialists when [what makes it difficult]. Help me identify: (1) what patterns in these escalations could AI learn to handle or pre-sort, (2) what should always stay with a human expert, and (3) how the specialist's time could be redirected to higher-value work if routine escalations dropped by half."
Review the response — does it match your intuition about where the real expertise bottleneck lives?
Share your escalation pattern and one insight in the group — the variety across roles shows where AI has the most room to help.

trends.title: Expert knowledge is becoming scalable — without losing the judgment behind it
trends.body: Axios reports that Twin1 AI emerged from stealth with $20 million in funding to build AI systems that preserve and scale individual professionals' expertise across an organization. Unlike generic assistants, these digital twins are grounded in the user's actual work context — emails, meetings, documents, decisions — preserving the judgment, relationships, and institutional knowledge that make specialists irreplaceable. Already deployed with professional services firms including Linklaters and Orrick, the model points toward a future where growing an organization's capability doesn't always require growing headcount (Axios, August 2026).

slants.strategy: Institutional knowledge is a strategic asset that walks out the door every time someone leaves. Building systems that capture and scale specialist judgment protects that investment.
slants.leaders: Develop your team by making senior expertise accessible to junior members through structured knowledge capture — not just shadowing or documentation, but systems that preserve how your best people think.
slants.operations: Identify the one or two people whose absence creates an immediate bottleneck. Their expertise is your scaling constraint — and now there are concrete approaches to extending it.
slants.pm: Projects slow down when they depend on one specialist's availability. Building the team's collective expertise into accessible systems reduces single-point-of-failure risk on every timeline.
slants.admin: The institutional knowledge you carry — who to call, how things actually work, what the real priorities are — is exactly the kind of expertise organizations are learning to value and scale.

steps: Think about the one person in your team or department who everyone goes to for a specific kind of question. What do they know that isn't written down anywhere?

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "On my team, one person is the go-to expert for [describe their specialty]. The knowledge they carry that isn't documented includes [list what you can — context, relationships, judgment calls, history]. Help me design a lightweight system to capture and share this expertise: what questions should I ask them, how should the answers be structured, and where should the knowledge live so others can access it without always interrupting the expert?"
Try one element of the system this week — even a single documented decision framework counts.
Share what you learned about capturing expertise in the group — the challenge of preserving judgment, not just facts, is universal.

trends.title: The trust barrier keeping sensitive work off AI just dropped
trends.body: OpenAI announced zero data retention for its frontier models, meaning eligible enterprise customers' prompts and responses are not retained after processing and are not available to OpenAI personnel or used for training. For teams that have been cautious about running contracts, strategy documents, or financial analyses through AI, this removes the most commonly cited objection. The broader signal: AI providers are now competing on enterprise trust, and organizations that limited AI to low-stakes tasks can begin expanding into work where the leverage is highest (OpenAI, August 2026).

slants.strategy: Revisit your AI governance framework — the categories of work you classified as too sensitive for AI may need updating now that zero-retention options exist at the frontier tier.
slants.leaders: If your team avoids AI for anything involving client data or strategy, update the conversation. The privacy landscape shifted — check whether your guidelines still reflect the actual risk.
slants.operations: Processes involving sensitive documents — contracts, compliance reviews, vendor assessments — that were excluded from AI pilots can now be reconsidered with zero-retention guarantees in place.
slants.pm: Project deliverables that touch confidential data no longer need to be carved out of AI-assisted workflows by default. Check with your security team whether updated policies open new scope.
slants.admin: Sensitive communications and documents you handle — executive scheduling, contract routing, confidential correspondence — may now be fair game for AI assistance under updated data policies. Ask your IT team what's changed.

steps: Think about one task you regularly do at work where you avoid AI because the content feels too sensitive — a contract, a personnel matter, a strategy document, anything.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "I work as a [your role]. I currently avoid using AI for [describe the sensitive task] because of data privacy concerns. Without me sharing any actual sensitive content, help me think through: (1) what questions I should ask my IT or security team about our AI data policies, (2) what a safe pilot would look like if the policies allow it, and (3) what guardrails I should put in place even with zero-retention guarantees."
Review the questions it generates — bring one or two to your IT team this week.
Share which category of sensitive work you'd most like to bring AI into — and what's holding you back — in the group. The patterns reveal where organizations can unlock the most value.

homework.title: Find your next great book in 5 minutes flat.
homework.body: End-of-summer reading lists are everywhere, but most of them are generic. Tonight, skip the bestseller lists and let AI interview you instead. Use any free AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity):
homework.prompt:
"Before you recommend anything, interview me. Ask me 5 questions about what I've read and enjoyed recently, what I'm in the mood for right now, and what I absolutely don't want. Then, based only on my answers, give me 3 book recommendations ranked by how confident you are I'll love them. For each one, tell me in one sentence why it fits what I told you."

The technique — asking AI to interview you before it answers — works for any recommendation problem. Restaurants, podcasts, gifts, vacation destinations, even career moves. When you let AI gather context first instead of guessing from a one-line request, the quality of its answers jumps dramatically. You're teaching it to think like a good friend who knows you, not a search engine ranking by popularity.

2026-08-23.intro: Three signals heading into a new week: a model that maps where AI value is compounding, a tooling shift that makes multi-model AI strategies practical, and a change in how leaders talk about AI and teams that tells you more than any forecast.

trends.title: A new model shows which capabilities AI will grow — and which it will compress
trends.body: Forrester released a model this week scoring more than 200 technology and service markets on how AI will reshape them. The pattern is clear: skills-based services like consulting, implementation, and creative work face the most pressure, while categories focused on AI governance, security, and enablement are positioned to grow. The useful question isn't whether AI will affect your work — it's whether the specific value you deliver is in a compounding category or a compressing one.

slants.strategy: Map your team's deliverables against the model's four categories. The exercise isn't about predicting headcount changes — it's about knowing where to invest next.
slants.leaders: If your team delivers skills-based services internally, start the conversation about expanding into governance and enablement before someone else frames it for you.
slants.operations: Process governance, compliance tracking, and documentation moved from overhead to growth category in Forrester's model. That's a shift worth owning.
slants.pm: Projects that build AI governance and enablement infrastructure are entering a stronger funding environment. Know which of yours qualifies.
slants.admin: Coordinating AI tools across teams, tracking vendor compliance, managing rollout logistics — those are growing service categories in this model, not shrinking ones.

steps: Pick one deliverable your team regularly produces — an internal report, a recurring analysis, a process you manage.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste this prompt: "I deliver [describe the deliverable] for my organization. Evaluate whether AI is more likely to compress this service's value (because AI can replicate the underlying skill) or compound it (because it enables, governs, or secures AI adoption). Give me your reasoning in three bullets."
Read the response and note whether you agree with the assessment.
Share your deliverable, its likely trajectory, and whether you agreed with AI's reasoning in the group.

trends.title: The case for using more than one AI model just got easier to make
trends.body: Ramp launched an AI model router this week that lets organizations switch between models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and others through a single API — optimizing for cost, speed, or quality per task. Companies already using it have reduced AI inference costs by 40% on average without changing output quality. The bigger signal: the tooling layer between your team and AI providers is maturing fast. Picking one AI vendor is becoming less important than knowing which tasks need which model tier (TechCrunch, August 2026).

slants.strategy: A multi-model strategy reduces vendor lock-in and lets you optimize AI spending per use case. If your current approach is one vendor for everything, that's leaving money and capability on the table.
slants.leaders: Don't force your team to pick one AI tool. The routing layer means each workflow can use what works best — and switching costs just dropped to near zero.
slants.operations: Model routing turns AI vendor management from a procurement decision into an optimization problem. Match simple tasks to cheaper models and complex ones to frontier models.
slants.pm: A 40% cost reduction on AI inference means more projects clear the ROI threshold. Revisit any AI initiative that stalled on unit economics.
slants.admin: You don't need to become an expert in every AI tool. Routing services handle model selection automatically — your job is knowing which tasks to send through the system.

steps: List three tasks your team currently uses AI for (or could). Categorize each as simple (summarizing, formatting), medium (drafting, analyzing), or complex (strategy, multi-step reasoning).

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste this prompt: "I have three AI tasks at different complexity levels: simple ([describe]), medium ([describe]), and complex ([describe]). For each, recommend whether I need a frontier model or whether a faster, cheaper model would produce the same quality. Explain what I'd gain and lose by matching model tier to task complexity."
Look at the response — does it change your assumption about needing the most powerful model for everything?
Share your three tasks and which model tier AI recommended for each in the group.

trends.title: Leaders are learning a better way to talk about AI and teams
trends.body: Axios reports a notable shift in how executives frame AI and workforce decisions. Where early adopters led with replacement metrics — Klarna's CEO publicly boasted AI was doing the work of 700 agents — the new playbook separates AI adoption from headcount messaging. Patreon's CEO frames restructuring as strategic, not AI-driven; Microsoft's chief people officer states that eliminated roles are 'not being replaced by AI.' The shift reflects a hard-won lesson: how you communicate AI's role in your organization shapes whether your team sees opportunity or threat (Axios, August 2026).

slants.strategy: Your AI communication strategy is itself a strategic asset. How you frame AI internally determines whether your best people lean in or start updating their resumes.
slants.leaders: Separate the AI story from the headcount story — not because they're unrelated, but because combining them tells your team the wrong thing about their future.
slants.operations: When you communicate process changes involving AI, lead with what's expanding — scope, quality, speed — rather than what's shrinking. The framing shapes adoption.
slants.pm: How you introduce AI-augmented workflows to project teams sets the tone. Position the tool as a capability upgrade for the team, not a signal about future staffing.
slants.admin: When new AI tools arrive in your workflow, you're often the first to notice how they're described internally. If the messaging feels threatening rather than empowering, flag it — your perspective shapes how the rest of the team receives it.

steps: Think about how AI has been introduced or discussed in your organization — in emails, town halls, or team meetings. Was the framing positive, neutral, or anxiety-inducing?

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste this prompt: "I'm a [your role] and my organization is adopting AI tools for [describe one area]. Help me write a two-paragraph internal message to my team introducing this change. The message should: (1) be honest about what's changing, (2) emphasize how this makes their work better rather than smaller, and (3) invite questions instead of shutting them down."
Review the draft. Does it sound like something your team would trust — or does it read like corporate spin?
Share your draft or key phrases in the group — seeing how different roles frame the same kind of change is the most useful part.

homework.title: Your Monday morning routine could use a second opinion.
homework.body: The start of a new week is when most people think about how their mornings should go — and then do the same thing they did last week. Tonight, try something different with a free AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity):
homework.prompt:
"Here's my typical Monday morning routine, from alarm to starting work: [describe yours honestly — including the parts you're not proud of]. Suggest a better version that gets me to my desk more focused and less rushed. Then argue against your own suggestion — what might not actually work for someone with my real constraints?"

That second step — argue against your own suggestion — is one of the most useful prompting habits you can build. It pushes AI past the polished 'ideal day' answer and into advice that fits your actual life.

2026-08-24.intro: Three patterns to start your week: strategy is becoming a system you design rather than a meeting you survive, your team's AI tools have outgrown your governance, and the training gap holding back AI adoption is simpler to fix than most leaders think.

trends.title: Strategy is becoming a system — and your role in it is shifting
trends.body: HBR's August issue argues that AI isn't just a tool for executing strategy — it's reshaping how strategy gets made. The key insight: AI expands the capacity of the strategy-making system itself by widening the option set, stress-testing plans through structured debate free from internal politics, and maintaining richer competitive models than any planning team could build alone. The shift for strategists is clear: less time building baseline analyses, more time exercising the judgment that determines which options actually fit your organization (HBR, August 2026).

slants.strategy: Your value is moving from building the strategic analysis to pressure-testing AI-generated options against organizational realities only you understand.
slants.leaders: Give your strategy team access to AI scenario-planning tools — the advantage isn't having better data, it's exploring more options before committing.
slants.operations: AI can maintain continuously updated competitive and market models. The quarterly strategy refresh can become a living process instead of a last-minute scramble.
slants.pm: Strategic planning cycles are compressing. Projects that depend on annual planning approvals need a faster path as AI-assisted strategy becomes more iterative.
slants.admin: When strategy meetings shift from presenting analyses to debating AI-generated options, meeting prep changes too — framing the right questions matters more than formatting the right deck.

steps: Think about one strategic decision your team is currently weighing or recently made — a resource allocation, a process change, a new initiative.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste this prompt: "We're deciding whether to [describe the decision]. Generate five alternative approaches we haven't considered, then argue against the two strongest options from the perspective of a skeptical executive."
Review the alternatives. Did AI surface an option your team hadn't discussed?
Share the most surprising alternative in the group — and whether the counterargument changed your thinking.

trends.title: Your team already adopted AI — now you can turn that into a strategic advantage
trends.body: Zylo's 2026 SaaS Management Index found that the average organization now spends $1.2 million a year on AI-native applications — up 108% year over year. But the real finding is what IT doesn't see: 77% of IT leaders discovered AI-powered tools and features they didn't know their teams were using, and 78% reported unexpected charges tied to AI consumption. The gap between AI adoption and AI governance isn't closing — it's widening (Zylo, 2026).

slants.strategy: Untracked AI spending is a strategic blind spot. You can't optimize what you can't measure — and right now, most organizations can't see a third of their AI footprint.
slants.leaders: Your team is already using AI tools you haven't approved. The practical question isn't whether to allow it — it's whether to govern it before the next budget review surfaces surprises.
slants.operations: Audit your team's actual AI tool usage before the next renewal cycle. Consumption-based AI pricing makes costs less predictable — knowing what's running is the first step to managing it.
slants.pm: If your project budget doesn't account for AI tool costs, you're likely undercounting. Build in a buffer for consumption-based AI features that charge by usage, not by seat.
slants.admin: You're often the first to notice when a new tool shows up in the workflow. That visibility is valuable — flagging unknown AI tools early helps the team avoid surprise costs and security gaps.

steps: Open a blank note and list every AI tool you've personally used for work in the past month — including free tiers, browser extensions, and features built into tools you already use.
Mark each one: "Approved by IT", "Not sure", or "Definitely not approved."

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste this prompt: "I use [number] AI tools at work, but only [number] are formally approved. What questions should I ask my IT or security team to understand which tools are safe to keep using and which I should stop?"
Share your count in the group — how many were approved versus not? The aggregate picture is usually eye-opening.

trends.title: The AI training gap costs trillions — and the fix is simpler than most programs assume
trends.body: IDC's workforce readiness report puts a number on the AI skills gap: $5.5 trillion in lost productivity, delayed products, and missed revenue globally. Over 90% of enterprises expect critical skills shortages this year. But the biggest barrier to closing the gap isn't budget or access — it's time. 41% of employees say they can't find time to learn AI skills during the workday, even when training is available. Only a third of employees received any AI training in the past year (IDC via Workera, 2026).

slants.strategy: If your AI strategy doesn't include protected learning time, you're planning around a workforce that doesn't exist yet. The readiness gap is a strategy gap.
slants.leaders: Carve out dedicated learning time for your team — even 30 minutes a week. The top barrier to AI upskilling isn't resistance or budget. It's that people literally can't find the hours.
slants.operations: The fastest way to close the ops-side skills gap: pair one AI-fluent team member with one who isn't, on a real task. Learning by doing beats training modules every time.
slants.pm: Build AI learning into project timelines as part of the work, not as an add-on after delivery. Teams that learn the tool while doing the work retain more than those who take a course and forget.
slants.admin: You don't need a formal AI course to start building fluency. The 10-minute challenges in this group are exactly the kind of low-pressure practice that works — and you're already doing them.

steps: Think about the last time you learned a new tool or skill at work. How did you actually learn it — a formal course, a colleague, trial and error, or something else?

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste this prompt: "I want to get better at using AI for [one task you do regularly]. Design a 5-day learning plan where I spend no more than 15 minutes per day. Each day should teach me one specific technique I can apply immediately to my real work."
Pick Day 1 from the plan and try it right now.
Share your 5-day plan or Day 1's technique in the group — crowdsourcing learning plans is one of the fastest ways to find what actually works.

homework.title: It's Monday — let AI plan your dinners for the week in 10 minutes.
homework.body: The hardest part of meal prep isn't the cooking — it's deciding what to make. Tonight, stop scrolling recipes and let AI do the thinking. Open any free AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity):
homework.prompt:
"I need to plan dinners for this week. Here's what I'm working with: [list what's already in your fridge and pantry, your budget, how many people you're feeding, and any dietary restrictions]. Give me 5 dinner options ranked by how little grocery shopping I'd need to do. For the top pick, give me a step-by-step recipe."

That ranking instruction — ranked by how little shopping I'd need — teaches AI to optimize for your real constraint instead of giving you five equally impractical ideas. Try swapping in other ranking criteria next time: fastest prep time, fewest dishes to wash, most kid-friendly.

2026-08-25.intro: Three patterns worth watching this week: AI is saving workers a full day but most organizations have no plan for it, governing AI agents is harder than building them, and the productivity multiplier from daily AI practice now has a number behind it.

trends.title: AI saves workers a full day each week — but most organizations have no plan for what to do with it
trends.body: BCG's fourth annual AI at Work survey of nearly 12,000 workers found that 42% of regular AI users save a full workday each week. But the strategy gap is stark: 66% report getting limited or no guidance on how to use the time saved. Companies with a clear AI strategy see 25 percentage points more impact — while simply buying better tools adds only 5. The bottleneck isn't adoption. It's direction (BCG, June 2026).

slants.strategy: You're the person who defines what freed-up time gets redirected toward. Without that answer, the productivity gains evaporate into busywork.
slants.leaders: Ask your team what they're doing with the time AI is saving them. If the answer is more of the same, the strategy needs work.
slants.operations: The time savings are real — 42% report gaining a full day back. The ops question is whether that time is being reallocated to higher-value work or absorbed by more meetings.
slants.pm: If AI is saving your team a day per week, your project timelines and capacity models should reflect it. Otherwise you're planning around the old math.
slants.admin: When AI saves time in your workflow, deciding what to do with it is your call — not a policy someone else writes. That's a real opportunity to take on higher-value work.

steps: Estimate how much time AI saves you personally each week — even a rough guess counts. Is it 30 minutes? Two hours? A full day?

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste this prompt: "I save approximately [X hours per week] using AI at work. Right now, that time goes to [describe what you currently do with it]. Suggest three higher-value ways I could redirect that time based on my role as a [your role], ranked by strategic impact."
Pick the suggestion that surprised you most and try redirecting your saved time there for one day this week.
Share your time estimate and where you're redirecting it in the group — the variety of answers is always eye-opening.

trends.title: Gartner's first Hype Cycle for Agentic AI puts governance at the center
trends.body: Gartner published its first-ever Hype Cycle dedicated to agentic AI, mapping over 30 technologies — and the standout finding isn't about capability. It's about control. Only 17% of organizations have deployed AI agents, but over 60% plan to within two years. Gartner predicts more than 40% of those projects will be canceled by end of 2027, primarily because organizations deployed agents without a governance plan, not because the technology failed (Gartner, 2026).

slants.strategy: Before your organization scales AI agents, someone needs to own the governance framework. If that person doesn't exist yet, that's a strategic gap worth raising now.
slants.leaders: Define the guardrails before the pilot ends. An agent that sends a client communication or writes to a production system without a human checkpoint is a different risk profile than a chatbot.
slants.operations: Your SOPs for AI tools need a new chapter. An agent that executes tasks autonomously requires different controls than a tool that suggests answers for a human to review.
slants.pm: Agentic AI projects need a governance milestone before the deployment milestone. Building it into the plan early avoids the retrofit when compliance calls.
slants.admin: If your team is experimenting with AI agents, tracking which ones have access to which systems is already part of your coordination work — and it's becoming more valuable, not less.

steps: List the AI tools your team currently uses that can take actions on their own — sending emails, updating records, scheduling meetings, or generating documents without a human clicking approve.
For each one, note whether there's a formal policy governing what it can and can't do.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste this prompt: "I have [number] AI tools that can take autonomous actions in my workflow. Help me draft a simple one-page governance checklist: what should each tool be allowed to do, what requires human approval, and who owns the policy?"
Share your checklist draft or your count of ungoverned tools in the group — the total is usually higher than anyone expects.

trends.title: AI super-users are 5x more productive — and the pattern behind it is surprisingly simple
trends.body: Writer's 2026 enterprise survey of 2,400 workers and executives found that AI super-users are 5x more productive than their peers, and 92% of C-suites are actively investing in developing this group. But the gains aren't spreading evenly: only 29% of organizations see significant ROI from AI overall, because the productivity boost concentrates in the people who've built a daily habit — not those who tried it once and moved on (Writer, 2026).

slants.strategy: The ROI gap isn't a technology problem — it's a practice problem. Organizations seeing returns are the ones where AI use became a daily habit, not a quarterly experiment.
slants.leaders: Identify your team's early AI adopters and give them a visible role: mentoring one colleague each. Peer learning scales the productivity gains faster than any formal training program.
slants.operations: A small ops team using AI daily can outperform a larger team that isn't. That changes how you think about capacity planning and headcount requests.
slants.pm: If some team members are 5x more productive with AI than others, your resource estimates need to account for that variance — or you'll consistently mis-scope.
slants.admin: You don't need to become a power user overnight. The pattern in the data is clear: the people who got productive started with one task, got comfortable, then expanded. Start with one.

steps: Rate your own AI fluency honestly: "Never used it", "Tried it once or twice", "Use it weekly", or "Use it daily."

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste this prompt: "I'm a [your role] who currently uses AI [your frequency]. Give me one specific task I do regularly that I could start doing with AI this week, and write me the exact prompt I'd use to get started."
Try the AI-generated prompt on that one task before the end of the day.
Share your starting fluency level and the task you tried in the group — the mix of starting points is always wider than people expect.

homework.title: Tonight, let AI play sleep coach — and find out what your evening routine is actually doing to your rest.
homework.body: Most of us know we should sleep better but aren't sure which specific habits are helping and which are quietly working against us. Open any free AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity) and try this:
homework.prompt:
"Act as a sleep scientist. Here's what my typical evening looks like from dinner to bedtime: [describe your routine — when you eat, screen time, caffeine cutoff, what you do in the last hour, when you go to bed, when you wake up]. Based on the research, tell me which two habits are working for me and which two are most likely hurting my sleep quality. Then give me one small change I can try tonight."

That opening line — act as a sleep scientist — is called a persona prompt. It focuses the AI's response through a specific lens of expertise, so you get targeted advice instead of generic tips. Try swapping in other roles: act as a nutritionist, act as a financial planner, act as a patient teacher.

2026-08-26.intro: Today's throughline: the AI conversation is moving from 'are we using it' to 'can we prove it, speed it up, and teach it well' — three very different signals that all point to the same shift toward maturity.

trends.title: AI spending keeps climbing, but the earnings bump isn't moving yet — and that's useful information
trends.body: McKinsey's newest State of AI survey found that more companies are deploying more AI than ever, betting the payoff is coming — but 37 percent of respondents attribute at least some EBIT impact to AI use, about the same share as in 2025. In plain terms: adoption is way up, but the number of people who can point to a real earnings bump hasn't moved. That's not bad news — it's a clear signal for anyone in strategy or planning about where to focus next.

slants.strategy: This is your cue to build a simple before/after measurement habit into every new AI initiative instead of waiting for a big annual review to ask if it worked.
slants.leaders: Use this data to set honest expectations with your team and your boss — 'we're still building the muscle to measure this' is a stronger message than overpromising a number you can't back up.
slants.operations: Pick one workflow already running on AI and instrument it this week so you have real before/after numbers instead of a guess next time someone asks about ROI.
slants.pm: Add a measurement checkpoint to your next AI-related project charter now, while it's cheap to add, rather than trying to reconstruct impact after the fact.
slants.admin: Start logging how much time AI tools save you on recurring tasks — that small log becomes real evidence your team can point to.

steps: Pick one task you or your team does regularly with AI help.

Open your company-approved AI tool and ask: "Help me design a simple before/after way to measure the business impact of using AI for [describe the task]. Give me 3 metrics I could track, ranked by how easy they are to measure."
Pick the easiest metric from the list and write down today's baseline number.
Put a reminder on your calendar 30 days out to check the number again.
Share the metric and baseline you picked in the group — someone else can probably reuse it.

trends.title: One automaker cut AI delivery time from six months to four days
trends.body: Toyota North America built an internal AI platform and now has over 50 production-ready agents running, using a system that shrank the typical build cycle from six months down to just four days. The team is also tracking the return on those agents directly, treating AI performance as a real line item rather than a side experiment.

slants.strategy: This is the case for building one reusable agent platform instead of funding a dozen one-off pilots that never talk to each other.
slants.leaders: When delivery cycles shrink this much, small teams can ship what used to take a full team — start thinking now about which people you can free up for higher-value work.
slants.operations: Borrow the idea of an 'observability board' for your own AI workflows — visibility into what's working saves you from debugging in the dark.
slants.pm: Recalculate your resourcing assumptions for AI-assisted projects — if delivery windows are shrinking industry-wide, your timeline estimates should shrink too.
slants.admin: Ask your team if there's a reusable template or config for repeat requests instead of rebuilding the same thing from scratch every time.

steps: Identify one task on your team that gets rebuilt from scratch every time — a report, a briefing doc, an intake form.
Ask your AI tool: "Turn this repeatable task into a reusable template I can fill in each time: [describe the task in general terms, no confidential details]. Give me a fill-in-the-blank version."
Review the draft template and adjust the wording so it sounds like your team, not a generic bot.
Save the template somewhere your team can find and reuse it.
Share the template in the group so others can borrow it too.

trends.title: Anthropic just made AI literacy free — and gave it a clear definition
trends.body: Anthropic's new Claude Academy is a free learning platform designed to help people understand AI, use Claude more effectively and build practical AI skills for work and everyday use, live now with no sign-in required. The real insight underneath it: Anthropic frames good AI skill as knowing what to hand off to AI and what to keep for yourself — not just knowing more prompts.

slants.strategy: Fold a free literacy resource like this into your workforce planning now — it's a zero-cost way to close the skills gap most teams assume needs a big budget.
slants.leaders: Set a simple team standard — everyone completes one free module this quarter — and you've built a shared baseline without asking finance for anything.
slants.operations: Use this as a chance to write down, as a team, which tasks you consistently hand to AI and which you keep — that shared list becomes your operating standard.
slants.pm: Have new project team members complete a quick module before kickoff so everyone starts a project with the same AI ground rules.
slants.admin: This is a fast, free way to become the go-to person on your team for AI questions — a few short courses can put you ahead of most colleagues.

steps: Think of one task you currently always do yourself, start to finish.
Ask your AI tool: "Ask me questions about this task, then tell me whether it's something AI could handle, something I should keep, or a hybrid. Task: [describe the task]."
Answer its questions honestly — don't skip ahead to the answer.
Read its recommendation and decide whether you agree with the split it suggests.
Share what you learned in the group, especially if the answer surprised you.

homework.title: let AI plan your next weekend with you, not for you
homework.body: Pick a free tool — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity — and use it to plan a small trip or outing you've been meaning to take. The trick is to make it ask you questions before it gives you an answer, so you get options that actually fit you.
homework.prompt: I want to plan a weekend trip within 3 hours of [your city] for under $400. Ask me clarifying questions first, then give me 3 ranked options with pros and cons for each.

2026-08-27.intro: Three things worth sitting with on a Thursday: the personal productivity gains from AI are proven, but organizations haven't figured out how to make them add up yet — and the two missing pieces are institutional knowledge and manager support.

trends.title: Personal AI productivity is proven — the organizational payoff is the next unlock
trends.body: McKinsey's 2026 State of AI survey of 1,719 executives puts a number on the gap everyone senses: 80% of individual workers report productivity gains from AI, but only 6% of organizations see significant earnings impact. Ninety percent of function-level use cases remain stuck in pilot mode. The gains are real at the desk — they just aren't compounding across the org chart yet.

slants.strategy: This is a design problem, not a tool problem — map where individual productivity gains are disappearing between teams.
slants.leaders: Pick one team already seeing individual gains and ask what they'd need to make those gains visible at the business-unit level.
slants.operations: You can spot the handoff points where one person's AI-assisted output sits in a queue built for the old pace.
slants.pm: Track cycle time alongside output quality — if AI is making people faster but the project still takes the same number of weeks, the bottleneck is in the process.
slants.admin: Your view across teams is exactly what's needed here — you see where work speeds up and where it slows back down.

steps: Think of one task you've personally sped up with AI in the last month. Write it down, along with roughly how much time it saved.
Now ask yourself: did that time savings change anything downstream? Did the next step in the process move faster because you finished sooner?

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste this: "I sped up [your task] using AI, but the downstream process didn't get faster. What are three possible reasons my time savings aren't compounding into team-level results?"
Read the response and identify the one reason that feels most true for your team.
Share that reason in the group — and whether you have any ideas for unblocking it.

trends.title: The most valuable thing you can train AI on might already be in your building
trends.body: Thomson Reuters just launched its own AI model, trained on decades of proprietary legal, tax, and regulatory content for $40 million. The result matches frontier models on domain tasks at a fraction of the inference cost — not because the architecture is novel, but because the training data is. The signal for every organization: your accumulated institutional knowledge is becoming your most strategic AI input.

slants.strategy: Start inventorying the institutional knowledge that's trapped in documents, SOPs, and senior employees' expertise — it's potential AI training data.
slants.leaders: Invest in capturing and structuring your team's knowledge now, while the people who hold it are still available to verify what AI produces from it.
slants.operations: The process documentation you've been maintaining isn't just compliance overhead anymore — it's the foundation for AI that actually understands how work moves here.
slants.pm: Lessons-learned databases and project templates are suddenly worth organizing well — they're the kind of structured knowledge AI can actually build on.
slants.admin: You know where the real institutional knowledge lives — the shared drive no one's cleaned, the procedures doc everyone references but nobody updates. That's the starting line.

steps: Pick one area where your team has deep, accumulated knowledge — a process you've refined over years, a set of decisions that follow unwritten rules, or a document library that holds real expertise.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste this: "If an organization wanted to build an AI system that understands how [your area] works, what kinds of documents and institutional knowledge would it need to capture first? List them in priority order."
Compare the response to what actually exists — is that knowledge captured somewhere, or does it live mostly in people's heads?
Share one item from the list that you realized isn't written down anywhere with the group.

trends.title: The manager — not the tool — is what decides whether AI adoption lifts a team
trends.body: Gallup's workforce study finds AI adoption pushing culture in both directions almost equally: among employees at companies using AI, 24% say culture improved and 25% say it got worse. The deciding variable is the manager. Where managers actively champion AI use, engagement sits at 48%; without that support, it drops to 30%. Meanwhile, half of CHROs say they lack confidence in their managers' readiness to guide employees on AI.

slants.strategy: Factor manager readiness into every AI rollout plan — a tool adoption without a people adoption strategy is a coin flip.
slants.leaders: You don't need to be an AI expert to lead here — you need to be visibly trying it and making space for your team to experiment alongside you.
slants.operations: When you share what worked and what didn't in your own AI experiments, you lower the barrier for everyone around you.
slants.pm: Build a five-minute AI tip into your next team meeting — normalizing the tool matters more than perfecting the workflow.
slants.admin: Every time you show a colleague a shortcut you found in an AI tool, you're doing exactly what the data says makes adoption work.

steps: Think about the last time you tried something new with AI at work. Did you share what happened — what worked, what surprised you, what flopped?

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste this: "I want to share a practical AI tip with my team at our next meeting. Give me three options for a 2-minute live demo that requires no prep and shows an immediately useful result. Assume the audience is new to AI and slightly skeptical."
Pick the one that fits your team best and try it yourself first.
Share it at your next team gathering — then tell the group how it landed.

homework.title: End-of-summer bucket list — but this time, structured enough to actually finish something.
homework.body: Summer's winding down and the year is two-thirds done. Somewhere in the back of your mind there's a list of things you keep meaning to do. Tonight, pull it out and give it some structure. Open any free AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity):
homework.prompt:
"I'm going to list everything I've been meaning to do — big and small, serious and fun. Organize them into categories, then rank each category by which item would make me happiest to have finished by December 31. For the top 3 overall, give me the single smallest next step I could take this week."

The technique here is structured decomposition — breaking a vague wish list into categories, priorities, and next actions. It turns "someday" into "this Saturday."

2026-08-28.intro: Three signals heading into the weekend: the talent pipeline is reshaping around AI in ways that favor organizations investing in their people, the era of faking AI skills is ending, and the value of your judgment has never been more visible.

trends.title: The talent pipeline is shifting — and it favors organizations that develop from within
trends.body: Stanford's updated analysis of millions of U.S. payroll records finds that young worker employment in AI-exposed fields is now 19% below trend — up from 13% a year ago, while experienced workers show no comparable gap. The effect operates through reduced hiring, not layoffs — and the implication is clear: organizations investing in developing their existing people have a growing advantage over those counting on an unchanged talent pipeline.

slants.strategy: Map which entry-level roles on your org chart carry the most AI-exposed skills — those are the positions where internal development paths matter most.
slants.leaders: Your current team members just became harder to replace externally. Invest in their growth now, while the development opportunity is still ahead of the competition.
slants.operations: Junior ops roles built around data entry, report generation, and routine analysis are shifting fastest — redesign them around the judgment and quality layer above the output.
slants.pm: If your project plans depend on hiring junior analysts or coordinators, factor in a tighter market — or scope the work for a smaller, more experienced team augmented by AI.
slants.admin: Your institutional knowledge and organizational judgment are exactly the skills the market is increasingly short of. That's not changing — it's accelerating.

steps: Think about the roles on your team that were originally designed for someone early in their career — the coordinator, the analyst, the junior specialist.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste this prompt: "I manage a team that includes entry-level roles like [describe them]. Given that AI can now handle much of the routine output these roles were designed for, help me redesign one of these positions to focus on judgment, quality control, and stakeholder communication — the parts AI can't do well."
Compare the redesigned role to the original. Would you hire differently for it?
Share your before-and-after role description in the group — the evolution tells you a lot about where value is heading.

trends.title: People stopped pretending to know AI — and real fluency is filling the gap
trends.body: A WalkMe survey finds the share of employees who admit to faking AI knowledge in meetings dropped from 45% to 28% in one year — but it also exposed what was hiding underneath. Ninety percent of workers say they feel confident using AI, yet only 25% say it works well on the first try. The pretending era is ending — the building-real-fluency era is just getting started.

slants.strategy: Confidence without competence is the current state of most AI adoption. The organizations that close that gap with structured daily practice will pull ahead.
slants.leaders: If your team says they're comfortable with AI but the results are inconsistent, that's not a tool problem — it's a practice problem. Build repetition into the workflow.
slants.operations: A 75% first-try failure rate means most people are doing extra rounds of editing and reprompting. That hidden rework is worth finding and fixing.
slants.pm: Factor in the learning curve when scoping AI-assisted work. A task that takes 10 minutes for a practiced user can take 40 for someone still building fluency.
slants.admin: Every time you get a better result from AI on your second or third attempt, you're building exactly the kind of practical fluency that separates confident from competent.

steps: Pick a task you've used AI for recently — something where you didn't get the result you wanted on the first try.

Open your company-approved AI tool and try the task again, but this time add: "Before you answer, ask me three clarifying questions about what I actually need, who the audience is, and what format works best."
Compare the two results. Was the second attempt closer to what you needed?
Share the difference in the group — and the clarifying question that made the biggest impact.

trends.title: When AI handles the first draft, your judgment becomes the product
trends.body: MIT's committee on AI in education published a finding with clear workplace implications: AI can now produce credible solutions to almost any standard written assignment — essays, analyses, problem sets, and code. If that holds at one of the most rigorous universities in the world, it holds in your office too. The premium is shifting fast — from producing the first draft to knowing whether the draft is right, complete, and suited to the actual need.

slants.strategy: Your planning team's edge isn't in generating analyses — it's in knowing which analyses matter and which assumptions to challenge.
slants.leaders: Develop your team's evaluation skills as deliberately as their production skills. Assessing AI output is becoming as important as creating work from scratch.
slants.operations: When anyone can generate a standard operating procedure with AI, the value shifts to the person who knows whether it actually reflects how work moves through the organization.
slants.pm: AI-generated project plans and risk registers look polished. The PM who knows which risks are real and which are boilerplate is worth more than the tool that produced the list.
slants.admin: You've always been the person who notices what's missing from a document — the context, the history, the unwritten rule. That eye is exactly what AI can't supply.

steps: Take a work product you created recently — a report, a memo, a plan, a summary. Make sure it contains nothing confidential.
Open your company-approved AI tool, describe the document's purpose in one sentence, and paste: "Write a first draft of [describe the document and its purpose]. Make it professional and thorough."
Compare AI's version to yours. Where did it get close, and where did it miss something only you would know?
Share the one thing AI missed in the group — those gaps are exactly where your judgment lives.

homework.title: Friday night, nothing at stake — let AI help you find the side project you'll actually stick with.
homework.body: The weekend is for things you choose, not things you're assigned. But finding the right hobby or side project usually stalls in the 'I don't know where to start' phase. Tonight, let AI narrow the options based on your actual life. Open any free AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity):
homework.prompt:
"I have about [X hours] of free time per week, a budget of roughly [$ amount] per month for hobbies, and I'm drawn to [list 2-3 interests — making things, learning, being outdoors, puzzles, cooking, whatever]. I've tried [anything you started and abandoned] before. Suggest five side projects or hobbies that fit those constraints, ranked by how quickly I'd feel a sense of progress. For the top pick, give me exactly what to do this weekend to get started."

The technique here is constraint-based filtering — instead of asking for a generic list, you give AI your real limitations upfront. The result is options you could actually pursue, not aspirational suggestions that assume unlimited time and money.

2026-08-29.intro: Three Saturday reads: AI agents are moving into the tools you already use, the organizations proving AI outcomes are pulling far ahead, and the era of demanding proof has quietly arrived.

trends.title: AI agents are becoming a built-in feature of your CRM
trends.body: Salesforce and Anthropic announced Claudeforce this week, making Claude the default reasoning engine across the Salesforce ecosystem. The launch ships with 37 prebuilt sales skills that let sellers query live CRM data, prep sales calls, review deals, and update records directly from Claude — without opening Salesforce. Agentforce workforce units grew 97% last quarter. Open beta arrives in September.

slants.strategy: When AI reasoning is embedded in your existing data layer, the strategic question shifts from 'which AI tool?' to 'which workflows should agents own first?'
slants.leaders: Ask your team which recurring CRM tasks they'd hand to an agent tomorrow — the answers will reveal where your process bottlenecks actually live.
slants.operations: Agent-ready CRM means your data quality matters more than ever. Clean data produces useful agent output; messy data produces confident mistakes.
slants.pm: Pipeline reviews, status updates, and deal tracking are exactly the kind of structured, repetitive work agents handle well — start scoping which reporting tasks you'd hand off.
slants.admin: You already know the CRM better than most. That makes you the person who spots when an agent's output doesn't match how things actually work here.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool and paste this prompt: "I use [name your CRM] daily. List five repetitive tasks I probably do in my CRM every week that an AI agent could handle. For each one, be specific about what the agent would do and what I'd still need to verify."
Review the list. Which task would you trust an agent with today, and which would need better data or clearer rules first?
For the one you'd trust, write a one-sentence acceptance criteria — what would the agent need to get right for you to stop doing it manually?
Share your top pick and your acceptance criteria in the group.

trends.title: The organizations measuring their AI are pulling four times ahead on customer satisfaction
trends.body: Talkdesk's new State of Agentic Automation in CX report surveyed 252 director-level decision makers and found a striking gap: 98% of organizations have deployed AI somewhere in their customer journey, but just 5% can clearly quantify its impact on business outcomes. Only 15% combine agentic AI with cross-departmental orchestration. The organizations at the highest maturity level are four times more likely to report major customer satisfaction gains.

slants.strategy: If your AI business case still says 'efficiency gains' without specific numbers, you're in the 95%. Define what 'working' looks like before the next budget cycle.
slants.leaders: Ask your team one question this week: 'How would we know if our AI deployment was actually improving outcomes?' If nobody has a clear answer, that's the priority.
slants.operations: The measurement gap is almost always a data-connection problem — if your AI touches customers in one system but outcomes live in another, the proof can't surface.
slants.pm: Build measurement milestones into every AI project plan — not just 'deployed' but 'producing measurable change in [specific metric] by [date].'
slants.admin: You see the customer journey across systems every day. That cross-functional visibility is exactly what most organizations are missing when they try to connect AI to results.

steps: Think of one AI-assisted process your team uses today — an automated response, a chatbot, an AI-generated summary, anything that touches a customer or internal workflow.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "We use AI for [describe the process]. Help me design three simple metrics to prove whether this deployment is actually improving outcomes — not just whether it's being used, but whether it's making things measurably better."
Pick the metric that would be most convincing to a skeptical executive.
Share that metric and how you'd measure it in the group.

trends.title: AI expectations are getting more realistic — and that's where real value starts
trends.body: BCC Research's AI Sentiment Index for July 2026, released this week, dropped from 77.86 to 75.10 — not because interest is fading, but because industries are applying stricter standards to separate routine improvements from genuine structural change. Chemicals, energy, and technology lead both adoption and spend. The signal: enterprises are moving past 'AI is exciting' into 'prove it works in our operations.'

slants.strategy: Cooling hype is your window. When AI stops being a boardroom buzzword, it becomes a planning tool — and that's where your skills matter most.
slants.leaders: The teams that thrive in the 'prove it' era are the ones already measuring. If you haven't set success criteria for your AI projects, now is the time.
slants.operations: This is your moment. Operations has always been about proof — cycle times, error rates, throughput. Apply those same standards to every AI deployment.
slants.pm: The shift from 'exciting pilot' to 'operational proof' is a project management challenge. Scope it, measure it, report on it — this is exactly what you do.
slants.admin: When the hype settles, the value of people who know how things actually work goes up. Your operational knowledge is what turns AI experiments into reliable processes.

steps: Think of one AI tool or process your team adopted in the last six months.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "My team started using AI for [describe it] about [X months] ago. Help me write three 'proof of value' questions I could answer with data we probably already have — to show whether this AI is actually improving our work, not just making it feel different."
Pick the question that would be easiest to answer with data you can access today.
Share your proof-of-value question in the group — and whether you already know the answer.

homework.title: Saturday night sorted — build a custom trivia night in 10 minutes.
homework.body: Whether it's two people or a full room, trivia is better when it's personal. Let AI build a round tuned to your actual group. Open any free AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity):
homework.prompt:
"I'm hosting a casual trivia night for [number] people. The group includes [describe ages, interests, inside jokes, or topics they'd enjoy]. Build me 4 rounds of 5 questions each — mix easy, medium, and hard so nobody feels left out. Include one wildcard round based on something only this specific group would find funny or impressive. Format it so I can read questions aloud with answers hidden below each one."

The technique here is audience-aware calibration — instead of asking for generic trivia, you're giving AI enough context about your specific group to tailor difficulty and topics. The result feels custom because it is.

2026-08-30.intro: A Sunday scan: hidden text can fool your AI email tools, enterprise AI spending finally has guardrails, and how people find information is quietly shifting in AI's favor.

trends.title: Hidden text can silently rewrite what your AI email tools tell you
trends.body: Forcepoint X-Labs demonstrated that hidden text in an email — invisible to you in Outlook — can silently rewrite what an AI summarizer tells you. In their proof of concept, invisible instructions shifted an invoice deadline by two weeks and deleted a name from the summary, with a 100% success rate across ten runs. The fix isn't fear — it's treating AI summaries the way you'd treat any unsigned memo: useful, but worth verifying when it matters.

slants.strategy: If your team uses AI-generated summaries to make decisions, build a habit of spot-checking the ones attached to deadlines, dollar amounts, or approvals.
slants.leaders: This is a good reason to ask your team: where are we trusting AI summaries without a second look? The answer shapes your next security conversation.
slants.operations: Any process that routes work based on an AI summary — ticket triage, invoice processing, escalation rules — needs a verification step for high-stakes items.
slants.pm: Add AI summary accuracy to your risk register for any workflow that depends on automated summaries to set priorities or deadlines.
slants.admin: You already double-check important details before acting on them. That instinct is now a security practice — and it's more valuable than ever.

steps: Think about the last time you relied on an AI-generated summary — an email recap, a meeting transcript, a document brief.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "I rely on AI-generated summaries for [describe the workflow]. What are three things I should always verify manually before acting on a summary, and why?"
Pick the one verification habit that would be easiest to add to your daily routine.
Share your new verification habit in the group — and whether the AI flagged something you hadn't thought of.

trends.title: Enterprise AI spending just got its first real guardrails
trends.body: Google Cloud this week added hard monthly spending caps for Gemini Enterprise that pause AI agent API calls when the budget hits its limit — with alerts at 50%, 80%, and 100% of the configured amount. They also launched pay-as-you-go pricing with no base subscription. The signal isn't about Google specifically — it's that enterprise AI cost governance is moving from 'track and hope' to 'cap and control.'

slants.strategy: If your AI pilots don't have spending caps yet, this is the template. Define the ceiling before the experiment scales, not after.
slants.leaders: Cost visibility changes the AI adoption conversation from 'should we try this?' to 'what is this experiment worth?' — which is the question you actually want to answer.
slants.operations: Hard caps that pause agent calls mean your runaway-cost scenario just got a safety net. Ask your cloud team whether your current AI deployments have equivalent controls.
slants.pm: Budget alerts at 50%, 80%, and 100% give you natural checkpoints to evaluate whether an AI workflow is delivering value proportional to its cost.
slants.admin: If you manage vendor invoices or cloud billing, knowing that AI spending can be capped and alerted means fewer surprise line items to chase down.

steps: Think about one AI tool or service your team pays for — or is evaluating.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "My team uses [name the AI tool or service]. Help me build a simple cost-tracking framework with three columns: what we're spending, what it's producing, and whether the value justifies the cost. Include one question I should ask monthly to catch spending that isn't delivering results."
Review the framework. Does your team currently track any of these things?
Share your one monthly question in the group — the one that would catch waste earliest.

trends.title: People are finding information differently — and what arrives is higher quality
trends.body: Brainlabs analyzed 54 advertisers across 14 months and found that organic search sessions fell 10.5% after AI Overviews became common, but visitors arriving from AI platforms convert at 1.5 times the rate. AI-driven key events rose 335%. The volume is shrinking, but the quality is going up — people who click through from an AI answer are further along in their thinking and more ready to act.

slants.strategy: Your competitive intelligence workflows built on traditional search may be missing what AI-first researchers find. Audit how your team discovers information, not just what they find.
slants.leaders: If your team still measures success by how many people visit a page, it's time to shift the metric to what visitors do when they get there.
