slants.operations: The internal knowledge base that ranks well in search may matter less than the one that answers the question directly. Structure your documentation for AI retrieval, not just keyword matching.
slants.pm: When your stakeholders arrive at a meeting having already asked an AI tool, the conversation starts further ahead. Prepare for questions that skip the basics.
slants.admin: The way people search for internal answers is changing too. If you maintain shared resources, clear structure and plain language help AI tools read and summarize them accurately.

steps: Pick a work-related question you'd normally search for — something about a process, a tool, or a best practice.
Search for it twice: once in a traditional search engine, and once in a free AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity).
Compare the two experiences. Which got you to a useful answer faster? Which required more clicking and scanning?
Share the comparison in the group — and whether the AI tool changed how you'd search for something next time.

homework.title: Sunday night kitchen adventure — let AI pick the one cooking skill worth learning tonight.
homework.body: You don't need another recipe. You need one technique that makes dozens of recipes better. Open any free AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity):
homework.prompt:
"I'd describe my cooking skill level as [beginner / comfortable / adventurous]. I mostly cook [type of food you usually make]. Pick one cooking technique I probably don't use that would most improve my everyday meals. Explain why it matters, walk me through it step by step like I've never done it before, and give me one simple dish to try it on tonight with ingredients I probably already have."

The technique here is targeted depth over breadth — instead of asking for a recipe list, you're asking AI to diagnose the single highest-leverage skill gap and teach it deeply. One technique fully understood beats ten recipes bookmarked and forgotten.

2026-08-31.intro: Monday reset: AI is reshaping how strategy gets made, enterprise agents are arriving faster than teams can govern them, and the transformation that works is about redesigning work — not cutting it.

trends.title: Strategy-making is being quietly rebuilt around AI
trends.body: HBR's August coverage explores how AI is changing the strategy process itself. AI can now generate and evaluate thousands of strategic options, build continually updated views of markets and competitors, and stress-test plans through structured debate free of internal politics. The organizations seeing real gains aren't bolting AI onto existing strategy rituals — they're building it into the process from the start.

slants.strategy: Your planning cycle can now include structured red-teaming at scale — not just one devil's advocate in the room.
slants.leaders: Give your strategy team permission to use AI as a sparring partner before the final deck is built, not after.
slants.operations: The competitive landscape scan that used to take a week can now update continuously — ask what that changes about your planning cadence.
slants.pm: AI-generated scenario analysis can feed directly into your risk registers and dependency maps.
slants.admin: You're often the first to spot when a plan doesn't match reality on the ground — AI can help you articulate that pattern faster.

steps: Pick a strategic question your team is currently working through — a market entry, a resource allocation decision, a process change.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "Here's a strategic decision we're considering: [describe it in 2–3 sentences, keeping it general enough to avoid confidential details]. Argue against this from three different perspectives: a skeptical CFO, a frontline operator, and a competitor. Be specific about which assumptions are weakest."
Read the three arguments. Identify one assumption you hadn't pressure-tested.
Share what surprised you most in the group — which perspective landed hardest?

trends.title: Gartner's first agentic AI hype cycle names what's real — and what's not ready
trends.body: Gartner released its inaugural Hype Cycle for Agentic AI, and the headline is a useful reality check: agentic AI sits at the Peak of Inflated Expectations. Only 17% of organizations have deployed agents, though over 60% plan to within two years. The telling signal is what else made the chart — governance, security, and cost-management tools now sit alongside core agent tech. Enterprises are learning to ask "how do we control this?" before "how do we scale this?"

slants.strategy: Use this hype cycle as a filter: which agent capabilities are production-ready today, and which are still two years out?
slants.leaders: The governance question is yours to own — setting guardrails now is cheaper than retrofitting them after a pilot scales.
slants.operations: If your team is evaluating agent tools, ask vendors where they sit on this hype cycle — and what their governance story is.
slants.pm: Agent projects need a governance plan from day one, not as a phase-two add-on.
slants.admin: You'll likely be among the first to use task-specific agents in daily workflows — your feedback on what works shapes what gets scaled.

steps: Think about one repetitive, rule-based workflow your team handles today — approvals routing, data entry, report generation, ticket triage.

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "I manage a workflow that involves [describe the steps briefly]. If an AI agent could handle parts of this autonomously, which steps would be safe to delegate, which would need human review, and what could go wrong?"
Review the response and note which steps the AI flagged as needing human oversight.
Share your workflow breakdown in the group — what did the AI say should stay human?

trends.title: The AI transformation that works is redesigning work, not replacing people
trends.body: A new HBR piece makes the case plainly: organizations focused on headcount reduction are getting less from AI than those redesigning how work gets done. The approach that delivers results starts by breaking roles into tasks, identifying where AI genuinely improves performance, and rebuilding processes around the right mix of human and machine. It's not about fewer people — it's about better-designed work.

slants.strategy: Map your team's work at the task level, not the role level — that's where the real AI opportunities live.
slants.leaders: Frame AI adoption as a work-design project, not a workforce-reduction project, and you'll get better results and stronger buy-in.
slants.operations: The processes that benefit most from AI aren't the ones with the most people — they're the ones with the most handoffs.
slants.pm: When scoping an AI initiative, start with a task inventory of the affected workflow — it changes what's actually automatable.
slants.admin: The parts of your role that feel most routine are the parts AI can take over — freeing you to do more of the judgment work that only you can do.

steps: Pick one role on your team — yours or someone else's — and list the 5–7 core tasks that fill a typical week.
Next to each task, write one label: "AI could draft this", "AI could review this", "AI could automate this", or "This needs a human."
Look at the split. Ask yourself: if AI handled the first three categories, what would this person spend their time on instead?
Share your task map in the group — and name the one task that surprised you most.

homework.title: Got a savings goal you keep meaning to start? Let AI build the plan in 5 minutes.
homework.body: Whether it's a trip, a new piece of furniture, or just a proper rainy-day fund — the hardest part is knowing how much to set aside and for how long. Let AI do the math and give you options. Try this in ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity (all free on the web):
homework.prompt:
"I want to save $[amount] for [your goal — a trip, a gadget, a holiday fund, an emergency cushion] by [target month and year]. I currently have $[what you've saved so far] set aside, and I can realistically put away about $[amount] per [week or month]. Give me 3 savings plans ranked from most comfortable to most aggressive, and tell me exactly what I'd need to cut or change in each one."

That last move — ranked options with explicit trade-offs — is one of the most useful prompting patterns you can learn. It turns AI from a single-answer machine into a decision-support tool.

2026-09-01.intro: Three Tuesday reads: AI chatbots are proving to be powerful fact-checking partners, giving AI agents a clear identity makes them trustworthy teammates, and the world's most valuable company just made AI its new CEO's day-one priority.

trends.title: AI chatbots are proving to be powerful fact-checking partners
trends.body: NPR partnered with NewsGuard to test six major chatbots against 30 false narratives pushed by China, Iran, and Russia. The result: chatbots debunked the falsehoods about three-quarters of the time, outperforming traditional search engines. Search engines failed to challenge a false narrative 18 out of 120 queries; chatbots failed just 12 out of 180. The edge isn't speed — it's synthesis. AI tools are better at reading context, weighing sources, and flagging contradictions than a ranked list of links.

slants.strategy: When AI is better at separating signal from noise than search, your competitive intelligence workflow deserves a second look.
slants.leaders: Encourage your team to cross-check important claims with an AI tool — not as a replacement for judgment, but as a faster first filter.
slants.operations: Any process that depends on web research for verification now has a stronger alternative sitting unused on your desktop.
slants.pm: Add AI-assisted verification as a step in your research phase — especially when a project decision rests on external data or market claims.
slants.admin: Next time you're fact-checking details for a briefing or report, try running the claim through an AI tool alongside your usual search — the comparison is eye-opening.

steps: Think of a claim, statistic, or piece of advice you've seen shared recently — something you weren't 100% sure about but didn't take time to verify.
Search for it in a traditional search engine and note what you find in the first few results.
Now open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "Is this claim accurate: [paste the claim]. Give me the evidence for and against, and cite your sources."
Compare the two experiences — which gave you a clearer, more trustworthy answer?
Share your comparison in the group — and whether you'll change how you verify information going forward.

trends.title: Giving AI agents a clear identity makes them trustworthy teammates
trends.body: VentureBeat published an analysis that reshapes how organizations should think about AI agent security: the first security control for autonomous agents isn't an API gateway — it's a unique identity with tracked permissions and accountability. Unlike chatbots, agents decide which tools to use, which APIs to call, and how to sequence actions on their own. That autonomy demands a security model built around who the agent is, not just where it connects.

slants.strategy: If your AI roadmap includes agents that take actions — not just answer questions — identity and permissions planning needs to start now, not after the pilot.
slants.leaders: Ask your security team one question: do we know which AI agents have access to which systems, and can we audit what they did? If the answer is vague, that's your priority.
slants.operations: Agents touching production systems without tracked identities create the same risk as unmanaged service accounts — invisible, powerful, and hard to audit after something goes wrong.
slants.pm: Every agent-based project plan should include an identity and permissions milestone alongside the technical build — treat it like defining roles and access for a new team member.
slants.admin: You already track who has access to what in your workflows. That same instinct applies to AI agents — if an agent can send an email or update a record, someone should know which one did it.

steps: List the AI tools your team uses that can take actions on their own — sending messages, updating records, generating documents, scheduling meetings.
For each one, ask yourself: if something went wrong, could I trace which tool did it and what permissions it had?

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "I manage a team that uses AI tools which can [describe the actions]. Help me draft a simple tracking checklist: what identity should each tool have, what permissions does it need, and how do we audit what it does? Keep it to one page."
Share your checklist draft in the group — the conversation about agent accountability is one most teams haven't had yet.

trends.title: Apple's new CEO starts day one with AI as the defining challenge
trends.body: John Ternus officially became Apple's CEO today, inheriting the world's most valuable company with a clear mandate: close the gap in artificial intelligence. His first product unveiling on September 9 will showcase a rebuilt Siri and the company's first foldable iPhone. When a company at Apple's scale makes AI the defining priority for a leadership transition, it signals something broader: AI capability is moving from a department initiative to the central business question.

slants.strategy: When AI becomes the defining metric for CEO performance at this scale, it's worth asking: is your organization's AI capability part of the leadership scorecard, or still sitting in a pilot report?
slants.leaders: AI fluency is becoming a core leadership expectation — not something you delegate to a technical team and check in on quarterly.
slants.operations: Apple's challenge is the same one every operations team faces at a different scale: integrating AI into existing products and workflows without breaking what already works.
slants.pm: Watch how Apple sequences its AI rollout over the next 100 days — the pattern of prioritizing, shipping, and iterating applies at any scale.
slants.admin: When AI becomes the top priority at a company this visible, it raises the bar everywhere. The good news: your practical AI experience is exactly what leadership teams need most.

steps: Think about how your own organization talks about AI at the leadership level. Is it a strategic priority with named owners, or still an experiment scattered across a few teams?

Open your company-approved AI tool and paste: "If our CEO made AI our organization's top priority tomorrow, what are three things that would need to change about how my team works? Be specific about process, skills, and decision-making."
Read the response and identify one change your team could start on this week — without waiting for a mandate from above.
Share that one change in the group — the best ideas often come from the people closest to the work.

homework.title: September is here — let AI sort your closet before the season changes.
homework.body: The weather is shifting, and somewhere in your closet there's a pile of things you haven't worn since last fall and another pile you wore all summer but probably shouldn't keep. Tonight, skip the overwhelm and let AI do the sorting logic. Open any free AI tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity):
homework.prompt:
"I'm doing a seasonal closet switch. Here's roughly what I have: [describe your wardrobe — how much, what types, what's stuffed in the back, what you wear constantly, what hasn't been touched in a year]. My climate is [your area]. My lifestyle is mostly [office / casual / active / mixed]. Tell me what to remove first, what to keep, and what one item I should add if I buy anything this fall. Be ruthless — I want a smaller, better closet, not a reorganized messy one."

The technique here is subtractive prompting — instead of asking AI to add ideas, you're asking it what to cut. It's one of the most underused prompting moves: start with everything you have and let AI tell you what to remove. Works for closets, meeting agendas, and project scopes alike.
